title: Scatter Diagrams and Correlation
content:
Scatter Diagrams and Correlation

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): scatter diagrams, types of correlation, line of best fit, interpolation vs extrapolation.

1. Correlation types

  • Positive: both increase (revision time vs score).
  • Negative: one increases, other decreases (price vs demand).
  • No correlation: random scatter.
  • Strength: strong (tight to a line) vs weak (loose).

2. Line of best fit

Balance points either side of the line; it need not pass through the origin. Use two well-separated points on your line (not necessarily data points) to estimate its gradient and equation.

Example: line through (10, 24) and (50, 60): m = 36/40 = 0.9 → y = 0.9x + 15. Key: x = the value on the horizontal axis (the variable you control); y = the value on the vertical axis; m = the gradient, the change in y per unit change in x, so it carries y's unit divided by x's; 15 = the intercept, the y value where the line crosses x = 0 — read it off the graph only if x = 0 is inside the data's range.

3. Using the line

Interpolation (inside the data range) is reliable; extrapolation (outside) is a risk — say so if asked.

4. Correlation ≠ causation

A third factor may drive both variables (ice-cream sales and drownings both rise with temperature). Describe relationships, don't over-claim.

5. Outliers

Points far from the trend: identify, and comment on their effect on the line; ignore them when drawing the best fit if instructed.

Exam tips: describe correlation in full ("strong positive linear correlation"); quote the equation only from two points on the drawn line, not raw data.

title: Hardware & Architecture
content:
Hardware & Architecture

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): von Neumann model, FDE cycle, registers, buses, RAM/ROM, secondary storage, embedded systems.

1. Von Neumann model

CPU (ALU, control unit, registers) + memory + I/O on shared buses; instructions stored as data (stored program concept).

2. Registers

RegisterRole
PCaddress of next instruction
MARaddress being read/written
MDRdata/instruction in transit
ACCALU results accumulator

3. FDE cycle

Fetch: PC → MAR; memory → MDR → CIR; PC + 1. Decode: control unit interprets opcode. Execute: ALU/registers act. Interrupts can pause between cycles.

4. Buses and performance

Address bus (one-way, width ⇒ addressable memory), data bus (two-way, width ⇒ bits per transfer), control bus. Performance factors: clock speed, cache size, core count — explain the effect, not just the name.

5. RAM vs ROM

RAM: volatile, read/write, holds running programs + data. ROM: non-volatile, read-only, bootstrap/firmware. Embedded systems: dedicated microprocessors inside devices (washing machines, engines) — one function, low cost, hard to update.

6. Secondary storage

  • Magnetic (HDD): platters, read/write heads; high capacity, cheap per GB, moving parts (shock-sensitive).
  • Optical (CD/DVD/Blu-ray): laser pits/lands; cheap, portable, slow, small capacity.
  • Solid state (SSD/flash): NAND cells; fast, silent, robust, no moving parts, more expensive per GB, finite write cycles.

Choose by use case: video editing (SSD), archive (optical/magnetic), tablets (flash).

Exam tips: trace FDE with register values; compare storage on capacity, speed, cost, durability, portability; always tie a performance factor to its effect.

title: Graphs of Linear Functions
content:
Algebra — Graphs

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): straight lines (gradient, intercept), key curves (quadratic, cubic, reciprocal, exponential), tangents, kinematic reading.

1. Straight lines

  • Gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). Key: m = gradient, the change in y for every 1 unit of x; (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) = any two points on the line, taken in the same order so m comes out positive when the line rises.
  • y = mx + c; parallel ⇒ equal m; perpendicular ⇒ m₁m₂ = −1. Key: y = the dependent variable; x = the independent variable; m = gradient; c = the y-coordinate where the line crosses the y-axis; m₁ and m₂ = the gradients of the two perpendicular lines.

Example: through (2, −1) parallel to y = 3x + 1: y + 1 = 3(x − 2) ⇒ y = 3x − 7.

2. Drawing curves

Table of values, plot, smooth curve. Parabola symmetry axis x = −b/2a. Recognise reciprocal y = 1/x (two branches) and exponential y = aˣ (through (0,1)).

3. Interpreting

  • Roots = x-intercepts; y-intercept from x = 0.
  • Turning points of quadratics by completing the square.

4. Tangents and rates

Gradient of tangent at a point = instantaneous rate: draw a large triangle, rise/run. Area under a speed–time graph = distance (trapezium estimate).

5. Graphical solutions

Simultaneous: intersection points. Quadratic = line: intersections give roots. Read off carefully to the accuracy allowed.

Exam tips: quote gradients as fractions where exact; when estimating a tangent gradient, use a triangle spanning at least 4 grid squares.

title: Reproduction
content:
Reproduction

Cambridge IGCSE 0610 (2023–2025): 16.1 asexual and sexual reproduction; 16.2 sexual reproduction in plants; 16.3 sexual reproduction in humans; 16.4 sexually transmitted infections.

1. Two strategies

Asexual reproduction produces genetically identical offspring from one parent (runners in strawberry, tubers in potato, binary fission in bacteria); it is fast and needs no mate but reduces variation. Sexual reproduction fuses gametes, so offspring vary, which helps survival when conditions change.

2. The flower

Sepals protect the bud; petals attract pollinators; stamens (anther and filament) are male; the carpel (stigma, style, ovary) is female. Pollination is the transfer of pollen to the stigma, by insects or wind. Fertilisation is the fusion of the male nucleus with the egg in the ovule. The ovule becomes the seed and the ovary the fruit; dispersal is by wind, water, animals or explosion.

3. Human reproduction

Sperm are made in the testes and travel through the sperm duct; the egg is released from an ovary into the oviduct, where fertilisation occurs. The zygote divides into an embryo, implants in the uterus lining and is nourished by the placenta, which also removes waste. The menstrual cycle is about 28 days: menstruation, repair, ovulation around day 14, then the lining thickens.

4. STIs

HIV weakens the immune system; chlamydia and gonorrhoea damage the reproductive tract and can cause infertility; syphilis and HPV are also transmitted sexually. Condoms reduce transmission, and screening and treatment prevent complications.

Exam focus

Q: Explain the difference between pollination and fertilisation in a flowering plant.

A: Pollination is the transfer of pollen from anther to stigma, which may be by insect or wind; fertilisation is the fusion of the male gamete nucleus with the egg nucleus inside the ovule.

title: Materials: Deformation
content:
Materials: Deformation

Hooke's Law

Up to the limit of proportionality, F = kx — extension is proportional to load. k is the spring constant (N m⁻¹). Key: F = applied load (N); x = extension from natural length (m); k = stiffness of that particular spring (N m⁻¹) — beyond the limit of proportionality the line bends, so the formula no longer applies.

Springs in series share the load (k_total < each); in parallel, k_total adds.

Stress, Strain, Young Modulus

  • Stress σ = F/A (Pa)
  • Strain ε = x/L (no unit)
  • Young modulus E = σ/ε (Pa) — a material property, independent of shape Key: σ = tensile stress = F/A (Pa); ε = tensile strain = x/L (no unit); F = load (N); A = cross-sectional area (m²); x = extension (m); L = original length (m) — because strain has no unit, E has the unit of stress.

Example: a wire of length 2 m, cross-section 1 × 10⁻⁶ m², extends 1 mm under 100 N: E = (F/A)/(x/L) = (10⁸)/(5 × 10⁻⁴) = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa — steel-like.

Force–Extension Graphs

  • Gradient of the linear region = k
  • Area under graph = elastic PE stored = ½Fx (for linear) = ½kx² Key: elastic PE in J; F = the load at that extension (N); x = extension (m); k = spring constant (N m⁻¹) — the ½ comes from the area of the triangle under a straight force–extension line.
  • Beyond the yield point the wire deforms plastically and will not return

Breaking Stress

The maximum stress a material withstands — strong materials have high breaking stress, stiff materials have high E.

Exam tips: convert mm to m and mm² to m² before substituting; the area under a stress–strain graph gives energy per unit volume.

title: Narrative Writing
content:
A narrative needs a character who wants something, obstacles that stand in the way, and a sequence of events that builds to a change. Writing well is about controlling what the reader knows and when.

Structure

A common shape is: opening hook, rising tension, a turning point, a climax, and a resolution. You do not need every stage to be long, but each should be clear.

The opening

  • Begin in the middle of action or with a striking detail.
  • Establish the character and a hint of the problem early.
  • Avoid long backstory before anything happens.

Tension

Tension comes from withholding information and controlling pace. Delay the answer to a question, slow the moment before a discovery, and let small threats build.

Techniques

  • End a section on a question or a small reveal.
  • Use short sentences at moments of danger.
  • Let the character misjudge a situation, so the reader worries.

Dialogue

Dialogue should reveal character and move the plot forward. Each speaker should sound distinct, and the reader should learn something from each exchange. Use punctuation correctly and begin a new line for each speaker.

Point of view

First person gives direct access to one mind, using I. Third person can be close to one character or wider in view. Choose one viewpoint and keep it consistent.

Ending

A satisfying ending resolves or meaningfully changes the central conflict. It can be open, but it should feel earned, not abandoned.

title: Sequences and Functions
content:
Algebra — Sequences and Functions

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): nth term (linear & quadratic), special sequences, function notation, composites, inverses.

1. Linear sequences

nth term = a + (n − 1)d. 5, 8, 11, … → 3n + 2. Check n = 1, 2, 3. Key: a = the first term; d = the common difference, the fixed step between terms; n = the position of the term, counted from 1.

2. Quadratic sequences

Second difference = 2a → an² + bn + c. 3, 8, 15, 24 … has second difference 2 → n² + bn + c; subtract n² → 2, 4, 6, 8 → 2n; so nth term = n² + 2n. Key: a, b and c = the coefficients to be found, with a read straight from the second difference; n = the term position.

3. Special sequences

Even/odd, triangular (½n(n+1)), squares, cubes, Fibonacci-type (each term = sum of previous two), geometric (×r). Key: n = the term position, so ½n(n+1) is the nth triangular number; r = the common ratio of a geometric sequence, the factor every term is multiplied by.

4. Function notation

f(x) = 2x − 5: f(3) = 1. Solve f(x) = 11 → x = 8.

5. Composite functions

fg(x) = f(g(x)) — g first. f(x) = 2x − 5, g(x) = x²: gf(2) = g(1) = 1; fg(3) = f(9) = 13.

6. Inverse functions

Swap x and y, rearrange. f(x) = 2x − 5 ⇒ f⁻¹(x) = (x + 5)/2. Domain of inverse = range of original. Verify: f⁻¹(f(x)) = x.

Exam tips: write the bracket order explicitly in composites; show the "swap and rearrange" line for inverses — answer-only scores little.

title: Inheritance
content:
Inheritance

Cambridge IGCSE 0610 (2023–2025): 17.1 chromosomes and genes; 17.2 monohybrid inheritance; 17.3 sex determination; 17.4 mutation.

1. Where the information lives

Chromosomes are DNA molecules; a gene is a length of DNA that codes for a protein. Humans have 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs, one of each pair from each parent. Alleles are alternative forms of a gene. Genotype is the allele combination; phenotype is the observable characteristic.

2. Monohybrid crosses

Use capital for dominant, lower case for recessive. A cross between two heterozygotes Tt × Tt gives 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt, so 3 tall : 1 short. A test cross with a homozygous recessive identifies whether a tall individual is TT or Tt.

Worked example. Both parents have brown eyes (Bb) but carry a blue allele. Offspring: 25% BB, 50% Bb, 25% bb, so the chance of blue eyes is 1 in 4.

3. Sex determination

Females are XX and males XY, so the father determines the sex: eggs are all X, sperm are half X and half Y. A cross gives a 1:1 ratio of girls to boys.

4. Mutation

A mutation is a change in the base sequence of DNA. Most are harmful or neutral; some are beneficial. Mutagens include radiation and some chemicals. Sickle-cell anaemia and cystic fibrosis are caused by gene mutations; Down syndrome results from an extra chromosome 21.

Exam focus

Q: Two heterozygous tall pea plants (Tt) are crossed. State the expected ratio of phenotypes.

A: 3 tall : 1 short, because the Punnett square gives TT, Tt, Tt and tt, and the first three are tall.

title: Persuasive and Argumentative Writing
content:
Argumentative writing sets out a clear position, supports it with reasons and evidence, and answers the opposing view. The tone should be measured and confident, not aggressive.

A clear thesis

Your thesis states your position in one sentence. It should be specific and arguable.

Weak and strong thesis statements

  • Weak: "Some people have views about school uniforms."
  • Strong: "School uniforms should be abolished because they limit self-expression without improving learning."

Building the argument

Each paragraph should develop one reason. Start with a topic sentence, give evidence or an example, and explain how the evidence supports your thesis.

Persuasive devices

  • Rhetorical questions make the reader consider a point, often expecting the answer you want.
  • Repetition of a key phrase reinforces your message.
  • A striking example makes an abstract point concrete.

Counter-argument

Acknowledge the opposing view and then rebut it. This shows awareness and makes your case stronger. Use a clear signpost such as "Some argue that... However, ..."

Register and audience

Choose a register that suits the audience and the form. A letter to the editor needs formal vocabulary, a measured tone and no contractions. Avoid slang and text-message abbreviations.

Connectives

Use connectives to show the logic of your argument. "However" introduces contrast, "consequently" introduces a result and "furthermore" adds a point.

title: Summary Writing
content:
A summary task tests whether you can select the relevant information and express it concisely in your own words. Accuracy and economy matter more than style.

Reading the task first

Read the question before the text. It tells you which points to select, and it sets the word limit. Mark the text lightly as you read, looking for the points the question asks for and ignoring examples and illustrations unless they are needed.

Selecting points

  • Include main points that answer the question directly.
  • Leave out anecdotes, examples and repeated ideas.
  • Keep the order logical, usually following the text's order unless the question asks otherwise.

Paraphrasing

Paraphrasing means rewriting an idea in your own words and sentence structure. Changing one or two words is not enough.

Techniques

  • Replace phrases with equivalent expressions, for example "in the not-too-distant future" becomes "soon".
  • Combine two sentences into one where the ideas are connected.
  • Use a general word for a list of specific examples where the question allows it.

Staying concise

Cut filler such as "in my opinion" or "it is important to note that". Each sentence should carry a required point. Count your words and stay within the limit.

Checking your summary

Read your summary alone. Does it answer the question? Could a reader understand it without the original text? Is every sentence necessary?

title: Alkenes
content:
Alkenes

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH11, Topic 5. Alkenes contain a carbon–carbon double bond, which makes them far more reactive than alkanes. Their addition reactions are a central part of organic synthesis.

Structure and bonding

  • A C=C double bond consists of one σ bond and one π bond. Key: C=C = the carbon–carbon double bond; σ (sigma) = the bond from the end-on overlap of orbitals, along the line joining the nuclei; π (pi) = the weaker sideways overlap of p orbitals, whose electron cloud lies above and below the C–C axis. The π bond is an electron cloud above and below the plane of the atoms, and it is the reactive part.
  • The carbons of a C=C bond are planar, with bond angles of about 120°. Key: 120° is the H–C=C bond angle expected from three electron regions around each double-bonded carbon (trigonal planar, 360° ÷ 3) — a measured angle far from 120° means the carbons are not both sp².

Addition reactions

  • Hydrogen adds across the double bond in the presence of a nickel catalyst to form an alkane.
  • Halogens (for example bromine water) add across the double bond: a colour change from orange to colourless is the test for an alkene.
  • Steam adds across the double bond in the presence of phosphoric acid to form an alcohol.
  • Hydrogen halides add to give halogenoalkanes; with unsymmetrical alkenes the Markovnikov rule predicts the major product.

Polymerisation

  • Addition polymers form when many alkene monomers join together. Poly(ethene) and poly(chloroethene) are examples.
  • The repeat unit is drawn with the double bond opened and the bonds extended through brackets.

Isomerism

  • Restricted rotation about the C=C bond allows E/Z isomers when each carbon carries two different groups.

Exam tip: when drawing a polymer, show the repeat unit with the bonds extending outwards, and do not leave a dangling double bond.

title: Differentiation
content:
Differentiation

Basic Rules

  • d/dx (xⁿ) = n xⁿ⁻¹
  • d/dx (k) = 0, d/dx (kx) = k Key: d/dx = differentiate with respect to x; k = a constant (it carries y's unit per unit of x); differentiating a constant kills it, and a linear term keeps its coefficient.

Example: y = 5x² − 3x gives dy/dx = 10x − 3.

Chain Rule

dy/dx = dy/du × du/dx. Key: dy/dx = rate of change of y with respect to x; u = an intermediate variable introduced to split the function; the chain rule multiplies the two rates, and du cancels like a fraction.

Example: y = (3x − 1)⁵: dy/dx = 5(3x − 1)⁴ × 3 = 15(3x − 1)⁴.

Tangents and Normals

The tangent gradient at a point is dy/dx there; the normal gradient is −1/(dy/dx).

Example: y = x² at (2, 4): tangent y = 4x − 4; normal has gradient −1/4.

Stationary Points

Set dy/dx = 0, then classify with the second derivative:

  • d²y/dx² > 0 → minimum
  • d²y/dx² < 0 → maximum
  • d²y/dx² = 0 → test either side

Example: y = x³ − 3x: dy/dx = 3x² − 3 = 0 at x = ±1; d²y/dx² = 6x, so a maximum at x = −1 and a minimum at x = 1.

Rates of Change

dy/dx is a rate: if V = 4/3 πr³, then dV/dr = 4πr² links volume change to radius change. Key: V = volume (m³); r = radius (m); dV/dr = the rate at which volume grows per metre of radius, so its unit is m³ ÷ m = m².

Exam tips: always restart gradients from the derivative at the exact point, and answer rate questions with units.

title: Energy, Work & Power
content:
Energy, Work & Power

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): stores and transfers, KE/PE, work, energy sources, power, efficiency.

1. Energy stores & transfers

Stores: kinetic, gravitational, elastic, chemical, nuclear, thermal. Transfer mechanisms: mechanically, electrically, heating, waves. Energy is conserved overall; transfers via work done.

2. Formulas

  • KE = ½mv²; PE = mgh. Key: KE = kinetic energy (J); m = mass (kg); v = speed (m s⁻¹); PE = change in gravitational potential energy (J); g = gravitational field strength (10 N kg⁻¹ on Earth); h = height gained (m).
  • Work W = Fd (force along displacement, joules). Key: W = work done (J); F = the component of force along the motion (N); d = displacement in that direction (m) — a force at right angles to the motion does no work.
  • Power P = W/t = E/t; P = Fv for constant speed. Key: P = power (W = J s⁻¹); W or E = work done or energy transferred (J); t = time taken (s); F = driving force (N); v = speed (m s⁻¹).

Example: 0.5 kg at 4 m/s: KE = 4 J. Lift 2 kg by 3 m: PE = 60 J (g = 10).

3. Energy sources

Renewable: solar, wind, hydro, geothermal, biofuel, tidal — replenished. Non-renewable: fossil fuels, nuclear — finite. Discuss reliability, cost, pollution for "evaluate" questions.

4. Efficiency

Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input (×100%). Sankey diagrams show losses. Key: efficiency is a ratio of two energies in the same unit (J), so it has no unit itself — multiply by 100 only to report a percentage, and it can never exceed 1 (100%).

Example: motor: 150 J useful from 600 J → 25%.

5. Energy-chain problems

Equating KE loss to PE gain: v = √(2gh) for frictionless drop; braking distance grows with v². Key: v = speed reached (m s⁻¹); g = gravitational field strength (10 N kg⁻¹); h = vertical drop (m) — mass cancels because it appears on both sides.

Exam tips: define work as "force × distance moved in the direction of the force"; use g = 10 unless told otherwise; efficiency is a ratio — no units.

title: Nuclear Physics
content:
Nuclear Physics

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): nuclear model, radioactivity, decay types, half-life, safety, fission/fusion (Extended).

1. The nuclear model

Nucleus (protons +, neutrons 0) with orbiting electrons (−). Nuclide notation ᴬ_Z X. Isotopes: same Z, different A. Rutherford scattering established the nuclear model; proton number Z, nucleon number A.

2. Radiation types

TypeNatureRange (air)Stopped by
alpha αhelium nucleus (2p2n)few cmpaper
beta β⁻fast electron~20–30 cmfew mm aluminium
gamma γEM wavevery farthick lead/concrete

Deflection in fields: α/β opposite, γ none. Ionising: α > β > γ. Background radiation: radon, cosmic, rocks, medical, fallout.

3. Decay equations

  • α: A −4, Z −2 (e.g. ²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + α).
  • β⁻: neutron → proton; A same, Z +1 (e.g. ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + β⁻).
  • γ: no change to A or Z.

Balance A and Z on both sides — that is the check. Key: in ²³⁸₉₂U the top number is the mass number A (protons + neutrons) and the bottom number is the atomic number Z (protons); an α particle is a helium nucleus with A = 4 and Z = 2, so emitting one lowers A by 4 and Z by 2; a β⁻ particle is an electron with A = 0 and Z = −1, so emitting one leaves A alone and raises Z by 1; γ radiation carries no mass or charge, so neither number changes.

4. Half-life

Time for half the unstable nuclei to decay (random process). Read from a decay curve or count halves: 80 → 40 → 20 over two half-lives.

Example: 800 Bq, half-life 2 h → 200 Bq after 4 h.

5. Safety and uses

Uses: medical tracers (β/γ), sterilisation, thickness gauge (β), dating (C-14), smoke alarms (α). Safety: distance, time, shielding, wear badges, store in lead. Handle with tongs; never point at people.

6. Fission and fusion (Extended)

Fission: heavy nucleus splits (U-235 + neutron), chain reaction controlled by moderators/control rods — power stations. Fusion: light nuclei join (stellar) — needs huge T/P; releases more energy per kg; no long-lived waste.

title: Logic Gates & Boolean Logic
content:
Logic Gates & Boolean Logic

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): six gates, truth tables, building/describing circuits, problem-to-logic mapping.

1. The six gates

ABANDORNANDNORXOR
0000110
0101101
1001101
1111000

NOT inverts. NAND = AND + invert; NOR = OR + invert; XOR = 1 when inputs differ.

2. Truth tables

2 inputs → 4 rows; 3 inputs → 8 rows. Work gate by gate, adding intermediate columns for sub-circuit outputs.

3. Problem → logic

Define inputs/outputs first. Alarm rings (X=1) if sensor P triggered AND (door D OR window W): X = P AND (D OR W). Then draw the circuit: OR first, then AND. Key: X = the output, 1 when the alarm rings and 0 when it is silent; P, D, W = the three inputs, each 1 when its sensor is triggered and 0 otherwise; AND gives 1 only when both its inputs are 1, OR gives 1 when either is — the brackets are the circuit order, not decoration.

4. Describing circuits

Write the expression from a diagram gate by gate; annotate output of each gate (X, Y) before combining.

Exam tips: check your truth table row count before writing; in problem questions, state "input P = 1 means sensor triggered" — definitions earn marks.

title: Processor Fundamentals
content:
The FDE Cycle

  • Fetch: PC → MAR; read memory → MDR; instruction → CIR; PC increments
  • Decode: control unit interprets the opcode
  • Execute: ALU/registers act; results stored; PC may be overwritten (jumps)

Registers

RegisterRole
PCaddress of next instruction
MARaddress being accessed
MDRdata in transit
CIRcurrent instruction
ACCaccumulator results

Buses

  • Address bus: one-way, CPU → memory (width sets addressable space)
  • Data bus: two-way, carries instructions/data
  • Control bus: timing and command signals

Interrupts

Signals that pause the current program (I/O complete, timer, errors). The CPU saves context, runs the ISR, then resumes — enabling multitasking.

Assembly and Addressing

Immediate (#5), direct (address holds value), indirect (address points to address), indexed (base + offset — arrays), relative (PC + offset — jumps).

Example: LDD 100 loads from 100 (direct); LDI 100 loads from the address stored at 100 (indirect).

Exam tips: trace register contents step by step in trace tables; explain the stored program concept — instructions as data in memory.

title: Entropy and Energetics
content:
Entropy and Energetics

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH14, Topic 12. Enthalpy alone does not decide whether a reaction happens. Entropy measures how energy and matter are spread out, and the Gibbs energy combines enthalpy and entropy to predict feasibility.

Entropy

  • Entropy S measures the disorder or the number of ways energy can be dispersed. Its standard unit is J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
  • Entropy increases when a solid melts or dissolves, when a liquid evaporates, and when the number of gas molecules increases.
  • Entropy decreases when gas molecules condense or when a crystal forms from solution.
  • Standard entropy values are given in data books. The entropy change for a reaction is ΔS = Σ S(products) − Σ S(reactants).

Gibbs free energy

  • The Gibbs energy change is ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, where T is in kelvin. ΔH is in J mol⁻¹ and ΔS in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, so convert ΔH from kJ to J before calculating.
  • A reaction is feasible when ΔG is negative. When ΔG = 0 the system is at equilibrium.

Total entropy change

  • The total entropy change is ΔS total = ΔS system + ΔS surroundings. For the surroundings, ΔS surroundings = −ΔH / T.

Temperature and feasibility

  • For a reaction with positive ΔH and positive ΔS, ΔG becomes negative above the temperature T = ΔH / ΔS. High temperature therefore makes the reaction feasible.
  • For a reaction with ΔH positive and ΔS negative, ΔG is always positive, so the reaction is never feasible.

Worked example

  • For CaCO3 → CaO + CO2, ΔH = +178 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = +161 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. The temperature at which ΔG = 0 is T = 178 000 / 161 = 1106 K, so the decomposition becomes feasible above about 1100 K.

Exam tip: always convert kJ to J before subtracting TΔS, and state the temperature in kelvin.

title: Measurement & Units
content:
Measurement & Units

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): 1.1 lengths & volumes; 1.2 density; 1.3 forces & motion context (measurements) — plus measurement techniques, SI units, scalars/vectors.

1. Measuring

  • Length: ruler (mm), vernier calipers (0.1 mm / 0.01 cm), micrometer screw gauge (0.01 mm).
  • Volume: measuring cylinder read at the meniscus bottom; regular solids by calculation; irregular by displacement (eureka can).
  • Time: stopwatch — human reaction time ±0.2 s; measure many oscillations and divide (e.g. 20 T).
  • Pendulum: T = time/oscillations; f = 1/T.

2. SI units and prefixes

QuantityUnitSymbol
lengthmetrem
masskilogramkg
timeseconds
currentampereA
temperaturekelvin (°C used)K

kilo 10³; centi 10⁻²; milli 10⁻³; micro 10⁻⁶; nano 10⁻⁹.

3. Scalars and vectors

Scalars: distance, speed, mass, energy, time. Vectors: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, weight, momentum. Vector addition by scale diagram (tip-to-tail) or by components.

4. Density

ρ = m/V (kg/m³ or g/cm³; 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³). Determining: mass on balance; volume by displacement. Floating: ρobject < ρfluid.

5. Accuracy and improvements

Avoid parallax (eye level with reading), zero errors (subtract the zero reading), measure multiple laps for small times. Suggest improvements by naming the error and the fix.

title: Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics
content:
Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics

Edexcel IAL Biology WBI14, Topic 6. Pathogens cause disease, and the immune system defends the body against them. Knowledge of microbes also allows antibiotics, vaccines and forensic DNA analysis.

Pathogens and antibiotics

  • Bacteria have 70S ribosomes, a cell wall made of peptidoglycan and circular DNA. Antibiotics such as penicillin block cell wall synthesis; others block 70S ribosomes.
  • Viruses have no cell structure of their own. They are obligate parasites that use the host cell machinery to replicate, so antibiotics do not act on them.
  • Antibiotic resistance spreads by natural selection. Bacteria with resistance alleles survive and reproduce, and the resistant population grows when antibiotics are overused.

Immune response

  • Phagocytes engulf pathogens by phagocytosis. Antigens on the pathogen surface are recognised as foreign.
  • B lymphocytes with complementary receptors undergo clonal selection and clonal expansion. Plasma cells produce antibodies, which bind to specific antigens.
  • T helper cells release cytokines that activate B cells and cytotoxic T cells. Cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells.
  • Memory cells persist after an infection, so the secondary response is faster and larger.

Vaccination

  • A vaccine contains an antigen, often as a weakened or inactivated pathogen, or a harmless fragment. It stimulates a primary response without causing the disease.
  • Herd immunity protects those who cannot be vaccinated when a high proportion of the population is immune.

HIV

  • HIV attacks and destroys helper T cells. Over time the immune system fails, and the person develops AIDS.
  • The virus carries RNA and uses reverse transcriptase to make DNA copies inside the host cell.

Forensic DNA profiling

  • Short tandem repeats (STRs) are short sequences that repeat a variable number of times at specific loci. The number of repeats differs between people.
  • PCR amplifies the STR regions from a small sample. The products are separated by gel electrophoresis, where DNA moves towards the positive electrode according to size.

Exam tip: when you explain antibiotic resistance, describe the variation, the selection pressure and the change in the population over generations.

title: Communication and Networking
content:
Transmission

  • Serial: one bit at a time — cheaper, reliable over distance
  • Parallel: multiple bits simultaneously — fast but suffers skew and crosstalk over long runs
  • Direction: simplex (one way), half-duplex (alternating), full-duplex (both ways)

Packets and Protocols

Data splits into packets with header (addresses, sequence) and trailer (checksum). A protocol is an agreed rule set — without one, devices cannot interpret signals.

  • TCP/IP stack: application → transport → network → link
  • HTTP/HTTPS: web transfer; HTTPS encrypts with TLS
  • FTP: file transfer; SMTP/POP3/IMAP: email

Network Types

  • LAN: small site, privately owned; WAN: large geographic scale (the internet)
  • Topologies: bus, star, mesh (star is most common — central switch)

Hardware

Routers join networks by IP; switches forward frames by MAC within a LAN; gateways translate protocols.

Client-Server vs Peer-to-Peer

Client-server: central services, easy administration, single point of failure. P2P: every node shares files directly — cheap, hard to manage (torrents, blockchain).

Exam tips: explain packet switching with header/trailer details; justify protocol choice per application (email vs streaming).

title: Electricity & Circuits
content:
Electricity & Circuits

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): simple circuits, current, p.d., resistance, series/parallel, electrical safety, practical electricity.

1. Circuit symbols & current

Conventional current: + → − (electron flow opposite). I = Q/t. Ammeter in series; voltmeter in parallel. Key: I = current (A); Q = charge flowed (C); t = time taken (s) — one amp is one coulomb per second.

2. Current, p.d., e.m.f.

  • Current: rate of charge flow; same everywhere in series.
  • p.d.: energy per coulomb across a component; e.m.f.: electrical energy per coulomb given by the source.

3. Resistance

  • R = V/I. Ohmic conductor: V ∝ I at constant temperature. Key: R = resistance (Ω); V = potential difference across the component (V); I = current through it (A) — one ohm is one volt per amp.
  • Series: R = R₁ + R₂ + …; same current; p.d. shares in proportion to R. Key: R = total resistance of the chain (Ω); R₁, R₂ = the individual resistors (Ω); in series the total always grows, and each p.d. is its share R/total × supply.
  • Parallel: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂; same p.d.; current splits (inverse-R share). Key: R = total resistance of the combination (Ω); R₁, R₂ = branch resistances (Ω); the total is always smaller than the smallest branch, because every extra path eases the flow.
  • Resistance ∝ length, ∝ 1/area (wires).

4. Components

Fixed/variable resistors, LDR (light ↑ R ↓), thermistor (T ↑ R ↓), diode/LED (one-way), relay, filament lamp (R grows as T rises — V–I curve flattens).

5. Power and energy

P = VI = I²R = V²/R; E = VIt. Fuse rating just above normal current; earth wire, double insulation, circuit breakers (trip quickly, resettable). Key: P = electrical power (W); V = potential difference (V); I = current (A); R = resistance (Ω); E = energy transferred (J); t = time the current flows (s) — the three forms of P are the same equation rearranged, so pick the one whose two quantities you know.

Example: 230 V, 2 A heater: P = 460 W; correct fuse 3 A or 5 A.

6. Digital electronics basics (syllabus 4.5 context)

Analogue vs digital; logic gates drive outputs from inputs (see CS link); sensors feed comparator-style circuits.

Exam tips: series: current same; parallel: p.d. same — say which before calculating; always compute total resistance first in mixed circuits.

title: Coordination, Response and Gene Technology
content:
Coordination, Response and Gene Technology

Edexcel IAL Biology WBI15, Topic 8. Nervous and hormonal systems coordinate the body, and plants respond to light and gravity using hormones. Gene technology uses enzymes to cut, join and copy DNA for medicine, research and agriculture.

Nervous coordination

  • A reflex arc passes information from a receptor along a sensory neurone, through a relay neurone in the spinal cord, and along a motor neurone to an effector. It is fast and does not need conscious control.
  • The resting potential is about −70 mV. The sodium-potassium pump moves three Na⁺ out and two K⁺ in, maintaining the gradient.
  • An action potential is a rapid depolarisation as voltage-gated sodium channels open, followed by repolarisation as potassium channels open. The myelin sheath allows saltatory conduction.
  • At a cholinergic synapse, an action potential causes Ca²⁺ to enter the presynaptic knob. Vesicles of acetylcholine fuse with the membrane, and the transmitter diffuses across the cleft and binds to receptors. Acetylcholinesterase breaks it down.

Hormonal coordination

  • Insulin is released from β cells when blood glucose is high. It increases glucose uptake and glycogenesis, and lowers blood glucose.
  • Glucagon is released from α cells when blood glucose is low. It stimulates glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
  • Adrenaline prepares the body for fight or flight by raising heart rate and glucose release.

Plant responses

  • Auxin is made in the shoot tip and moves to the shaded side of a shoot. Cells on that side elongate faster, so the shoot bends towards the light (positive phototropism).
  • Roots show positive gravitropism and shoots show negative gravitropism.

Gene technology

  • Restriction endonucleases cut DNA at specific palindromic sequences. Many leave sticky ends that are complementary to each other.
  • DNA ligase joins the sugar-phosphate backbone of two DNA fragments. Plasmids are used as vectors to carry the gene into bacteria.
  • Reverse transcriptase makes complementary DNA (cDNA) from mRNA, so the cDNA has no introns.
  • In PCR, the sample is heated to separate the strands, primers anneal, and Taq polymerase extends the new strands. Each cycle doubles the amount of DNA.

Exam tip: for a question on synapses, give the steps in order: action potential, calcium entry, vesicle fusion, diffusion, binding, and then removal of the transmitter.

title: Programming Paradigms and Low-Level
content:
Programming Paradigms and Low-Level

Paradigms

  • Procedural: programs as sequences of instructions in procedures — good for straightforward algorithms.
  • Object-oriented: classes encapsulate state (attributes) and behaviour (methods); supports encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism.
  • Declarative: state what is required, not how (SQL queries, logic programming).
  • Low-level: assembly maps closely to machine code; used where hardware control or timing precision is needed.

Assembly Essentials

The opcode names the operation (LDM load, STR store, ADD, CMP compare, JMP branch, IN/OUT for I/O). The operand names the data. The assembler translates mnemonics to machine code one-to-one; two-pass assemblers resolve forward references via the symbol table.

Addressing Modes

  • Immediate: operand is the constant itself, ADD #5.
  • Direct: operand is the memory address of the data.
  • Indirect: operand is the address OF the address; one extra memory read.
  • Indexed: effective address = base + index register; ideal for arrays. Key: effective address = the address the operand is actually fetched from (a memory address, not a value); the base register holds the start address of the block, usually the array's first element; the index register holds the offset of the wanted element — change only the index and the same instruction walks the array.
  • Relative: address given as an offset from the program counter; enables position-independent code.

Fetch-Execute

Fetch: PC gives address, instruction loads into the CIR, PC increments. Decode: control unit interprets the opcode. Execute: the operation runs, possibly updating registers or memory. Interrupts are checked at cycle boundaries.

Exam tips: trace short assembly programs register by register; compute effective addresses for each addressing mode; state one advantage of OOP for large systems.

title: Transition Metals and their Chemistry
content:
Transition Metals and their Chemistry

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH15, Topic 17. Transition metals form coloured complex ions, show variable oxidation states and act as catalysts. These properties come from partly filled d orbitals.

Complex ions and ligands

  • A ligand is a species with a lone pair that forms a dative bond to a metal ion. Water, ammonia and chloride are monodentate ligands.
  • Ethane-1,2-diamine is bidentate because it has two donor atoms. EDTA⁴⁻ is hexadentate.
  • The coordination number is the number of coordinate bonds to the central metal ion. Common shapes are octahedral (6), tetrahedral (4), square planar (4) and linear (2, e.g. [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺).

Colour

  • In a ligand field the five d orbitals split into two energy levels. Electrons absorb light to jump between them, and the colour seen is complementary to the colour absorbed.
  • The d-orbital splitting depends on the metal, its oxidation state and the ligands. Ligand exchange changes the colour.

Ligand substitution and isomerism

  • Concentrated HCl converts [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ (blue) into [CuCl₄]²⁻ (yellow-green, tetrahedral).
  • Excess aqueous ammonia converts Cu²⁺ into [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺, a deep blue complex. Key: [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 4NH₃ → [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ + 4H₂O — the copper ion starts with six water ligands; four ammonia molecules replace four of them and two waters remain, so four waters are released; the coordination number stays 6 throughout, the charge is +2 on both sides, and the colour deepens from pale blue to deep blue. A ligand exchange that keeps the coordination number the same changes the colour without changing the shape.
  • Square planar [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] shows cis-trans isomerism. The cis form is the anticancer drug cisplatin.

Catalysis

  • Heterogeneous catalysts (iron in the Haber process) work on a surface. Homogeneous catalysts such as Fe²⁺ in the iodide–peroxydisulfate reaction are in the same phase as the reactants.
  • In the MnO₄⁻ and ethanedioate reaction, Mn²⁺ is the product and catalyses the reaction, so the rate increases as it forms: this is autocatalysis.

Exam tip: when a ligand exchange is asked for, name both the shape and the colour change, and write the complex formula with its charge.

title: Numerical Measures of Central Tendency
content:
Central Tendency: Mean, Median and Mode

The Mean

For data x₁, ..., xₙ the mean is

  • x̄ = Σx/n

For a frequency table with midpoints x and frequencies f: x̄ = Σfx/Σf. The mean uses every value, so a single extreme value drags it — that is its main weakness.

The Median

The median is the middle value: position (n + 1)/2 for ordered raw data. With n even, average the two middle values. The median ignores the size of extreme values, so it describes skewed data more honestly. For grouped data, estimate the median by linear interpolation within the median class.

The Mode

The most frequent value. A dataset may have no mode or several. For grouped data the modal class is the one with the highest frequency density (frequency ÷ class width), not the highest frequency.

Effects of Data Changes

Adding a constant a to every value adds a to the mean and median (the mode too) but leaves the spread untouched. Multiplying every value by b multiplies mean and median by b.

Coding

Subtract a constant and divide by a convenient width: y = (x − a)/b. Then x̄ = b·ȳ + a. Coding simplifies arithmetic and always preserves the relationship — the coded mean decodes exactly. Key: x = the raw value (its own unit); a = the assumed mean, in that same unit; b = the coding divisor, also in that unit, so y is a plain number; x̄ = the decoded mean and ȳ = the mean of the coded values.

Example: data 2, 4, 4, 10: mean = 5, median = 4, mode = 4. Change 10 to 100: mean = 27.5, median and mode unchanged — the mean chased the outlier.

Exam tips: always state which average you used and why. When asked to compare two distributions, pair a central measure with a spread measure; a mean without a spread is only half an answer.

title: Biotechnology and Genetic Modification
content:
Biotechnology and Genetic Modification

Cambridge IGCSE 0610 (2023–2025): 21.1 biotechnology; 21.2 genetic modification; 21.3 industrial uses.

1. Using microorganisms

Yeast ferments glucose to ethanol and carbon dioxide: brewing, bread-making and biofuel. Bacteria make yoghurt and cheese from milk. Penicillium mould produces penicillin. The conditions are controlled: temperature, pH, oxygen and sterile equipment, because contamination ruins a batch.

2. Industrial fermentation

A fermenter provides a controlled environment with a stirrer, a water jacket for cooling, air supply and a pH monitor. Fermentation releases heat, so cooling is essential. Biogas from anaerobic digestion of waste is mainly methane and is used for cooking and electricity.

3. Genetic modification

A gene from one organism is cut out with an enzyme, inserted into a plasmid vector, and taken up by a host cell. Bacteria carrying the human insulin gene make insulin in bulk; GM crops carry genes for pest resistance or vitamin A. The steps are cut, insert, transform, select, culture.

4. Benefits and concerns

Benefits: medicine produced cheaply and safely, higher yields, less pesticide. Concerns: genes spreading to wild plants, effects on non-target insects, cost to small farmers, and ethical objections. Regulation exists because the risks are uncertain, not because the science is unsound.

Exam focus

Q: State two advantages of producing human insulin using genetically modified bacteria.

A: It can be produced in large quantities, and it is human insulin rather than animal insulin, so it is less likely to cause an immune reaction.

title: Diseases and Immunity
content:
Diseases and Immunity

Cambridge IGCSE 0610 (2023–2025): 10.1 diseases and immunity; 10.2 the body's defence; 10.3 vaccination.

1. Pathogens and transmission

A pathogen is a disease-causing organism: bacteria (cholera, tuberculosis), viruses (influenza, HIV), fungi (athlete's foot), protoctists (malaria). Transmission is by droplets, contaminated food or water, direct contact, vectors and blood. Cholera spreads through contaminated water; malaria by the female Anopheles mosquito; HIV by unprotected sex, shared needles or contaminated blood.

2. The body's defences

First line: skin, mucus, cilia, stomach acid, tears. Second line: phagocytes engulf pathogens non-specifically; lymphocytes produce antibodies specific to an antigen, and memory cells give long-lasting immunity. A fever and inflammation are part of the response.

3. Vaccination

A vaccine contains dead or weakened pathogens or their antigens, so lymphocytes produce antibodies without illness. Memory cells mean a real infection is fought before symptoms develop. Herd immunity protects those who cannot be vaccinated. Antibiotics kill bacteria but not viruses, and overuse selects resistant strains such as MRSA.

4. Reducing the spread

Clean water and sanitation (cholera), mosquito nets and draining standing water (malaria), condoms and screened blood (HIV), covering the mouth and ventilation (droplets), and completing antibiotic courses.

Exam focus

Q: Explain why a person who has had one vaccination may need a booster years later.

A: Antibody levels and memory cells fall over time, so a booster re-exposes the immune system and raises antibody levels again before infection.

title: Atoms, Elements and Compounds
content:
Atoms, Elements and Compounds

Cambridge IGCSE 0620 (2023–2025): 2.1 elements, compounds and mixtures; 2.2 atomic structure and the Periodic Table; 2.3 isotopes; 2.4 ions and ionic bonds; 2.5 simple molecules and covalent bonds; 2.6 giant covalent structures; 2.7 metallic bonding.

1. Pure substances and mixtures

An element contains one kind of atom; a compound contains atoms of two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions; a mixture contains substances not chemically joined and can be separated by physical means. Air, seawater and alloys are mixtures.

2. Inside the atom

ParticleRelative massChargeWhere
proton1+1nucleus
neutron10nucleus
electron1/1836−1shells

Proton number Z fixes the element; nucleon number A = protons + neutrons. Isotopes have the same Z and different A, and they differ only in neutron count, so their chemistry is identical while their mass and some physical properties differ. Relative atomic mass is the weighted average of the isotopes, which is why chlorine is 35.5.

3. Ionic bonding

A metal loses electrons to form a positive ion, a non-metal gains them to form a negative ion, and the ions are held in a giant lattice by electrostatic attraction. Sodium chloride: Na → Na⁺ + e⁻ and Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻. Properties follow from the lattice: high melting point, brittle, and it conducts only when molten or dissolved, because the ions must be free to move.

4. Covalent and metallic bonding

Non-metals share electron pairs. Simple molecules (H₂O, CO₂, CH₄) have weak forces between molecules, so they melt low. Giant covalent structures (diamond, graphite, silicon(IV) oxide) have very high melting points; diamond is hard because every carbon has four strong bonds, graphite is soft and conducts because its layers slide and each carbon has a delocalised electron. Metals are a lattice of positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons, which explains conduction and malleability.

Exam focus

Q: Explain why solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity but molten sodium chloride does.

A: In the solid the ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice and cannot move; when molten, the lattice breaks down and the ions are free to carry charge.

title: Circular Motion and SHM
content:
Circular Motion and SHM

Circular Motion Recap

Angular speed ω = 2π/T; v = ωr; a = ω²r = v²/r; F = mv²/r toward the centre. Key: ω = angular speed (rad s⁻¹); T = period of one revolution (s); r = radius of the circle (m); v = speed along the path (m s⁻¹); a = centripetal acceleration (m s⁻²); F = centripetal force (N); m = mass (kg).

Simple Harmonic Motion

Acceleration is proportional to displacement and opposite: a = −ω²x. Key: a = acceleration (m s⁻²); ω = angular frequency (rad s⁻¹); x = displacement from the equilibrium position (m) — the minus sign is the definition of SHM and is what examiners award the mark for.

Solutions: x = x₀ sin ωt (start at centre) or x = x₀ cos ωt (start at extreme), with ω = 2πf.

Velocity and acceleration:

  • v_max = ωx₀ at the centre
  • a_max = ω²x₀ at the extremes

Example: a pendulum with x₀ = 0.02 m, f = 0.5 Hz has a_max = (2π × 0.5)² × 0.02 ≈ 0.20 m s⁻².

Energy in SHM

E = ½mω²x₀² total (constant), exchanged between KE (max at centre) and PE (max at extremes). Key: E = total energy of the oscillator (J); m = mass (kg); ω = angular frequency (rad s⁻¹); x₀ = amplitude, the maximum displacement (m).

Damping and Resonance

Damping removes energy: light damping → slow decay; critical → fastest return without oscillation. Resonance: driving at the natural frequency gives maximum amplitude (microwave ovens, swing pushing, bridge disasters).

Exam tips: quote a = −ω²x as the defining condition; time period questions often need only T = 2π/ω.

title: Metals
content:
Metals

Cambridge IGCSE 0620 (2023–2025): 9.1 properties of metals; 9.2 uses of metals; 9.3 alloys; 9.4 reactivity series; 9.5 corrosion; 9.6 extraction.

1. Properties and uses

Metals are malleable, ductile, good conductors of heat and electricity, and have high melting points (mercury is the exception). Uses follow from properties: copper for wiring and pipes, aluminium for aircraft because it is light and corrosion-resistant, iron for structures because it is strong and cheap, gold for contacts because it does not corrode.

2. Alloys

An alloy is a mixture of a metal with other elements. Different-sized atoms disrupt the layers, so the alloy is harder and stronger than the pure metal but less malleable. Steel is iron with carbon; stainless steel adds chromium and nickel for corrosion resistance; brass is copper and zinc; bronze is copper and tin.

3. Reactivity series and displacement

Potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, (carbon), zinc, iron, (hydrogen), copper, silver, gold. A metal displaces any metal below it from a solution of its salt: iron + copper(II) sulfate gives copper + iron(II) sulfate. The series also decides extraction: metals above carbon are extracted by electrolysis, those below by reduction with carbon.

4. Extraction, corrosion and recycling

Iron is extracted in a blast furnace: coke burns to CO₂, CO₂ is reduced to CO, and CO reduces the iron ore (Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂); limestone removes the sandy impurities as slag. Aluminium is extracted by electrolysis of alumina dissolved in molten cryolite, which is expensive in electricity, so recycling aluminium saves about 95% of the energy.

Corrosion of iron needs oxygen and water; galvanising, painting and sacrificial protection prevent it. Recycling also conserves ore and reduces landfill.

Exam focus

Q: Explain why aluminium is extracted by electrolysis rather than by reduction with carbon.

A: Aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot displace it from its oxide; electrolysis of the molten oxide can supply enough energy to break the very strong bonds.

title: Organisms and their Environment
content:
Organisms and their Environment

Cambridge IGCSE 0610 (2023–2025): 19.1 energy flow; 19.2 food chains and webs; 19.3 cycles; 19.4 populations.

1. Energy through an ecosystem

The Sun is the source. Producers (plants) convert light to chemical energy; consumers eat them; decomposers break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil. Only about 10% of energy passes to the next trophic level, because most is lost as heat, in movement, and in uneaten or undigested parts. That is why food chains are short and why pyramids of numbers or biomass narrow upwards.

2. Food chains and webs

A food chain starts with a producer and ends with a top predator; the arrows show the direction of energy flow. A food web joins chains, so removing one species affects many. Interdependence means a change in one population alters others — a fall in aphids reduces ladybirds.

3. Cycles

Carbon cycle: photosynthesis removes CO₂; respiration, combustion and decomposition return it. Nitrogen cycle: nitrogen fixation by bacteria in root nodules and in the soil converts N₂ to nitrates; nitrification converts ammonium compounds to nitrates; denitrification returns N₂; decomposers release ammonium compounds.

4. Populations and sampling

A population is all the individuals of one species in an area; a community is all the populations. Quadrats estimate plant abundance (place randomly, count, multiply by area ratio); sweep nets and pitfall traps sample animals. Random sampling avoids bias; the mean of several quadrats is more reliable than one.

Exam focus

Q: Explain why only about 10% of energy passes to the next trophic level.

A: Energy is lost as heat from respiration, used in movement, and lost in uneaten and undigested material, so little remains to be stored as biomass.

title: Indices and Standard Form
content:
Number — Indices and Standard Form

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): index laws, negative and fractional indices, standard form arithmetic.

1. Index laws

  • aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ; aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ; (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ
  • a⁰ = 1; a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ; a^(1/n) = ⁿ√a; a^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)ᵐ Key: a = the base, any non-zero number; m and n = integers, with ⁿ√a meaning the nth root of a; these laws hold for every non-zero base, positive or negative.

Examples: 27^(2/3) = (³√27)² = 9; 5⁻² = 1/25; (2x³)² = 4x⁶.

2. Standard form

a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10.

  • 47 382 = 4.7382 × 10⁴; 0.0056 = 5.6 × 10⁻³
  • Multiplication: multiply a's, add powers. Division: divide a's, subtract powers.

Example: (3 × 10⁵) × (4 × 10⁻²) = 12 × 10³ = 1.2 × 10⁴.

3. Calculator use

Use the ×10ˣ key, not 10 ^; keep working in standard form and convert at the end. Give final answers in the form asked (often 3 s.f. standard form).

4. Solving index equations

Match bases: 2ˣ = 32 ⇒ 2ˣ = 2⁵ ⇒ x = 5. With different bases, rewrite (8 = 2³).

Exam tips: check a is in [1, 10) before writing standard form; in "multiply out" questions apply the power to every factor including coefficients.

title: Data Structures
content:
Arrays and Lists

Contiguous, indexed, O(1) access; fixed size. 2D arrays: element (i, j) — rows × columns.

Stack (LIFO)

push/pop/peek at one end. Uses: call stacks, undo, expression evaluation, DFS.

Example: evaluating 3 4 + : push 3, push 4, pop both, push 7.

Queue (FIFO)

enqueue at rear, dequeue at front. Uses: print queues, schedulers, BFS. A circular queue reuses vacated slots with head/tail pointers modulo capacity.

Linked List

Nodes with data + pointer. Insert/delete O(1) at a known node; search O(n). Traversal follows next pointers until null.

Hash Table

Hash function maps keys → index. Collisions resolved by chaining or open addressing. Average O(1) lookup, worst O(n).

title: Introduction to Kinetics and Equilibria
content:
Introduction to Kinetics and Equilibria

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12, Topic 9. Kinetics asks how fast a reaction goes, and equilibria asks how far it goes before the forward and backward reactions balance. Both depend on the same collision ideas.

Rates and collision theory

  • For a reaction to occur, particles must collide with enough energy (the activation energy, Ea) and in the correct orientation.
  • Increasing concentration or pressure increases the frequency of collisions. Increasing temperature raises the proportion of particles with energy above Ea, which has a larger effect than the increase in collision frequency.
  • A catalyst provides an alternative route with a lower Ea; it is not used up.

Measuring rates

  • Rates can be found from the gradient of a concentration–time graph at the start of the reaction (the initial rate).
  • Methods include measuring the volume of gas produced, the change in mass, or the time for a colour change to occur (1/time gives a relative rate).

Dynamic equilibrium

  • In a closed system, the forward and reverse rates become equal. Concentrations stop changing, but the reaction has not stopped.
  • Equilibrium constant Kc = [products]^n / [reactants]^m, with each concentration raised to the power of its coefficient. Kc is constant for a given temperature. Key: [products] and [reactants] = equilibrium concentrations (mol dm⁻³); n and m = the stoichiometric powers taken from the balanced equation (no units).

Le Chatelier's principle

  • If a system at equilibrium is disturbed, the position shifts to oppose the change.
  • Increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction. Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules. Adding a reactant shifts the position towards products.
  • A catalyst speeds up both directions equally, so it changes the rate of reaching equilibrium but not the equilibrium position or Kc.

Exam tip: say which direction is favoured and why, using the principle. Do not claim that a catalyst increases the yield.

title: Organic Chemistry
content:
Organic Chemistry

Cambridge IGCSE 0620 (2023–2025): 11.1 formulae; 11.2 fuels; 11.3 alkanes; 11.4 alkenes; 11.5 alcohols; 11.6 carboxylic acids; 11.7 polymers.

1. The families and their general formulae

Displayed and structural formulae must show every bond; the empirical formula is the simplest ratio and the molecular formula the actual count.

2. Alkanes and fuels

Alkanes are unreactive except for combustion and substitution with halogens in ultraviolet light. Fractions of crude oil are separated by fractional distillation, and larger molecules are cracked into smaller, more useful ones. Complete combustion gives CO₂ and H₂O; incomplete gives CO and soot.

3. Alkenes and addition reactions

The C=C bond is the reactive site. Bromine water is decolourised, which is the test that tells an alkene from an alkane. Ethene reacts by addition with hydrogen (to ethane), steam (to ethanol) and bromine (to dibromoethane). Ethanol is also made by fermentation of glucose from sugar with yeast.

4. Oxidation, esters and polymers

Ethanol is oxidised to ethanoic acid by acidified potassium dichromate(VI), which turns from orange to green. Carboxylic acids react with alcohols to give esters, which smell fruity. Addition polymerisation joins alkene monomers (poly(ethene) from ethene); condensation polymerisation joins monomers with loss of water (nylon, PET).

Exam focus

Q: Describe the test that distinguishes ethene from methane and state the result.

A: Add bromine water and shake; ethene decolourises it by addition across the double bond, while methane leaves the orange colour unchanged.

title: Hardware and Logic Gates
content:
Logic Gates

ABANDORNANDNORXOR
0000110
0101101
1001101
1111000

NOT inverts; NAND is 'AND then NOT'; XOR outputs 1 when inputs differ.

Boolean Algebra Laws

  • De Morgan: (A·B)′ = A′ + B′; (A + B)′ = A′ · B′
  • Distribution: A·(B + C) = A·B + A·C
  • Absorption: A + A·B = A Key: A, B and C are Boolean variables that hold 0 or 1; · means AND and + means OR, so these laws are algebra for logic, not arithmetic.

Example: simplify A + A′B = (A + A′)(A + B) = A + B.

Constructing Circuits

Truth table → Boolean expression → gates. A half adder: S = A XOR B, C = A AND B. Key: A and B = the two input bits; S = sum output bit; C = carry output bit; all four are 0 or 1.

Flip-Flops (Bistables)

  • SR latch: set/reset, invalid state S=R=1
  • JK: like SR but J=K=1 toggles
  • Clock signals synchronise state changes

Von Neumann Model

CPU (ALU, control unit, registers: PC, MAR, MDR, ACC) + memory + I/O, sharing one bus system; instructions fetched–decoded–executed in cycles.

Exam tips: write truth tables fully; simplify before drawing circuits to save gates, and name the law you use.

title: Database Systems
content:
Database Systems

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): limitations of file-based systems; relational concepts; SQL (SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, INNER JOIN, SUM, COUNT); DBMS features.

1. File-based problems

Data repetition (wasted space, inconsistency), fixed queries, no concurrent access control — solved by a DBMS with shared, structured tables.

2. Relational concepts

  • Table, record, field; primary key (unique); secondary key (indexed search field); foreign key links tables.
  • One-to-many relationships via foreign keys; no repeating groups (1NF mindset).

3. SQL

SELECT Title, Year FROM Films
WHERE Genre = 'Sci-Fi' AND Year > 2015
ORDER BY Year DESC;

SELECT Genre, COUNT(*) AS NumFilms, SUM(Rating) AS TotalRating
FROM Films
GROUP BY Genre;

SELECT s.Name, f.Title
FROM Students s INNER JOIN Loans l ON s.StudentID = l.StudentID
INNER JOIN Films f ON l.FilmID = f.FilmID;

WHERE filters rows; GROUP BY aggregates; JOIN combines on matching keys.

4. DBMS features

Data dictionary (schema, types, constraints), query processor, forms/reports, access rights (read/write per user), data integrity (validation rules), backup/recovery.

Exam tips: write SQL keywords uppercase; alias joined tables (s, l, f); when asked "why relational", cite reduced redundancy + flexible queries.

title: Work, Energy and Power
content:
Work, Energy and Power

Work

W = Fs cos θ — force × displacement in the force's direction. Unit: joule (J). Key: W = work done (J); F = magnitude of the force (N); s = displacement (m); θ = angle between the force and the displacement — at 90° the cosine is 0 and the force does no work.

Example: 100 N over 5 m in the same direction: W = 500 J. At 60°: 100 × 5 × cos 60° = 250 J.

Energy Forms

  • Kinetic energy: Ek = ½mv², in joules Key: m = mass (kg); v = speed (m s⁻¹) — v is squared, so doubling the speed quadruples the energy and the braking distance.
  • Gravitational PE: Ep = mgh, in joules Key: m = mass (kg); g = 9.81 N kg⁻¹; h = height gained above the chosen zero level (m) — the zero level is arbitrary, so only changes matter.
  • Elastic PE: ½kx² (spring, Hooke's law region)

Conservation of Energy

Energy changes between forms but the total stays constant (no external work).

Falling from height h: mgh = ½mv², so v = √(2gh) — independent of mass.

Example: a 0.5 kg ball dropped from 4 m hits at v = √(2 × 9.81 × 4) ≈ 8.9 m s⁻¹.

Power

P = W/t = Fv. Unit: watt (W = J s⁻¹). Key: P = power (W); W = work done (J); t = time (s); F = driving force (N); v = speed (m s⁻¹) — P = Fv applies when the force is along the motion.

Example: a 750 N runner at 6 m s⁻¹ outputs P = 4500 W.

Efficiency

Efficiency = useful output / total input × 100%. Key: both energies in the same unit (J), so efficiency has no unit; ×100 is only to report it as a percentage, and it can never exceed 100%.

Exam tips: energy questions are solved with energy, not kinematics, when forces vary; always ask 'where did the missing energy go?' — usually heat or sound.

title: Bonding and Structure
content:
Bonding and Structure

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH11, Topic 3. Bonding explains the physical properties of a substance: melting point, conductivity and solubility all follow from the type of bond and the way particles are packed.

Ionic bonding

  • Ionic bonds are the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in a giant lattice.
  • They have high melting points, are brittle and conduct only when molten or dissolved, because the ions are free to move.

Covalent bonding

  • A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between two atoms. Simple molecular substances have low melting points because only weak intermolecular forces are overcome.
  • Giant covalent structures such as diamond and silicon(IV) oxide need many strong bonds broken to melt, so they have very high melting points.
  • Graphite conducts because each carbon uses three electrons in bonding, leaving one delocalised electron per atom.

Electronegativity and polarity

  • Electronegativity is the ability of an atom to attract the bonding pair. The difference between two atoms gives a polar bond.
  • A molecule is polar only if its bond dipoles do not cancel. Shape decides this: CO2 is linear and non-polar, while H2O is bent and polar.

Shapes of molecules

  • Electron pairs repel each other, so they arrange themselves as far apart as possible. Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs.
  • Common shapes: linear (180°), trigonal planar (120°), tetrahedral (109.5°), and bent or pyramidal forms when lone pairs are present.

Metallic bonding

  • Metals consist of positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons, which explains conductivity, malleability and high melting points.

Exam tip: a question asking why a substance conducts must name the mobile particle — ions, delocalised electrons — not just "electrons".

title: Ethics, Security & Impact
content:
Ethics, Security & Impact

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): ethics & professional codes, security threats, malware, online safety, environmental/employment impact.

1. Ethics and codes

ACM/IEEE-CS/BCS codes: public interest, competence, integrity, privacy. Applying: identify the principle → apply to scenario → stakeholders affected → consequences.

2. Threats

  • Malware: virus (attaches, replicates via host), worm (self-spreads), trojan (disguised), spyware, ransomware.
  • Social: phishing (fake emails/sites), pharming (DNS/hosts redirect), shoulder surfing, brute force.
  • Technical: interception (packet sniffing), SQL injection (malicious input into queries), DoS (flooding services).

3. Defences

Antivirus/antispyware (scan, quarantine), firewalls (port/IP filtering), 2FA + biometrics, strong passwords + managers, encryption (HTTPS, VPN), access levels, patches/updates, user training.

4. Online behaviour

Digital footprint, cyberbullying, fake news, privacy settings, verification of sources.

5. Wider impact

Employment: automation displaces roles but creates IT jobs. Environment: e-waste, energy use vs paperless efficiency. Monitoring: workplace tracking, CCTV — balance with privacy laws (GDPR-style).

Exam tips: name the threat precisely (pharming ≠ phishing), then the matched defence; ethics answers need principle + application, not opinion.

title: Functions
content:
Functions

A function maps each input in the domain to exactly one output in the range.

Composite Functions

fg(x) means f(g(x)) — apply g first, then f. Order matters.

Example: f(x) = 2x + 1, g(x) = x². Then fg(x) = 2x² + 1 but gf(x) = (2x + 1)².

Inverse Functions

f⁻¹ reverses f: f⁻¹f(x) = x. To find it, swap x and y in y = f(x) and rearrange. Key: f⁻¹ = the inverse function; f⁻¹f(x) means "apply f, then undo it", which returns the original input; x stays in f's domain and the output stays in f's range.

Example: f(x) = 3x − 2 gives f⁻¹(x) = (x + 2)/3.

An inverse exists only if f is one-one. If not, restrict the domain (e.g. f(x) = x² for x ≥ 0 has f⁻¹(x) = √x). Graphically, y = f⁻¹(x) is the reflection of y = f(x) in the line y = x, and the range of f becomes the domain of f⁻¹.

Transformations

NotationEffect on y = f(x)
f(x) + atranslation up by a
f(x + a)translation left by a
a f(x)vertical stretch, factor a
f(ax)horizontal stretch, factor 1/a
−f(x)reflection in the x-axis
f(−x)reflection in the y-axis

Exam tips: state the domain of any inverse; when combining transformations, translations inside the bracket act in the opposite direction to the sign.

title: Binomial Distribution
content:
The Binomial Distribution

When Binomial Applies

X ~ B(n, p) counts successes in n independent trials when:

  • a fixed number n of identical trials,
  • each trial ends in success or failure,
  • constant success probability p,
  • trials are independent.

Check all four before using the model — "justifying a binomial model" is a real exam question.

The Formula

P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ʳ for r = 0, 1, ..., n. The ⁿCᵣ counts which r of the n trials were the successes. Key: X = number of successes; n = number of independent trials (a count); p = probability of success on one trial (0 to 1); r = the observed number of successes; ⁿCᵣ = n! / (r!(n − r)!), the number of ways to choose which trials succeeded.

Example: X ~ B(5, 0.3). P(X = 2) = ¹⁰C₂? No — ⁵C₂ × 0.3² × 0.7³ = 10 × 0.09 × 0.343 = 0.3087.

Cumulative Probabilities

P(X ≤ 2) = P(0) + P(1) + P(2). "At least" questions convert by the complement: P(X ≥ 2) = 1 − P(X ≤ 1). Keep one extra decimal place in intermediate steps to avoid rounding drift.

Expectation and Variance

  • E(X) = np and Var(X) = np(1 − p) Key: n = number of trials; p = success probability; E(X) = the mean number of successes (a count); Var(X) = its variance — always smaller than the mean, because (1 − p) is under 1.

For X ~ B(20, 0.4): E(X) = 8 and Var(X) = 4.8.

Modelling Decisions

If trials are dependent (drawing without replacement from a small population) binomial is not appropriate. If p changes between trials it is not binomial. When n is large and p small, the binomial is approximately Poisson — but at A2 you usually stay exact.

Exam tips: identify n and p in words before touching the calculator. For P(X ≥ k) always rewrite as 1 − P(X ≤ k − 1). Tables give cumulative values — use them rather than summing by hand.

title: Molecules, Transport and Health
content:
Molecules, Transport and Health

Edexcel IAL Biology WBI11, Topic 1. Living things are built from a small set of biological molecules. Their structure decides how they are used, how substances move in and out of cells, and how diet affects health.

Carbohydrates

  • Monosaccharides such as glucose, fructose and galactose are the building blocks. Glucose is the main respiratory substrate.
  • Disaccharides form by a condensation reaction that releases water and creates a glycosidic bond. Maltose is glucose + glucose, sucrose is glucose + fructose, and lactose is glucose + galactose.
  • Starch (amylose and amylopectin) stores glucose in plants. Glycogen stores glucose in animals. Cellulose is a straight chain of beta-glucose with hydrogen bonds between chains, giving strength.

Lipids and proteins

  • A triglyceride is one glycerol with three fatty acids joined by ester bonds. Phospholipids have a hydrophilic head and two hydrophobic tails.
  • Amino acids join by peptide bonds to form polypeptides. Tertiary structure is held by hydrogen, ionic, disulfide and hydrophobic interactions.

Enzymes

  • Enzymes have an active site with a shape complementary to the substrate. Rate rises with temperature until the enzyme denatures, and pH changes can alter the active site.

Transport

  • Diffusion moves substances down a concentration gradient without energy. Facilitated diffusion uses carrier or channel proteins. Active transport moves substances against a gradient and uses ATP.
  • Water moves by osmosis from a less negative water potential to a more negative water potential.
  • Large, multicellular organisms need exchange surfaces with a large surface area to volume ratio, such as alveoli and the villi of the small intestine.

Health

  • Body mass index (BMI) = mass (kg) ÷ height² (m²). Diet, exercise and cholesterol intake affect the risk of cardiovascular disease. Key: BMI = body mass index in kg m⁻²; mass in kilograms; height in metres, already squared.

Exam tip: when you describe a transport process, state whether it needs energy, whether it uses a protein, and which way the gradient points.

title: Mensuration — Area and Volume
content:
Mensuration — Area and Volume

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): units, perimeter/area (incl. sectors), surface area, volume of standard solids, composite shapes.

1. Units

1 m² = 10 000 cm²; 1 m³ = 1 000 000 cm³; 1 litre = 1000 cm³. Convert area/volume factors carefully (square/cube the length factor).

2. Area

  • Triangle ½bh; trapezium ½(a + b)h; parallelogram bh. Key: b = base and h = the perpendicular height for the triangle and parallelogram; a and b are the two parallel sides of the trapezium; all lengths share one unit, so every area comes out in square units.
  • Circle A = πr²; sector area = (θ/360)πr²; arc = (θ/360) × 2πr. Key: r = radius (same length unit as the arc); θ = the angle at the centre in degrees; A is in square units, while the arc stays in the length unit of r.
  • Composites: split, calculate, add/subtract.

3. Volume and surface area

  • Cuboid V = lbh; prism V = cross-section × length.
  • Cylinder V = πr²h; SA = 2πr² + 2πrh.
  • Pyramid V = ⅓ × base area × h.
  • Cone V = ⅓πr²h; SA = πr² + πrl, with l² = r² + h².
  • Sphere V = (4/3)πr³; SA = 4πr².

Key: for every solid in this list: r = radius, h = vertical height, l = slant height (with l² = r² + h² for a cone), b = a base length; V comes out in cubic units and SA in square units of that same length.

4. Problem solving

Flow/filling: volume ÷ rate = time. Packing: divide volumes (check edge alignment). Nets for surface area: label every face before adding.

Exam tips: keep π on the calculator until the final answer; for sector problems ask "fraction of the full circle?"; quote units in every answer.

title: Programming and Algorithms
content:
Design Approaches

  • Top-down (stepwise refinement): decompose into modules — planned structure
  • Object-oriented: classes encapsulating state + behaviour — reusability
  • WAD (write all down): rapid prototyping — evolves during coding

Pseudocode Conventions

DECLARE x : INTEGER
IF x > 10 THEN ... ELSE ... ENDIF
WHILE ... ENDWHILE
FOR i ← 1 TO n ... NEXT i
FUNCTION f(a) RETURNS INTEGER

Searching

  • Linear: check each item, O(n), works unsorted
  • Binary: halve a sorted list each step, O(log n)

Example: 1,000,000 items: binary search needs ≤ 20 comparisons.

Sorting

AlgorithmBestAverageIdea
BubbleO(n)O(n²)swap neighbours
InsertionO(n)O(n²)insert into sorted prefix
MergeO(n log n)O(n log n)divide and merge

Merge sort example: [5,2,9,1] → [5,2][9,1] → [2,5][1,9] → [1,2,5,9].

Recursion

A function calling itself with a base case. Factorial: f(0)=1, f(n)=n·f(n−1). Stack frames handle state. Key: f(n) = n factorial, the product 1 × 2 × … × n (no units); n = a non-negative integer; the base case f(0) = 1 is what stops the recursion.

Exam tips: state the Big-O and justify it; for traces, tabulate variable changes per iteration.

title: Simplifying, Expanding and Factorising
content:
Algebra — Simplifying and Expanding

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): substitution, collecting like terms, expanding brackets, factorising (common factor, quadratics, difference of two squares), algebraic fractions.

1. Substitution

a = 3, b = −2: 2a² − b = 2(9) + 2 = 20. Always bracket substituted negatives.

2. Collecting like terms

5x + 3y − 2x + y = 3x + 4y. Terms need identical letter parts (x² and x are not like terms).

3. Expanding

  • Single: 3(2x − 5) = 6x − 15.
  • Double: (x + 3)(x − 4) = x² − x − 12 (grid or FOIL).
  • Cubic products: (x+2)³ = x³ + 6x² + 12x + 8.

4. Factorising

  • Common factor: 6x²y − 9xy² = 3xy(2x − 3y).
  • Quadratics: x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3) (two numbers ×6, sum −5).
  • Harder: 6x² + 7x + 2 = (3x + 2)(2x + 1) — split the middle term.
  • Difference of two squares: 9x² − 25 = (3x − 5)(3x + 5).

5. Algebraic fractions

Factorise top and bottom fully, then cancel: (x² − 9)/(x + 3) = (x − 3). To add, use a common denominator: 1/(x+1) + 2/(x−1) = (3x + 1)/((x+1)(x−1)). Key: x = the variable, a real number in the same unit as the expression; the cancelled form is equal to the original only where the cancelled factor is not zero, so x ≠ −3 there, and the sum is defined only for x ≠ −1 and x ≠ 1 — state that with the answer.

Exam tips: always factorise out the highest common factor including the number; check expansion by substituting x = 1 into both forms.

title: Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7
content:
Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12, Topic 8. Redox reactions involve electron transfer. The same ideas explain the reactions of metals with water and acids, and the displacement reactions of the halogens.

Oxidation states

  • Oxidation state is the charge an atom would have if all bonds were ionic. Elements are 0, simple ions equal their charge, and the sum of oxidation states equals the overall charge.
  • Oxidation is an increase in oxidation state (loss of electrons); reduction is a decrease (gain of electrons).
  • The oxidising agent is reduced; the reducing agent is oxidised.

Redox equations

  • Half-equations balance atoms, then charge, with electrons added to show the transfer. Combine them so that electrons cancel.
  • Example: MnO4⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H2O, and acidified manganate(VII) decolourises when it is reduced. Key: MnO4⁻ = the manganate(VII) ion; H⁺ = the acid that supplies the protons; e⁻ = an electron, on the left because the ion is being reduced; Mn²⁺ = the manganese(II) ion left in solution; H2O = water, made from the oxygens and protons. The equation balances atoms and charge: −1 + 8 − 5 = +2 on each side.

Group 1 and Group 2

  • Reactivity increases down Group 1 because the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is lost more easily.
  • Group 2 metals form M²⁺ ions. Reactivity with water increases down the group: magnesium reacts slowly with cold water, while calcium reacts steadily.
  • The solubility of Group 2 hydroxides and sulfates changes down the group: magnesium sulfate is soluble, barium sulfate is not.

Group 7

  • Halogens are non-metals that form X2 molecules. Oxidising power decreases down the group: chlorine displaces bromide and iodide ions, bromine displaces iodide ions.
  • Halide ions are reducing agents, and reducing power increases down the group. Concentrated sulfuric acid is reduced by HI to hydrogen sulfide, because iodide ions are strong reducing agents.

Tests for halide ions

  • Silver nitrate solution forms precipitates: chloride gives white, bromide cream, iodide yellow. Dilute ammonia distinguishes the first two.

Exam tip: when balancing a redox equation in acid, add H⁺ and H2O before counting electrons, and always check that charge and atoms balance on both sides.

title: Operating Systems
content:
Operating Systems

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): OS roles, memory/process management, hardware–software layer, interrupts, buffers, utility software.

1. What an OS does

Manages memory, processes/files, I/O via drivers, security (users, permissions), and provides the UI (CLI/GUI) between user, applications and hardware.

2. Memory and process management

  • Paging/segmentation move programs in/out; virtual memory extends RAM to disk when RAM is full.
