  • Multitasking: scheduler gives each process time slices; context switching saves/restores state.

3. Interrupts and buffers

Interrupts signal events (I/O complete, timer); CPU saves context, services via ISR, resumes. Buffers hold data in transit (printing) so slow devices don't block the CPU; spooling queues jobs.

4. Utility software

Disk formatter, defragmenter (reduces head movement on HDDs; unnecessary for SSD), backup scheduler, compression, antivirus, file compression.

5. UI and drivers

CLI: precise, scriptable, low overhead. GUI: icons/windows, discoverable, more resources. Device drivers translate OS calls to hardware specifics — each device needs its own.

Exam tips: "manage" verbs earn marks: manages memory, manages processes, manages peripherals; explain virtual memory by RAM-full scenario, not definition alone.

title: Characteristics and Classification of Living Organisms
content:
Characteristics and Classification of Living Organisms

Cambridge IGCSE 0610 (2023–2025): 1.1 characteristics of living organisms; 1.2 classification; 1.3 features of organisms; 1.4 dichotomous keys.

1. The seven characteristics

Remember MRS GREN: movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion, nutrition. Every living organism shows all seven; a virus shows none outside a host cell, which is why it is not classified as living.

2. The classification hierarchy

Kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species. The binomial name uses genus and species, written in italics with a capital genus (Homo sapiens). Organisms in the same species can interbreed to produce fertile offspring.

The five kingdoms are animals, plants, fungi, protoctists and prokaryotes (bacteria). Viruses are placed outside the kingdoms because they are not cells.

3. Features of the main groups

  • Animals: multicellular, no cell wall, feed heterotrophically; vertebrates have a backbone, invertebrates do not.
  • Plants: multicellular, cellulose cell walls, chlorophyll, photosynthesise.
  • Fungi: cell walls of chitin, no chlorophyll, feed by absorbing dissolved nutrients (yeast, moulds, mushrooms).
  • Protoctists: mostly single-celled with a nucleus (Amoeba, Chlorella).
  • Prokaryotes: no nucleus, loop of DNA, no membrane-bound organelles (bacteria).

Vertebrate classes: fish (scales, gills), amphibians (moist skin, eggs in water), reptiles (dry scaly skin, shelled eggs), birds (feathers, beaks), mammals (hair, mammary glands).

4. Using a key

A dichotomous key asks one question at a time with two mutually exclusive answers, each leading to another question until the organism is named. Good keys describe visible features, not habitat or behaviour.

Exam focus

Q: State two features that distinguish fungi from plants.

A: Fungi have cell walls made of chitin rather than cellulose, and they have no chlorophyll, so they cannot photosynthesise and feed heterotrophically.

title: Formal Writing: Register and Linking Words
content:
Formal writing uses a measured register: full forms instead of contractions, precise vocabulary, and connectives that show how ideas relate. Using the right register is as important as using correct grammar.

Formal and informal register

Informal writing uses slang, contractions and abbreviations. Formal writing avoids them.

  • Informal: Hey, we can't go tomorrow.
  • Formal: We are unable to attend the meeting tomorrow.

Linking words

Linking words show the relationship between ideas.

  • Addition: moreover, furthermore, in addition
  • Contrast: however, nevertheless, although
  • Result: consequently, therefore, as a result
  • Sequence: first, then, meanwhile
  • Similarity: similarly, likewise

Choosing a connective

Ask what the relationship is. If the second idea contradicts the first, use a contrast word. If it follows from the first, use a result word. Avoid starting every sentence with the same word.

Opening and closing formal letters

  • Use Dear Sir or Madam when you do not know the name.
  • Use Dear followed by a name when you do.
  • End with Yours faithfully for Dear Sir or Madam, and Yours sincerely for a named person.

Checking an essay

Remove contractions. Replace casual words with precise ones. Check that each connective matches the logic between the sentences.

title: Arithmetic, Place Value and Estimation
content:
Number — Arithmetic and Place Value

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): 1.1 integers & place value; 1.2 fractions/decimals/percentages context; 1.3 powers & roots; HCF/LCM.

1. Types of number

  • Integers: … −2, −1, 0, 1, 2 … Primes: exactly two factors; 2 is the only even prime; 1 is not prime.
  • HCF = product of common prime factors (lowest powers); LCM = all prime factors (highest powers).

Example: 60 = 2²×3×5 and 84 = 2²×3×7 ⇒ HCF = 2²×3 = 12; LCM = 2²×3×5×7 = 420.

2. Place value

In 47 382 the digit 7 has value 7000. Rounding to significant figures: keep n digits, round using the next digit (≥5 up).

Estimation: round inputs to 1 s.f. first — 39.2 × 5.98 ≈ 40 × 6 = 240.

3. Order of operations

BIDMAS. 3 + 4 × 2² = 3 + 16 = 19. Insert brackets yourself when translating words: "3 added to the product of 4 and 2²" = 3 + (4 × 2²).

4. Negative numbers and calculators

Bracket negatives when substituting. Know the ×10ˣ, x², √, ˣ√ and fraction keys; give answers to 3 s.f. unless told otherwise.

5. Bounds (Extended)

Measured to nearest u: UB = +u/2, LB = −u/2. Division p/q: max = UBp ÷ LBq. Key: u = the unit the reading was rounded to (the same unit as the measurement); UB = upper bound; LB = lower bound; the subscripts p and q say which quantity each bound belongs to.

Example: 45 cm (nearest cm) in 6 s (nearest s): max speed = 45.5 ÷ 5.5 = 8.27 m/s (3 s.f.).

Exam tips: show prime-factor trees for HCF/LCM; always state rounding units (3 s.f., 1 d.p.); bounds answers quote both limits.

title: Solving Equations
content:
Algebra — Equations

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): linear equations, simultaneous equations, quadratic formula, completing the square, forming equations from words.

1. Linear equations

3(x − 2) = x + 4 → 3x − 6 = x + 4 → 2x = 10 → x = 5. With fractions, multiply through by the LCD first.

2. Forming equations

Translate shapes/situations: "rectangle length 3 cm more than width, perimeter 34" → 2w + 2(w + 3) = 34 → w = 7.

3. Simultaneous equations

  • Elimination: 2x + y = 7 and x − y = 2 → add → 3x = 9 → x = 3, y = 1.
  • Substitution for linear–quadratic: substitute y = 2x into x² + y² = 20 → 5x² = 20 → x = ±2.

4. Quadratics by formula

x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a. Key: a, b and c are the coefficients of ax² + bx + c = 0, with a ≠ 0 (no units); ± gives the two roots; the discriminant b² − 4ac decides how many real roots exist.

Example: 2x² − 4x − 3 = 0 → x = (4 ± √(16 + 24))/4 = 2.58 or −0.58 (2 d.p.).

5. Completing the square

x² + bx + c = (x + b/2)² − (b/2)² + c. x² − 6x + 5 = (x − 3)² − 4 → minimum at (3, −4). Use for turning points and for solving when factorising fails. Key: b and c are the coefficients of the quadratic (no units); the squared bracket makes the turning point readable straight off — the graph is at its lowest or highest where x + b/2 = 0.

Exam tips: substitute answers back to verify; in word problems define the unknown clearly ("let w = width in cm"); give quadratic solutions to the accuracy demanded.

title: Nuclear Physics
content:
Nuclear Physics

The Nucleus

Protons + neutrons (nucleons). Nuclide notation: ᴬZX — Z protons, A nucleons. Isotopes share Z, differ in N.

Nuclear densities are enormous (~10¹⁷ kg m⁻³) — nearly all mass in a tiny volume.

Radioactive Decay

Random and spontaneous:

TypeWhat changesStopped by
alphaZ − 2, A − 4paper
beta-minusZ + 1, A samemm of aluminium
gammanothingthick lead

Half-life: time for half the nuclei to decay. N = N₀ e^(−λt), λ = ln 2 / t½. Key: N = nuclei remaining after time t; N₀ = nuclei present at the start; λ = decay constant (s⁻¹), the probability per second that any one nucleus decays; t = elapsed time (s); t½ = half-life (s); ln 2 = 0.693.

Example: a sample with t½ = 10 days: after 30 days, 1/8 of the original activity remains.

Mass–Energy

E = mc². Mass difference Δm in nuclear reactions becomes energy; binding energy = energy released assembling the nucleus. 1 u ≈ 931 MeV. Key: E = energy released (J); m = the mass that disappears (kg); c = speed of light (3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹); Δm = mass of the separate nucleons minus the mass of the nucleus (kg); binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron, which is why both fission and fusion release energy.

Fission and Fusion

Both release energy by moving toward iron (peak binding energy per nucleon): heavy nuclei split (fission, reactors), light nuclei merge (fusion, stars).

Exam tips: balance Z and A on both sides of every equation; activity questions use A = λN, not guesswork with halves.

title: Membranes, Proteins, DNA and Gene Expression
content:
Membranes, Proteins, DNA and Gene Expression

Edexcel IAL Biology WBI11, Topic 2. DNA holds the code for proteins. Gene expression copies that code into mRNA and then builds the protein. Cell membranes control what enters and leaves the cell.

Cell membranes

  • The fluid mosaic model describes a phospholipid bilayer with proteins that move within it.
  • Cholesterol stabilises the membrane and reduces its fluidity at high temperature. Glycoproteins and glycolipids on the outer surface act as cell recognition sites.
  • Channel and carrier proteins control facilitated diffusion and active transport.

DNA structure and replication

  • DNA is a double helix of two antiparallel strands. Each nucleotide has a deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate and one base: adenine, thymine, cytosine or guanine.
  • Adenine pairs with thymine (two hydrogen bonds) and cytosine pairs with guanine (three hydrogen bonds).
  • Replication is semi-conservative: each new molecule has one original strand and one new strand. Helicase unwinds the helix, and DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to the 3' end of the new strand.

Protein synthesis

  • Transcription takes place in the nucleus. RNA polymerase makes a complementary mRNA copy of one gene. RNA contains uracil instead of thymine.
  • Translation takes place on ribosomes. A codon is three bases on mRNA that codes for one amino acid. tRNA carries a specific amino acid and has an anticodon that matches the codon.
  • The genetic code is degenerate: several codons can code for the same amino acid. It is also universal and non-overlapping.

Mutations

  • A substitution changes one base. It may be silent, or it may change one amino acid.
  • A deletion or insertion of one or two bases causes a frameshift that alters every codon after the mutation.

Exam tip: when you explain a mutation, say what happens to the codon, then to the amino acid, then to the protein's shape and function.

title: Energy Flow, Ecosystems and the Environment
content:
Energy Flow, Ecosystems and the Environment

Edexcel IAL Biology WBI14, Topic 5. Energy enters most ecosystems as light, is fixed by photosynthesis and then passes along food chains. Nutrients cycle, and human activity can disrupt those cycles.

Photosynthesis and limiting factors

  • The light-dependent reactions take place on the thylakoid membranes. Light energy splits water (photolysis), releases oxygen and makes ATP and reduced NADP.
  • The light-independent reactions (the Calvin cycle) take place in the stroma. CO₂ is fixed by the enzyme RuBisCO onto ribulose bisphosphate, and the product is reduced to make triose phosphate.
  • Light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature are limiting factors. The factor that is in shortest supply limits the rate.

Energy transfer through trophic levels

  • Gross primary productivity is the total energy fixed by plants. Net primary productivity is the energy left after respiration.
  • Energy is lost between trophic levels: in respiration, as heat, in faeces and urine, and in parts of organisms that are not eaten. Only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is usually passed on.
  • Energy pyramids are always the right way up, because energy is lost at each step.

Nutrient cycles

  • In the carbon cycle, photosynthesis removes CO₂ from the air and respiration, decomposition and combustion return it.
  • Nitrogen fixing bacteria in root nodules convert nitrogen gas into ammonium ions. Nitrifying bacteria convert ammonium to nitrate, and denitrifying bacteria return nitrogen gas to the air.

Human impact

  • Fertiliser run-off causes eutrophication. Algae grow rapidly, block light, and then die. Decomposers use up the oxygen, and fish and other animals die.
  • Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane absorb infrared radiation and raise the temperature of the Earth.
  • Pesticides and persistent chemicals become more concentrated at higher trophic levels, which is called biomagnification.

Exam tip: when you explain a limiting factor, name the factor, state which reaction it slows, and say why the rate falls.

title: Sequences and Series
content:
Sequences and Series

Arithmetic Progressions (AP)

Terms increase by a common difference d.

  • nth term: uₙ = a + (n − 1)d
  • Sum: Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d]

Example: AP 5, 8, 11: the 20th term is 5 + 19 × 3 = 62. Key: 5 = a, the first term; 3 = d, the common difference; 19 = n − 1, because the 20th term sits 19 steps after the first.

Geometric Progressions (GP)

Terms multiply by a common ratio r.

  • nth term: uₙ = arⁿ⁻¹
  • Sum: Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r)
  • Sum to infinity (|r| < 1 only): S∞ = a/(1 − r)

Example: a = 8, r = 1/2 gives S∞ = 8/(1/2) = 16. Key: a = the first term of the GP; r = the common ratio (each term × r); S∞ = the sum to infinity, which only exists while |r| < 1 — otherwise the series diverges.

Binomial Expansion

(1 + x)ⁿ = 1 + nx + n(n − 1)/2! x² + n(n − 1)(n − 2)/3! x³ + …, valid for |x| < 1.

For positive integer n, coefficients come from Pascal's triangle: (1 + 2x)⁴ = 1 + 8x + 24x² + 32x³ + 16x⁴.

Exam tips: identify a, d or r first; for "sum to infinity" questions check |r| < 1 explicitly, and for binomial expansions give terms up to the power asked (usually x² or x³).

title: Coordination and Response
content:
Coordination and Response

Cambridge IGCSE 0610 (2023–2025): 14.1 nervous control; 14.2 the eye; 14.3 hormones; 14.4 homeostasis; 14.5 tropisms.

1. The reflex arc

Stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone in the spinal cord → motor neurone → effector → response. The relay neurone in the spinal cord allows a reflex without waiting for the brain, which is faster and protects the body. Impulses cross synapses with neurotransmitters.

2. The eye

Light passes the cornea and pupil to the lens, which focuses it on the retina; rods detect low light and cones colour. In bright light the iris muscles make the pupil smaller; in dim light it widens. To focus on a near object, the ciliary muscle contracts and the lens becomes fatter; for a distant object it relaxes and the lens thins.

3. Hormones and homeostasis

Hormones travel in blood and act more slowly than nerves. Insulin lowers blood glucose by converting it to glycogen in the liver; glucagon raises it. Adrenaline raises heart rate and breathing in emergencies. Thyroxine controls metabolic rate; ADH controls water reabsorption; oestrogen and testosterone control secondary sexual characteristics.

Homeostasis keeps temperature, glucose and water constant. Temperature control uses sweating, vasodilation and vasoconstriction, shivering and hairs standing up.

4. Tropisms

Phototropism: shoots grow towards light because auxin accumulates on the shaded side and stimulates elongation. Geotropism: roots grow downwards towards gravity, anchoring the plant and reaching water. These are examples of plant responses without a nervous system.

Exam focus

Q: Explain why a reflex action is faster than a deliberate response.

A: The reflex pathway passes through a relay neurone in the spinal cord and bypasses the brain, so there are fewer synapses and less processing before the effector responds.

title: Integration
content:
Integration

Indefinite Integrals

Reverse the power rule and add a constant: ∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1) + c (n ≠ −1). Key: n = the power of x, any number except −1 (where division by n + 1 would fail); c = the constant of integration, carrying the same unit as y; dx = integrate with respect to x.

Examples: ∫ x³ dx = x⁴/4 + c; ∫ 1/x dx = ln|x| + c; ∫ sin x dx = −cos x + c; ∫ e^x dx = e^x + c.

Definite Integrals

∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = [F(x)]ₐᵇ = F(b) − F(a). Constants of integration cancel. Key: F = any antiderivative of f; a = lower and b = upper limit, both values of x; the result is the signed area under the curve between them, in y-units × x-units.

Example: ∫₀¹ 6x² dx = [2x³]₀¹ = 2.

Areas Under Curves

Area between a curve and the x-axis = ∫ₐᵇ y dx, where y ≥ 0. If the curve dips below the axis, split the integral at the roots and add the absolute values.

Example: area between y = x² − 4 and the x-axis: roots ±2, and the area is |∫₋₂² (x² − 4) dx| = 32/3.

Trapezium Rule

A ≈ h/2 [y₀ + 2(y₁ + … + yₙ₋₁) + yₙ], h = (b − a)/n. More strips → better estimate; always an over-estimate for convex curves. Key: h = width of each strip (unit of x); y₀ … yₙ = the strip heights (unit of y); n = the number of strips (a count); a and b = the limits of x; A = the estimated area.

Exam tips: never forget +c on indefinite integrals; for areas with negative regions, sketch first and split.

title: Congruence and Similarity
content:
Geometry — Congruence and Similarity

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): congruence criteria, similar shapes, scale factors for length/area/volume, symmetry.

1. Congruence

Criteria: SSS, SAS, ASA (AAS), RHS. State the criterion used when proving triangles congruent, then transfer matching sides/angles.

2. Similarity

Equal angles + sides in proportion. Scale factor k = corresponding new ÷ old. Key: k = scale factor, a length divided by a length so it has no unit; lengths scale by k, areas by k² and volumes by k³.

Example: triangles with sides 4, 6, 8 and 6, 9, 12: k = 1.5.

3. Length, area, volume factors

Length ×k; area ×k²; volume ×k³ — including reverse problems.

Example: volumes 250 cm³ and 2000 cm³: k³ = 8 ⇒ k = 2 ⇒ areas ×4.

4. Area/volume calculations from similarity

Find k from a matching length pair, then apply the right power. Watch hidden pairs (radii, heights, slants).

5. Symmetry

Line symmetry (reflect) and rotational symmetry order — for 2-D shapes and 3-D solids (prisms, cubes, pyramids).

Exam tips: write the matching-vertex order in similarity statements (△ABC ~ △DEF); choose which k-power applies before calculating.

title: Organisation of the Organism
content:
Organisation of the Organism

Cambridge IGCSE 0610 (2023–2025): 2.1 cell structure; 2.2 levels of organisation; 2.3 size and magnification.

1. Plant and animal cells

StructureFunctionPlantAnimal
nucleuscontains chromosomes, controls the cellyesyes
cytoplasmsite of chemical reactionsyesyes
cell membranecontrols what enters and leavesyesyes
cell wallcellulose, supports the cellyesno
chloroplastcontains chlorophyll, photosynthesisyesno
vacuolelarge, permanent, stores sapyessmall or absent

2. From cell to organism

Cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism. A tissue is a group of similar cells doing one job (muscle tissue); an organ combines tissues for a function (stomach); a system combines organs (digestive system).

3. Specialised cells and their shapes

  • Root hair cell: long thin extension, large surface area for water uptake.
  • Palisade mesophyll: packed with chloroplasts near the leaf surface.
  • Red blood cell: no nucleus, biconcave, packed with haemoglobin.
  • Ciliated cell: tiny hairs sweep mucus (trachea, oviduct).
  • Sperm and egg cells: one is motile, the other stores food for the embryo.
  • Nerve cell: long to carry impulses; muscle cell: contracts.

4. Magnification

Magnification = drawing size / actual size. Keep the units consistent: 1 mm = 1000 µm. A cell 50 µm wide drawn 10 mm across is ×200. Convert the other way for actual size: actual = image / magnification.

Exam focus

Q: A cell is examined and shown to have a cell wall and many chloroplasts. State two things it cannot be.

A: It cannot be an animal cell (it has a wall and chloroplasts) and it cannot be a fungal or bacterial cell (fungi have no chloroplasts, bacteria have no membrane-bound chloroplasts or nucleus).

title: Further Algebra
content:
Further Algebra

Polynomial Division and the Remainder Theorem

Divide to rewrite p(x) = (x − a)q(x) + r. The remainder when dividing by (x − a) equals p(a). Key: p(x) = the polynomial being divided; q(x) = the quotient (one degree lower than p); a = the value substituted; r = the remainder, a constant in p(x)'s own unit — and it is exactly p(a).

Example: p(x) = x³ − 2x² + 5. p(2) = 8 − 8 + 5 = 5, so dividing by (x − 2) leaves remainder 5.

If p(a) = 0, then (x − a) is a factor — that is the factor theorem. Divide out fully to reduce a cubic to a quadratic and factorise completely.

The Modulus Function

|x| measures distance from zero: |x| = x for x ≥ 0, −x for x < 0. Its graph is V-shaped.

Solving |2x − 1| = 5: split into 2x − 1 = 5 or 2x − 1 = −5, giving x = 3 or −2.

Inequalities: |2x − 1| < 5 becomes −5 < 2x − 1 < 5, so −2 < x < 3.

Partial Fractions

Reverse of combining fractions — needed before binomial expansion of rational functions.

  • Repeated linear: (4x + 1)/(x + 1)² = A/(x + 1) + B/(x + 1)²
  • Distinct linear: (7x + 4)/(x + 1)(x + 2) = A/(x + 1) + B/(x + 2) Key: A and B = the constants to be found (pure numbers), chosen so the split is identical to the original fraction for every x; the method then integrates each simple piece separately.

Example: cover the (x + 1) factor with x = −1: B = 3; then compare coefficients for A = 4.

Exam tips: for |ax + b| > c, remember two separate regions; check factor-theorem roots by substitution before long division.

title: Kinetics
content:
Kinetics

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH14, Topic 11. Kinetics links the rate of a reaction to the concentrations of the reactants, and the rate constant to temperature. Rate equations come from experiments, not from the balanced equation.

Rate equations and order

  • The rate equation has the form rate = k[A]^m[B]^n. The powers m and n are the orders with respect to A and B, and they must be found from experimental data. Key: rate = reaction rate (mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹); k = rate constant, whose units depend on the overall order; [A], [B] = concentrations (mol dm⁻³); m, n = orders (no units).
  • A first-order reaction has rate proportional to concentration: doubling [A] doubles the rate. A second-order reaction gives a quadrupled rate when [A] doubles.
  • A zero-order reaction has a rate that does not depend on the concentration of that reactant, because the reactant is not involved in the rate-determining step or the reaction surface is saturated.
  • The overall order is the sum of the individual orders.

Initial rates

  • Using the initial rates method, keep all but one concentration constant and compare the rates. The ratio of rates gives the order for the changed reactant.

Rate constant and units

  • The rate constant k is the proportionality constant in the rate equation. Its units depend on the overall order: for rate in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹, a first-order k is in s⁻¹ and a second-order k is in dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.
  • k changes only with temperature (and with a catalyst, which lowers Ea). Concentration changes alter the rate, not k.

Half-life

  • For a first-order reaction, the half-life is constant and given by t½ = ln 2 / k = 0.693 / k. Key: t½ = half-life (s); ln 2 = 0.693, a number with no units; k = first-order rate constant (s⁻¹).

Arrhenius equation

  • The Arrhenius equation k = A e^(−Ea/RT) relates the rate constant to temperature. Taking natural logarithms gives ln k = ln A − Ea/(RT). Key: A = pre-exponential factor (same units as k); Ea = activation energy (J mol⁻¹); R = gas constant (8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹); T = temperature (K).
  • A plot of ln k against 1/T is a straight line with gradient −Ea/R, which allows the activation energy to be found.

Mechanisms

  • A reaction mechanism is a series of steps. The slowest step is the rate-determining step, and the rate equation is predicted from its stoichiometry.

Exam tip: when asked for the rate equation, use the data and state the order for each reactant; do not simply copy the coefficients from the balanced equation.

title: Kinematics
content:
Kinematics

Definitions

  • Displacement s: distance in a given direction (vector)
  • Velocity v: rate of change of displacement, v = ds/dt Key: s = displacement (m, signed); t = time (s); ds/dt = the gradient of the displacement–time graph, so v is in m s⁻¹.
  • Acceleration a: rate of change of velocity, a = dv/dt Key: v = velocity (m s⁻¹); t = time (s); a is in m s⁻² and is the gradient of the velocity–time graph.

Graphs

  • Gradient of a displacement–time graph = velocity
  • Gradient of a velocity–time graph = acceleration
  • Area under a velocity–time graph = displacement
  • Area under an acceleration–time graph = change in velocity

SUVAT (uniform acceleration only)

EquationMissing
v = u + ats
s = ut + ½at²v
v² = u² + 2ast
s = ½(u + v)ta

Sign convention matters: take up as positive and g = −9.81 m s⁻² for falling objects.

Projectiles

Resolve into independent components: horizontal at constant velocity (s = ut), vertical under gravity (SUVAT).

Example: a ball fired at 20 m s⁻¹ at 30°: uₓ = 20 cos 30° ≈ 17.3 m s⁻¹, u_y = 20 sin 30° = 10 m s⁻¹. Time of flight = 2u_y/g ≈ 2.04 s; range = uₓ × t ≈ 35 m. Key: u = initial speed (m s⁻¹); uₓ and u_y = its horizontal and vertical components (m s⁻¹), found with cos and sin of the launch angle; g = 9.81 m s⁻²; t = time of flight (s) — horizontal and vertical motion are solved separately.

Exam tips: state which direction is positive; projectile questions are two separate 1-D problems joined by time.

title: Organic Chemistry: Arenes
content:
Organic Chemistry: Arenes

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH15, Topic 18. Benzene is an arene. Its delocalised ring of six π electrons makes it stable, so it reacts by electrophilic substitution rather than addition.

Structure and stability

  • Benzene is C₆H₆ with a planar ring. All six C–C bonds are the same length (0.139 nm), intermediate between single and double bonds.
  • The measured enthalpy of hydrogenation is about −208 kJ mol⁻¹, compared with −360 kJ mol⁻¹ for a hypothetical cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene. The difference, about 150 kJ mol⁻¹, is the delocalisation energy.

Electrophilic substitution

  • The π electron cloud is electron-rich, so the ring is a nucleophile and attacks electrophiles.
  • Nitration: concentrated HNO₃ and concentrated H₂SO₄ at about 50 °C. The electrophile is NO₂⁺, and nitrobenzene forms.
  • Halogenation: Br₂ with an AlBr₃ or FeBr₃ halogen carrier. The carrier polarises Br₂ to give Br⁺.
  • Friedel–Crafts alkylation uses a haloalkane and AlCl₃ to add an alkyl group. Friedel–Crafts acylation uses an acyl chloride and AlCl₃ to form a phenyl ketone.

Directing effects

  • Alkyl groups, including –CH₃, direct a second substituent to the 2- and 4- (ortho and para) positions.
  • A –NO₂ group directs to the 3- (meta) position.
  • –OH and –NH₂ are strongly activating: phenol reacts with bromine water at room temperature to give a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol.

Side-chain oxidation

  • Hot, acidified KMnO₄ oxidises an alkyl side chain on the ring to a carboxylic acid group. Methylbenzene forms benzoic acid.

Exam tip: when describing a mechanism, show the electrophile, the arenium intermediate with its positive charge spread over the ring, and the loss of H⁺ to restore the delocalised ring.

title: Electric Fields and Capacitance
content:
Electric Fields and Capacitance

Coulomb's Law

F = q₁q₂/(4πε₀r²). Field strength E = F/q (N C⁻¹); for a point charge E = q/(4πε₀r²). Key: F = force between the charges (N); q₁, q₂ = the two charges (C); ε₀ = permittivity of free space (8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹); r = separation (m); E = field strength (N C⁻¹); q = the charge feeling the force (C) — like charges repel, so keep the signs.

Uniform Fields

Between parallel plates: E = V/d, constant. Key: E = uniform field strength between the plates (V m⁻¹, the same as N C⁻¹); V = potential difference across them (V); d = plate separation (m) — the field is uniform, so the force on a charge is the same everywhere between them.

Example: 2 kV across 5 mm: E = 400 kV m⁻¹. An electron feels F = eE ≈ 6.4 × 10⁻¹⁴ N toward the positive plate.

Potential

V = W/q, scalar; E = −dV/dr. Potential energy of q at V is qV.

Capacitance

C = Q/V (farads). Energy stored: W = ½QV = ½CV². Key: C = capacitance (F); Q = charge stored on one plate (C); V = p.d. across the capacitor (V); W = energy stored (J) — the ½ is there because the voltage rises from zero as the charge is added.

Combinations: parallel adds (C = C₁ + C₂); series: 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ (opposite to resistors).

Example: 10 μF and 20 μF in series: 1/C = 1/10 + 1/20 → C ≈ 6.7 μF.

Charging and Discharging

Exponential: V = V₀ e^(−t/RC). Time constant RC: after one RC, V falls to 37%. Half-life t½ = 0.69 RC. Key: V = p.d. at time t (V); V₀ = initial p.d. (V); R = resistance in the discharge path (Ω); C = capacitance (F); t = time since discharge began (s); RC = time constant (s); e = 2.718; 0.69 = ln 2.

Exam tips: field points from high to low potential; in discharge problems identify which quantity (V, Q or I) decays — all share the same exponential factor.

title: Web Technologies and Security
content:
Web Technologies and Security

The Three Layers

  • HTML gives structure and content: elements, attributes, forms for user input.
  • CSS gives presentation: selectors, properties, responsive layout.
  • JavaScript gives client-side behaviour: validation before submission, DOM updates without reload.

Server-side scripting (PHP) runs on the server: reads form fields ($_POST), queries the database, outputs HTML. The client never sees PHP source.

SQL Injection

An attack where crafted input changes the meaning of a query. If a login query concatenates the username directly, entering X OR 1=1 can match every row. Defences: parameterised queries (prepared statements) that separate code from data, validation, and least-privilege database accounts.

Encryption

  • Symmetric: one shared key (AES). Fast, but key distribution is the weak point.
  • Asymmetric: public/private key pair (RSA). Anyone encrypts with the public key; only the holder decrypts with the private key. Slower, so used to exchange a symmetric session key.
  • SSL/TLS combines both: certificates verify the server, asymmetric key exchange establishes a symmetric session key, then traffic is encrypted. HTTPS = HTTP over TLS on port 443.

Hashing vs Encryption

Hashing (e.g. SHA-256) is one-way: passwords should be stored hashed with a unique salt, never encrypted reversibly.

Exam tips: explain why parameterised queries stop injection; describe the TLS handshake in three steps; distinguish hashing from encryption with password storage as the example.

title: Energetics
content:
Energetics

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12, Topic 6. Energetics explains why reactions release or absorb heat, and it provides the enthalpy data that later decides whether a reaction is feasible.

Enthalpy change and types of reaction

  • The enthalpy change ΔH is the heat energy transferred at constant pressure. Exothermic reactions have a negative ΔH; endothermic reactions have a positive ΔH.
  • Standard conditions are 100 kPa and a stated temperature, usually 298 K, with substances in their standard states.
  • Important definitions include standard enthalpy of formation, combustion and neutralisation. Each is written for one mole of the stated substance.

Measuring enthalpy changes

  • In a calorimetry experiment, q = m × c × ΔT, where m is the mass of solution (usually assumed to be 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ for water-based solutions).
  • Convert heat to enthalpy change using moles: ΔH = −q / n. The sign is negative for an exothermic reaction.
  • Sources of error include heat loss to the surroundings and incomplete combustion; the answer is always lower than the data book value for combustion.

Hess's law

  • The total enthalpy change is independent of the route taken. Enthalpy cycles let you find an unknown ΔH from known values.
  • For formation values: ΔH = Σ ΔHf(products) − Σ ΔHf(reactants).

Bond enthalpies

  • Breaking bonds is endothermic; making bonds is exothermic. ΔH ≈ Σ bonds broken − Σ bonds formed.
  • Bond enthalpies are averages over many compounds, so values from bond enthalpy calculations differ from accurate formation data.

Entropy and free energy (introduced)

  • A reaction that increases disorder (more gas molecules, for example) has a positive entropy change, which favours spontaneous change.

Exam tip: a common mistake is to use the wrong sign for ΔH. Always check whether the process is releasing or taking in heat before writing the value.

title: Measures of Variation and Standard Deviation
content:
Measures of Variation

Range and Quartiles

The range is max − min — quick but destroyed by a single outlier. Quartiles split ordered data into quarters: Q₁ at position (n + 1)/4, Q₃ at 3(n + 1)/4 (raw data). The interquartile range, IQR = Q₃ − Q₁, is the spread of the middle 50% and resists outliers. Outliers are commonly flagged as values beyond Q₁ − 1.5·IQR or Q₃ + 1.5·IQR. Key: n = the number of data items (a count); Q₁ and Q₃ = the lower and upper quartile values, in the same unit as the data; the IQR and the 1.5·IQR fences share that unit.

Variance and Standard Deviation

For raw data:

  • variance s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/n (the definitional form)
  • equivalently s² = Σx²/n − x̄² (the computational form)
  • standard deviation s = √(variance) Key: s = standard deviation, back in the unit of the data because the square root undoes the squaring; variance is the mean square deviation, so it carries that unit squared.

The standard deviation shares the units of the data; the variance does not. For frequency tables use Σf(x − x̄)²/Σf, or Σfx²/Σf − x̄².

Grouped Data

Use class midpoints as x. The result is an estimate — grouping discards within-class detail.

Combining and Scaling Datasets

Multiplying every value by b multiplies s by |b| and the variance by b². Adding a constant changes nothing in the spread. Two merged datasets: compute combined Σx and Σx² from each part, then apply the computational formula.

Example: data 1, 3, 4, 5, 7: mean 4, Σx² = 100, so variance = 100/5 − 16 = 4 and s = 2.

Exam tips: state units for s. When comparing consistency, the dataset with the smaller standard deviation (relative to its mean) is the more consistent. Always give the comparison sentence, not just the two numbers.

title: Quantum Physics
content:
Quantum Physics

Photons

E = hf = hc/λ, h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. Key: E = energy of one photon (J); h = Planck constant (J s); f = frequency (Hz); c = speed of light (3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹); λ = wavelength (m).

Example: green light 550 nm: E ≈ 3.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J ≈ 2.3 eV.

The Photoelectric Effect

Light above a threshold frequency ejects electrons instantly; intensity alone does nothing below f₀.

  • Einstein: hf = φ + KE_max (φ = work function) Key: hf = photon energy (J); φ = work function, the minimum energy needed to free an electron from that metal (J); KE_max = maximum kinetic energy of an emitted electron (J) — no emission at all if hf is below φ, whatever the intensity.
  • KE_max = eV_s (stopping potential) Key: e = elementary charge (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C); V_s = stopping potential, the reverse p.d. that just stops the fastest electrons (V); eV_s is therefore in joules.

Example: sodium φ = 2.3 eV needs λ < 540 nm; 400 nm light gives KE_max = 3.1 − 2.3 = 0.8 eV.

Wave–Particle Duality

de Broglie: λ = h/p = h/(mv). Key: λ = de Broglie wavelength of the particle (m); h = Planck constant (J s); p = momentum (kg m s⁻¹); m = mass (kg); v = speed (m s⁻¹) — heavier and faster particles have shorter wavelengths. Electrons diffract like waves — electron microscopes exploit short electron wavelengths.

Example: an electron at 10⁶ m s⁻¹: λ ≈ 0.7 nm.

Energy Levels and Line Spectra

Atoms absorb/emit photons matching level gaps: hf = E₁ − E₂. Emission lines are bright; absorption dark.

Example: the Hα line: 3 → 2 transition, 656 nm.

Exam tips: one photon interacts with one electron — that is why intensity cannot release electrons below threshold; convert eV ↔ J with 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹.

title: Oscillations and Waves II
content:
Oscillations and Waves II

Progressive vs Stationary

Progressive waves transfer energy; stationary waves store it in loops. Stationary patterns arise from two identical waves travelling in opposite directions (reflections on strings, air columns).

PropertyProgressiveStationary
Amplitudesame for all pointsvaries: nodes zero, antinodes max
Phasevaries along wavesame within a loop, π flip across nodes
Energytransferredtrapped

Harmonics

A string fixed at both ends: f₁ = v/2L, then 2f₁, 3f₁… Closed pipes resonate at odd multiples; open pipes at all multiples.

Superposition Applications

  • Young's double slit: x = λD/a — evidence light is a wave Key: x = fringe spacing (m); λ = wavelength (m); D = slit-to-screen distance (m); a = slit separation (m) — interference cannot be explained by particles travelling in straight lines, so it is the wave evidence.
  • Diffraction grating: d sin θ = nλ — resolution of spectra
  • Noise-cancelling headphones: destructive interference of antiphase sound

Polarization Applications

Polaroid sunglasses cut glare from horizontal surfaces; stress analysis in plastics; LCD screens control light with twisted polarizers. Malus' law I = I₀cos²θ. Key: I = intensity after the analyser (W m⁻²); I₀ = intensity reaching it; θ = angle between the polarising directions (°) — at 90° the cosine is zero and the light is blocked.

Exam tips: 'explain' marks want the physics: path difference, phase, node/antinode conditions — not just formula substitution.

title: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table
content:
Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH11, Topic 2. The periodic table is not a list to memorise: its rows and columns follow directly from how electrons fill shells and sub-shells.

Atoms, isotopes and mass spectrometry

  • Protons and neutrons make up the nucleus; the mass number is protons plus neutrons, and the atomic number is the number of protons.
  • Isotopes have the same number of protons and different numbers of neutrons, so the same chemistry but a different mass.
  • Relative atomic mass is the weighted mean of isotopic masses. In a mass spectrum, abundance is read from the peak heights.

Electron configuration

  • Electrons fill orbitals in order of energy: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d and so on, each orbital holding at most two electrons with opposite spins.
  • Write configurations such as 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ for neon; for transition metals the 4s electrons are lost before the 3d electrons when forming ions.

Periodic trends

  • Ionisation energy increases across a period because nuclear charge rises with similar shielding, and falls down a group as the outer electrons sit further from the nucleus.
  • Atomic radius falls across a period and rises down a group.
  • Successive ionisation energies reveal the group of an element: a large jump appears after the outer-shell electrons are removed.

Electron arrangement and the table

  • Period number = highest principal quantum number in use; group number relates to the number of outer electrons. Key: n = the principal quantum number, 1, 2, 3 … labelling the electron shell and its energy; the period is the highest n occupied in the ground state; the group is the outer-electron count for groups 1–2 and that count plus 10 for groups 13–18.
  • Blocks: s-block (groups 1-2), p-block (groups 13-18), d-block (transition metals).

Exam tip: when explaining an ionisation energy trend, name the factor (nuclear charge, shielding, distance) and say which way it changes.

title: Formulae, Equations and Amount of Substance
content:
Formulae, Equations and Amount of Substance

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH11, Topic 1. The mole is the bridge between the mass you can weigh and the number of particles a reaction actually uses, so every quantitative question in the course depends on it.

Relative masses and the mole

  • Relative atomic mass (Ar) and relative molecular mass (Mr) are based on the carbon-12 scale.
  • One mole contains the Avogadro constant, 6.02 × 10²³ particles, and the molar mass in g mol⁻¹ equals Mr numerically.
  • Moles: n = m / M. Rearrange to find mass (m = n × M) or molar mass (M = m / n). Key: n = amount of substance (mol); m = mass (g); M = molar mass (g mol⁻¹).

Empirical and molecular formulae

  • Convert percentage (or mass) composition to moles, divide by the smallest value and multiply until the ratios are whole numbers.
  • The molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula: n = Mr / Mr(empirical formula). Key: n = the whole-number multiple (no units); Mr = relative molecular mass, which has no unit either, because it is a ratio against ¹²C.

Equations and reacting masses

  • Balance equations by conserving each element, then use the coefficients as mole ratios.
  • Limiting reagent: work out the moles each reactant could give, then take the smallest.
  • Percentage yield = actual yield / theoretical yield × 100. Key: both yields are expressed in the same unit (usually g), so the percentage carries no unit.

Solutions and gases

  • Concentration c = n / V, with V in dm³ (cm³ ÷ 1000). Titration data follow the same route. Key: c = concentration (mol dm⁻³); n = amount of solute (mol); V = volume of solution (dm³).
  • At room temperature and pressure one mole of gas occupies 24 dm³, so n = V / 24. Key: n = amount of gas (mol); V = gas volume at rtp (dm³); 24 = the volume one mole occupies at rtp (dm³ mol⁻¹).

Exam tip: write the unit on every line of working, and check that your final answer has the same number of significant figures as the least precise data given.

title: Reading for Information and Inference
content:
Reading questions reward two different skills: finding information that is stated, and working out what is implied. Keep them apart when you plan an answer.

Information: what the text says

Information questions ask for facts the writer states directly. Locate the key words in the question, scan the text for matching ideas, and copy only the words you need. Do not add personal comment unless the question asks for it.

Scanning for key words

  • Underline the nouns and verbs in the question.
  • Look for synonyms, because the text rarely repeats the question's exact words.
  • Check the line reference if one is given, then read a sentence either side to confirm the context.

Inference: what the text suggests

An inference is a conclusion supported by evidence. The writer does not state it, so you must show how the evidence points to it.

Building a strong inference

  • Choose a precise quotation or a short phrase.
  • Explain what the word or phrase suggests, using a verb such as suggests, implies or hints.
  • Link the suggestion back to the character, mood or idea the question asks about.

Common mistakes

  • Retelling the plot instead of explaining the evidence.
  • Quoting a long passage with no comment.
  • Stating a fact when the question asks for a feeling or an opinion.

Exam approach

Answer the information questions quickly and accurately, because they are worth marks for precision. Spend the most time on inference questions: one well-explained quotation usually earns more than three vague ones.

title: Algorithms & Programming
content:
Algorithms & Programming

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): pseudocode, flowcharts, standard algorithms (linear/bubble), trace tables, validation & verification.

1. Pseudocode

OUTPUT "Enter n"
INPUT n
IF n MOD 2 = 0 THEN
  OUTPUT "even"
ELSE
  OUTPUT "odd"
ENDIF

FOR i ← 1 TO 10
  total ← total + i
NEXT i

WHILE total < 100
  total ← total + n
ENDWHILE

FUNCTION square(x : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
  RETURN x * x
ENDFUNCTION

Assignment ←, comparison =, MOD/DIV for remainders/quotients.

2. Flowchart symbols

Terminator (oval), process (rectangle), decision (diamond), input/output (parallelogram), flow lines with arrows.

3. Standard algorithms

  • Linear search: check each item until found/end — works unsorted.
  • Bubble sort: repeated adjacent swaps; largest bubbles to the end each pass; n−1 passes max; early exit when no swaps.
  • Counting/totaling patterns; max/min with a running best value.

4. Trace tables

One column per variable; log every assignment in order; watch loop counters and reassignments.

x ← 1; total ← 0
WHILE x <= 4
  total ← total + x * 2
  x ← x + 1
ENDWHILE  // total = 20

5. Validation vs verification

  • Validation: automatic checks on data — range (exam mark 0–100), length (password ≥ 8), type, format (postcode pattern), presence (field not empty), check digit (barcode).
  • Verification: data matches the source — double entry, visual/proof reading.

6. Testing

Normal (typical), abnormal (rejects invalid), boundary (extremes just inside/outside). Test data tables list input → expected output.

Exam tips: write pseudocode with ENDIF/NEXT/ENDWHILE terminators; in trace tables record the condition result too; boundary choices need "just above/below/at" values.

title: Probability
content:
Probability

Basic Rules

For an event A with P(A) = p: 0 ≤ p ≤ 1, and P(A′) = 1 − P(A). For mutually exclusive events, probabilities add: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B). For events that can occur together, subtract the overlap:

  • P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) Key: P = a probability, a number from 0 to 1 with no unit; A ∪ B = "at least one of A, B"; A ∩ B = "both", which is subtracted once because adding P(A) and P(B) counts it twice.

Venn Diagrams

Draw the universe first, then the events. Fill from the intersection outwards: if P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.25, then only-A = 0.35, only-B = 0.25, neither = 0.15. Every region must sum to 1.

Tree Diagrams

Branch probabilities multiply along a path; outcomes at the end of complete paths add. Draw one branch set per stage of the experiment. For two draws without replacement from a bag of 5 red and 3 blue: P(RR) = (5/8)(4/7) = 20/56.

Conditional Probability

P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) — the probability of A given that B has occurred. The condition shrinks the sample space. Key: P(A | B) = the probability of A once B is known; P(A ∩ B) = the probability that both occur; P(B) = the probability of the condition, which must not be zero.

Example: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4, P(A ∩ B) = 0.2. Then P(A | B) = 0.2/0.4 = 0.5, so A and B are independent since P(A | B) = P(A).

Independence

A and B are independent exactly when P(A ∩ B) = P(A)·P(B). Do not confuse independent (no influence on probabilities) with mutually exclusive (cannot co-occur). Mutually exclusive events with non-zero probabilities are never independent.

Exam tips: convert every "given that" into a conditional. With trees, label the second-stage branches with conditional probabilities; they are usually different from the first stage when drawing without replacement.

title: Intermolecular Forces
content:
Intermolecular Forces

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12, Topic 7. Intermolecular forces are the attractions between molecules, not the bonds inside them. They determine boiling points, solubility and how molecules pack together.

Types of intermolecular force

  • London (instantaneous dipole–induced dipole) forces exist in all molecules. They grow with the number of electrons, so larger molecules have higher boiling points.
  • Permanent dipole–dipole forces occur between polar molecules, where the partial positive and negative charges attract one another.
  • Hydrogen bonding is a strong dipole–dipole attraction. It occurs when H is bonded to N, O or F and attracts a lone pair on another N, O or F.

Effect on physical properties

  • Boiling point depends on the strength of intermolecular forces: more energy is needed to separate molecules that attract strongly.
  • Water boils at a much higher temperature than hydrogen sulfide because hydrogen bonding is much stronger than the dipole forces between H2S molecules.
  • Branched alkanes have lower boiling points than straight-chain isomers because they have a smaller surface area for London forces.

Solubility

  • Substances dissolve when the new attractions between solute and solvent replace the attractions within each.
  • Polar solvents such as water dissolve ionic and polar solutes; non-polar solvents dissolve non-polar solutes.
  • Ethanol is miscible with water because its –OH group forms hydrogen bonds with water.

Ideal and real gases

  • A real gas deviates from ideal behaviour at high pressure and low temperature, because molecules have volume and attract one another.

Exam tip: when comparing boiling points, name the type of intermolecular force, state whether it is stronger or weaker, and say how much energy is needed to overcome it. Do not say that "bonds break" when a liquid boils.

title: Electrochemistry
content:
Electrochemistry

Cambridge IGCSE 0620 (2023–2025): 4.1 electrolysis; 4.2 hydrogen–oxygen fuel cells; 4.3 rusting.

1. What electrolysis is

An electric current drives a non-spontaneous reaction in an electrolyte — a molten ionic compound or an aqueous solution. The positive anode attracts anions, where oxidation (loss of electrons) happens; the negative cathode attracts cations, where reduction (gain) happens. Remember "PANIC": Positive Anode, Negative Is Cathode.

2. Molten compounds

Molten lead(II) bromide gives bromine at the anode and lead at the cathode, because there is only one cation and one anion present. This is the cleanest case and the one to quote when asked what electrolysis of a molten salt produces.

3. Aqueous solutions and the reactivity series

In water there are always H⁺ and OH⁻ competing. At the cathode, a metal below hydrogen in the reactivity series is deposited; a reactive metal such as sodium or potassium is not, and hydrogen is given off instead. At the anode, halides are discharged in preference to hydroxide, so concentrated sodium chloride solution gives chlorine; with a dilute or non-halide solution, oxygen is produced.

Copper(II) sulfate with copper electrodes is the exception worth knowing: the anode dissolves and copper is deposited at the cathode, so the blue colour stays the same. That is copper refining.

4. Fuel cells and rusting

A hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell produces electricity with water as the only product, which is why it is used where exhaust must be clean. Rusting needs both oxygen and water; salt speeds it up, and painting, greasing, galvanising or sacrificial protection (zinc, magnesium) prevents it. Sacrificial protection works because the more reactive metal corrodes instead.

Exam focus

Q: State the products at each electrode when concentrated aqueous sodium chloride is electrolysed, and explain the anode product.

A: Cathode: hydrogen. Anode: chlorine. Chloride ions are discharged in preference to hydroxide ions because the solution is concentrated, and chlorine is formed by oxidation of Cl⁻.

title: Stoichiometry
content:
Stoichiometry

Cambridge IGCSE 0620 (2023–2025): 3.1 formulae; 3.2 relative masses of atoms and molecules; 3.3 the mole and the Avogadro constant; 3.4 calculations using moles; 3.5 concentration.

1. Formulae and relative mass

Work out an empirical formula from percentage composition by dividing each percentage by its Ar, then dividing by the smallest. Molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula. Relative formula mass Mr is the sum of Ar values: Mr(CaCO₃) = 40 + 12 + 3(16) = 100.

2. The mole

One mole contains 6.02 × 10²³ particles and has a mass equal to Mr in grams. Three conversions carry almost every calculation:

  • n = m / Mr (mass in g)
  • n = V / 24 dm³ at room temperature and pressure, for gases
  • n = c × V, with c in mol/dm³ and V in dm³, for solutions

3. Using an equation

The balancing numbers are mole ratios. For 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, two moles of hydrogen need one mole of oxygen. A typical route: mass → moles of the known substance → moles of the required substance by ratio → mass or volume.

Worked example. What mass of magnesium oxide forms when 2.4 g of magnesium burns? n(Mg) = 2.4 / 24 = 0.10 mol. The ratio is 2Mg : 2MgO, so n(MgO) = 0.10 mol. Mr(MgO) = 40, so m = 0.10 × 40 = 4.0 g.

4. Concentration and yield

Concentration in g/dm³ converts to mol/dm³ by dividing by Mr. Percentage yield = actual / theoretical × 100; percentage purity = mass of pure substance / mass of sample × 100. A yield below 100% is normal: reversible reactions, side reactions and losses on transfer.

Exam focus

Q: 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide neutralises 20.0 cm³ of hydrochloric acid. Find the acid concentration.

A: n(NaOH) = 0.100 × 0.0250 = 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol; the ratio is 1:1, so n(HCl) is the same; c = 2.50 × 10⁻³ / 0.0200 = 0.125 mol/dm³.

title: Gas Exchange in Humans
content:
Gas Exchange in Humans

Cambridge IGCSE 0610 (2023–2025): 11.1 breathing; 11.2 the respiratory tract; 11.3 gas exchange; 11.4 smoking.

1. The mechanics of breathing

Inhaling: the diaphragm contracts and flattens, the external intercostal muscles lift the ribs up and out, the thorax volume increases and pressure falls, so air rushes in. Exhaling is largely passive: muscles relax, volume falls and pressure rises. The lungs contain no muscle; they follow the thorax.

2. From trachea to alveoli

Air passes the trachea, bronchi, bronchioles and alveoli. The trachea is kept open by C-shaped cartilage rings; the lining has cilia and mucus to trap dust and bacteria. Alveoli are the exchange surface and they are built for it: a huge total surface area, walls one cell thick, a moist lining, a dense capillary network and a short distance to blood.

3. Gas exchange

Oxygen diffuses from the alveolar air, where its concentration is higher, into blood, then into red cells. Carbon dioxide diffuses the other way and is exhaled. Breathing maintains the concentration gradients. Inhaled air is about 21% oxygen and 0.04% carbon dioxide; exhaled air is about 16% oxygen and 4% carbon dioxide, and is warmer and saturated with water vapour.

4. Smoking

Tar paralyses cilia and irritates the lining, causing a smoker's cough; nicotine is addictive and raises heart rate; carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin, reducing oxygen transport; carcinogens cause mutations and lung cancer; emphysema destroys alveolar walls, reducing surface area and causing breathlessness.

Exam focus

Q: State two features of alveoli and explain how each helps gas exchange.

A: Their walls are one cell thick, giving a short diffusion distance, and their millions of tiny sacs give a large surface area for diffusion.

title: States of Matter
content:
States of Matter

Cambridge IGCSE 0620 (2023–2025): 1.1 solids, liquids and gases; 1.2 diffusion — particle arrangement, kinetic theory, changes of state.

1. The three states, in particles

StateArrangementMotionShape / volume
solidclose, regular latticevibrate about fixed positionsfixed both
liquidclose, irregularslide past each otherfixed volume, takes container shape
gasfar apart, randomfast, straight linesfills the container

2. Changes of state and their names

Melting (s → l) and boiling (l → g) take in energy; freezing (l → s) and condensing (g → l) release it. Evaporation happens below the boiling point, from the surface, and is faster with a higher temperature, larger surface area and moving air. Sublimation is solid → gas directly, as iodine and carbon dioxide do.

During melting and boiling the temperature stays constant: the energy supplied breaks forces between particles instead of raising kinetic energy. That plateau is why a heating curve has flat sections.

3. Kinetic theory and pressure

Gas pressure comes from particles colliding with the walls. Heating at constant volume raises the average speed, so collisions are more frequent and harder: pressure rises. Compressing a fixed mass at constant temperature raises pressure because each collision is more frequent. The kelvin scale is needed for gas calculations: T(K) = θ(°C) + 273.

4. Diffusion

Diffusion is the spreading of particles from high to low concentration by random motion. It is fastest for light particles at high temperature: ammonia (Mr 17) travels faster than hydrogen chloride (Mr 36.5), so the white ring of ammonium chloride forms nearer the HCl end. Bromine vapour and potassium manganate(VII) in water are the standard demonstrations.

Exam focus

Q: Explain why a gas exerts a higher pressure when its temperature is raised at constant volume.

A: Particles gain kinetic energy and move faster; they hit the walls more often and with greater force per collision, so pressure rises.

title: Organic Chemistry: Carbonyls, Carboxylic Acids and Chirality
content:
Organic Chemistry: Carbonyls, Carboxylic Acids and Chirality

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH14, Topic 15. Aldehydes and ketones contain the carbonyl group, C=O. Their reactions are nucleophilic addition, and the products can be carboxylic acids, alcohols or molecules with a chiral centre.

Carbonyl compounds

  • An aldehyde has the C=O group at the end of a chain (RCHO). A ketone has it inside the chain (RCOR). Key: R = an alkyl group (CH₃, C₂H₅ …); C=O = the carbonyl group; CHO = the aldehyde end group, whose hydrogen is written out because it is the one the nucleophile is judged against; COR = a carbonyl carbon carrying two carbon groups — which is why a ketone cannot be oxidised further.
  • The carbon of C=O is slightly positive, so nucleophiles attack it. Ketones are less reactive than aldehydes because the two alkyl groups donate electron density.

Reactions and tests

  • Hydrogen cyanide adds across C=O. For ethanal, CH3CHO + HCN gives 2-hydroxypropanenitrile.
  • Sodium tetrahydridoborate(III) (NaBH4) reduces aldehydes to primary alcohols and ketones to secondary alcohols.
  • 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNPH) gives an orange or yellow precipitate with any carbonyl compound.
  • Tollens' reagent gives a silver mirror with aldehydes but not with ketones.
  • The iodoform test gives a yellow precipitate of triiodomethane with compounds containing CH3CO– or CH3CH(OH)– groups, such as propanone.

Carboxylic acids

  • Carboxylic acids contain –COOH and are weak acids. They are more acidic than alcohols because the carboxylate ion is stabilised by delocalisation.
  • Carboxylic acids react with alcohols in the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid to form esters, in a reversible esterification.
  • Primary alcohols are oxidised to carboxylic acids by heating with acidified potassium dichromate(VI) under reflux.

Chirality

  • A chiral carbon atom has four different groups attached. Molecules with a chiral centre exist as a pair of enantiomers.
  • Enantiomers have identical physical properties except their effect on plane-polarised light: one rotates it clockwise and the other anticlockwise by the same amount.
  • An equimolar mixture of the two enantiomers is a racemic mixture, which is optically inactive.

Exam tip: when describing a nucleophilic addition, show the nucleophile attacking the carbon of C=O and the oxygen gaining the negative charge.

title: Prepositions and Collocations
content:
Prepositions (in, on, at, for, of) and collocations (words that naturally go together) are not always logical, so they are best learned in phrases rather than one word at a time.

Time prepositions

  • At: a clock time or a specific moment (at 10 a.m., at night).
  • On: a day or a date (on Monday, on 5 May).
  • In: a month, a year or a longer period (in June, in 2020).

Example: The meeting is on Monday at 10 a.m.

Prepositions after adjectives and verbs

Many adjectives and verbs take a fixed preposition:

  • interested in
  • good at
  • depend on
  • listen to
  • belong to

Learn these as complete phrases.

Collocations

Collocations are common word pairings. Learn the verb that goes with the noun:

  • make a decision, make an effort, make a mistake
  • do homework, do the washing, do research
  • take a break, take a photo, take part

Using make where do is needed, or the reverse, is one of the most common errors for learners.

Strategy

  • Keep a notebook of phrases, not single words.
  • Record the preposition or verb with each noun or adjective.
  • Read widely and notice which words appear together in good writing.

title: Chemical Energetics
content:
Chemical Energetics

Cambridge IGCSE 0620 (2023–2025): 5.1 exothermic and endothermic reactions; 5.2 using enthalpy changes.

1. Two directions of energy

An exothermic reaction releases energy to the surroundings, so the mixture warms (combustion, neutralisation, adding water to anhydrous copper(II) sulfate). An endothermic reaction takes energy in, so it cools (thermal decomposition, dissolving ammonium nitrate). The sign convention: ΔH is negative for exothermic, positive for endothermic.

2. Reading a reaction profile

Every profile has reactants on one side, products on the other, and a hump in between. The hump height from reactants is the activation energy Ea — the minimum energy colliding particles need. For an exothermic reaction the products sit lower than the reactants; for an endothermic reaction they sit higher. ΔH is simply products minus reactants.

3. Bond energy arithmetic

Breaking bonds takes energy in; making bonds gives it out. ΔH = energy to break bonds in reactants − energy released making bonds in products. If breaking costs more than making releases, the reaction is endothermic. A catalyst lowers Ea but never changes ΔH, because the reactants and products are unchanged.

4. Measuring the change

A simple calorimeter: measure the temperature rise of a known mass of water, then use q = m c ΔT with c = 4.2 J/(g °C) and divide by the moles reacting. Energy is lost to the surroundings, so the measured value is always smaller than the data-book value; insulation and a lid reduce the loss.

Exam focus

Q: A reaction has ΔH = −890 kJ/mol. Is it exothermic or endothermic, and what happens to the temperature of the mixture?

A: Exothermic, because ΔH is negative. Energy is transferred to the surroundings, so the temperature rises.

title: Computational Thinking and Problem-Solving
content:
Computational Thinking and Problem-Solving

Thinking Ahead, Abstractly, Systematically

  • Abstraction: keep essential features, drop detail — a metro map ignores street geometry.
  • Decomposition: split the problem into sub-problems solved independently.
  • Thinking ahead: pre-plan inputs, outputs and reusable components; pre-calculate tables where possible.

Recursion

A recursive routine calls itself with a smaller input and a base case that stops the recursion. Elegant for trees and divide-and-conquer, but each call consumes stack space — deep recursion can overflow. Any recursion can be rewritten with a loop and explicit stack.

Searching and Sorting

  • Linear search: O(n), works unsorted.
  • Binary search: O(log n), needs sorted data.
  • Bubble sort: O(n²) average; simple; detects a sorted pass.
  • Insertion sort: O(n²) average; fast on nearly-sorted data.
  • Merge sort: O(n log n) always; needs extra memory.

Testing

White-box tests trace internal paths; black-box tests check specification behaviour. Choose normal, boundary and erroneous data. Dry runs use trace tables recording variables line by line; a trace of recursion should log each call and its return.

Exam tips: write the base case before the recursive call in pseudocode; give the Big-O with a one-line justification; construct a trace table for a small loop or recursive call.

title: Astronomy and Cosmology
content:
Astronomy and Cosmology

Luminosity and Intensity

Luminosity L is total power radiated (W). Intensity at distance d: I = L/(4πd²) — the key to distances. Key: I = intensity received (W m⁻²); L = luminosity of the star (W); d = distance from the star (m); 4πd² is the surface area of the sphere the light has spread over.

Standard candles (Cepheid variables, Type Ia supernovae) have known L, so measuring I gives d.

Example: the Sun: I = 1370 W m⁻² at d = 1.5 × 10¹¹ m gives L ≈ 3.9 × 10²⁶ W.

Wien and Stefan–Boltzmann

  • Wien: λ_max T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K — hotter stars are bluer Key: λ_max = wavelength of peak emission (m); T = surface temperature (K); the constant 2.9 × 10⁻³ has unit m K, so λ_max and T are inversely proportional.
  • Stefan: L = σAT⁴, σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ Key: L = luminosity (W); σ = Stefan–Boltzmann constant (5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴); A = surface area of the star (m²), 4πr² for a sphere; T = surface temperature (K) — the fourth power is why temperature dominates.

Hubble's Law

Galaxies recede with v = Hd, H₀ ≈ 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹. Redshift z = Δλ/λ ≈ v/c for small z. Key: v = recessional speed (m s⁻¹); H₀ = Hubble constant (s⁻¹); d = distance to the galaxy (m); z = redshift, a ratio with no unit; Δλ = observed minus emitted wavelength (m); λ = emitted wavelength (m); c = speed of light (3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹).

Example: a galaxy at 100 Mpc recedes at v = 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ × 100 × 3.09 × 10²² ≈ 6800 km s⁻¹.

The Big Bang

Evidence: Hubble expansion, cosmic microwave background (2.7 K), hydrogen/helium abundance. Age estimate: t ≈ 1/H₀ ≈ 14 billion years. The fate question: critical density, Ω.

Exam tips: convert Mpc to metres (×3.09 × 10²²) before Hubble arithmetic; distinguish redshift of light from distance ladder methods.

title: Vectors
content:
Vectors

Components and Arithmetic

A vector a = 3i + 4j has magnitude |a| = √(3² + 4²) = 5. Parallel vectors are scalar multiples; unit vector = a/|a|. Key: i and j = the unit vectors along the x- and y-axes, each of length 1; 3 and 4 = the components (same unit as the axes); |a| = the magnitude, back in that unit; a/|a| = a direction with length exactly 1.

Position and Direction

The line through point A with direction d: r = a + t d. Two lines are parallel if their directions are multiples. Key: r = the position vector of any point on the line; a = the position vector of the fixed point A; d = the direction vector; t = a free scalar parameter — sweep t and you walk the whole line.

Example: r = (1, 2) + t(3, −1).

Scalar (Dot) Product

a · b = |a||b| cos θ = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂. Key: a · b = the scalar product, which has the units of length squared; |a|, |b| = the magnitudes; θ = the angle between the two vectors, in degrees or radians as the question uses; a₁, a₂ and b₁, b₂ = their components.

Perpendicular ⇔ a · b = 0. Parallel ⇔ cross-multiplied components are equal (in 2D: a₁b₂ − a₂b₁ = 0).

Example: (2, 3) · (−6, 4) = −12 + 12 = 0, so they are perpendicular.

Angle Between Vectors

cos θ = (a · b)/(|a||b|).

Example: between (1, 0) and (1, 1): cos θ = 1/(1 × √2), θ = 45°.

Lines and Points

Foot of perpendicular from P to a line, intersection of two lines, and shortest distances all come from dot products and parameter t.

Exam tips: write column vectors cleanly; check answers by substituting the found t back into both position vectors; keep exact surd magnitudes rather than decimals.

title: Differentiation II
content:
Differentiation II

Product and Quotient Rules

  • (uv)′ = u′v + uv′
  • (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v²

Example: y = x² e^x gives dy/dx = 2x e^x + x² e^x = e^x(2x + x²).

Standard Derivatives

  • sin x → cos x; cos x → −sin x; tan x → sec²x
  • e^x → e^x; ln x → 1/x

Chain Rule Everywhere

d/dx [ln(3x)] = 3/(3x) = 1/x; d/dx [e^(2x)] = 2e^(2x); d/dx [sin²x] = 2 sin x cos x.

Implicit Differentiation

Differentiate both sides w.r.t. x, treating y as a function of x (terms in y pick up dy/dx).

Example: x² + y² = 25 → 2x + 2y(dy/dx) = 0 → dy/dx = −x/y.

Parametric Curves

For x = f(t), y = g(t): dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt). Key: t = the parameter (often time, in seconds); dy/dt and dx/dt = the rates of change with respect to t; their quotient is the rate of y per unit x, because dt cancels like a fraction.

Example: x = t², y = t³ gives dy/dx = 3t²/2t = 3t/2.

Exam tips: quote the rule you use; for tangent/normal on parametric curves, find t at the point first, and simplify implicit answers using the original equation.

title: Web Technologies
content:
Web Technologies

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): HTML structure/tags, CSS styling, JS interactivity, the DOM, microprocessors/controllers in web context.

1. HTML

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head><title>Page</title></head>
<body>
  <h1>Heading</h1>
  <p>Paragraph with <strong>bold</strong> text</p>
  <img src="pic.jpg" alt="description">
  <a href="https://example.com">Link</a>
  <table><tr><td>cell</td></tr></table>
</body>
</html>

Head holds metadata/title; body holds visible content; hypertext links via <a href>.

2. CSS

p { color: red; font-size: 14px; }
.highlight { background-color: yellow; }
#header { text-align: center; }

Element, class (.) and id (#) selectors; inline vs external stylesheets; separation of content (HTML) from presentation (CSS).

3. JavaScript and the DOM

document.getElementById("demo").innerHTML = "Hello";
document.getElementsByClassName("item")[0].style.color = "blue";

DOM = the browser's object model of the page; JS reads/changes it for interactivity (validation, sliders, dynamic text). Events (click, submit) trigger functions.

4. How pages load

URL → DNS lookup → server request → HTML parsed → assets fetched → DOM built → render. Layers: structure (HTML) → presentation (CSS) → behaviour (JS).

Exam tips: write tags with correct closing pairs; explain DOM operations as "find element by id … then change property"; separate structure/presentation/behaviour in answers.

title: Acid-base Equilibria
content:
Acid-base Equilibria

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH14, Topic 14. Acids and bases are defined by proton transfer. The strength of an acid is given by its dissociation constant, and pH calculations, buffers and titrations all follow from it.

Strong and weak acids

  • A strong acid dissociates completely in water, so [H⁺] equals the acid concentration. For 0.010 mol dm⁻³ HCl, [H⁺] = 0.010 and pH = 2.00. Key: [H⁺] = hydrogen ion concentration (mol dm⁻³); pH = −log₁₀[H⁺], and pH itself has no unit.
  • A weak acid dissociates only partly. For HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻, Ka = [H⁺][A⁻] / [HA]. Key: Ka = acid dissociation constant (mol dm⁻³); [HA] = concentration of the undissociated acid (mol dm⁻³); A⁻ = the conjugate base.
  • pKa = −log10 Ka. A smaller pKa means a stronger acid. Key: pKa has no unit because Ka, a concentration, is taken logarithmically; the smaller the pKa, the stronger the acid.

pH calculations

  • pH = −log10[H⁺]. For a base, find pOH = −log10[OH⁻] and use pH = 14.00 − pOH at 298 K. Key: [OH⁻] = hydroxide ion concentration (mol dm⁻³); pOH has no unit; 14.00 = −log₁₀ Kw at 298 K.
  • Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶ at 298 K. Key: Kw = ionic product of water, whose units are (mol dm⁻³)², and it is fixed once the temperature is 298 K.
  • For a 0.050 mol dm⁻³ NaOH solution, [OH⁻] = 0.050, pOH = 1.30 and pH = 12.70.

Buffers

  • A buffer contains a weak acid and its conjugate base (for example ethanoic acid and sodium ethanoate). It resists large pH changes.
  • The pH of a buffer is given by pH = pKa + log([A⁻] / [HA]). When [A⁻] = [HA], pH = pKa. Key: [A⁻] = conjugate-base concentration (mol dm⁻³); [HA] = weak-acid concentration (mol dm⁻³); the log is base 10, so the ratio must be dimensionless.
  • Adding a small amount of strong acid is absorbed by the conjugate base, so the pH changes only slightly.

Titrations and indicators

  • Strong acid with strong base: the equivalence point is pH 7.
  • Weak acid with strong base: the equivalence point is above pH 7, so phenolphthalein (pH 8.3 to 10) is suitable.
  • Strong acid with weak base: the equivalence point is below pH 7, so methyl orange (pH 3.1 to 4.4) is suitable.
  • Choose an indicator whose colour change lies within the steep vertical section of the titration curve.

Exam tip: when pH is asked for a weak acid, calculate [H⁺] from Ka and the concentration before taking the logarithm.

title: Pressure & Density
content:
Pressure & Density

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): pressure & pressure differences in fluids, density review (Extended pressure-depth).

1. Pressure basics

p = F/A (Pa = N/m²). Increase F or decrease A to raise pressure; explain applications (snowshoes, knives, hydraulic press). Key: p = pressure (Pa = N m⁻²); F = force acting perpendicular to the surface (N); A = area over which it acts (m²).

2. Liquids

  • Pressure increases with depth: p = ρgh (Extended). Key: p = pressure due to the liquid (Pa); ρ = density of the liquid (kg m⁻³); g = gravitational field strength (10 N kg⁻¹); h = vertical depth below the surface (m) — the shape of the container does not appear, so it does not matter.
  • Same level, same liquid ⇒ same pressure (hydrostatic paradox).
  • Hydraulic systems transmit pressure — force multiplier: F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂.

3. Atmospheric pressure

~10⁵ Pa at sea level; demonstrated by collapsing can, mercury barometer 760 mmHg; decreases with altitude.

4. Density revisited

ρ = m/V; floating condition; upthrust = weight of displaced fluid (qualitative). Key: ρ = density (kg m⁻³); m = mass (kg); V = volume (m³); an object floats when its own density is less than the fluid's, because the upthrust then equals its weight before it is fully submerged.

5. Gas pressure (particle model)

Particles collide with walls → force per area. Volume ↓ at same T ⇒ pressure ↑ (more frequent collisions). Temperature ↑ ⇒ faster particles ⇒ more frequent, harder impacts.

title: Transport in Plants
content:
Transport in Plants

Cambridge IGCSE 0610 (2023–2025): 8.1 transport in xylem; 8.2 transpiration; 8.3 translocation.

1. Two tissues, two directions

Xylem carries water and mineral ions from the roots upwards. Its vessels are dead, hollow cells with lignified walls, which stop them collapsing and give support. Phloem carries sugars and amino acids from sources (leaves) to sinks (roots, fruits, growing tips); its cells are living, with sieve plates and companion cells.

2. Water uptake

Root hair cells increase the surface area for osmosis; water moves in because the root hair cell has a lower water potential than the soil solution. Mineral ions are taken up by active transport against their gradient.

3. Transpiration

Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from leaves, mostly through stomata. It is faster when the air is warm, dry and moving, and when light is bright (stomata open for photosynthesis). The cohesion-tension theory explains the pull: evaporation from mesophyll cells creates tension, water molecules cohere in a continuous column, and water is drawn up the xylem.

Wilting is a protective response: the leaves droop, reducing surface area and light exposure, so less water is lost. A potometer measures water uptake as a proxy for transpiration.

4. Translocation

Sugars made in the leaves are loaded into phloem, raising solute concentration; water follows by osmosis and the pressure pushes sap towards sinks. This is why bark damage (which removes phloem) starves the roots.

Exam focus

Q: Explain why a plant wilts on a hot, sunny day and why this helps.

A: Transpiration exceeds uptake, so cells lose turgor and the leaves droop. Drooping reduces the exposed surface area and light interception, so less water is lost and the plant is more likely to survive.

title: Earth & Space
content:
Earth & Space

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): Earth & Solar System; stars & the Universe (Extended).

1. Earth, Moon, Sun

Earth rotates 24 h (day/night), orbits 365¼ d (year + leap). Moon orbits Earth ~27.3 d; phases from viewing angle; lunar/solar eclipses when aligned. Seasons from axial tilt (23.5°), not distance.

2. Solar system

Planets (Mercury → Neptune), dwarf planets (Pluto), moons, asteroids, comets (eccentric orbits, tails away from Sun), natural satellites. Gravity keeps orbits; orbital speed & radius relate to the central mass.

3. Orbital motion

Orbital speed v = 2πr/T. T grows with r (Kepler trend). Comets speed up near the Sun (ellipse, Sun at focus). Key: v = orbital speed (m s⁻¹); r = orbital radius, measured from the centre of the body being circled (m); T = time for one full orbit (s); 2πr = the circumference travelled each period.

4. Stars (Extended)

Star formation: nebula → protostar (gravity, KE→thermal) → main sequence (hydrogen fusion: H→He, radiation pressure balances gravity) → red giant → white dwarf (Sun-mass) or supergiant → supernova → neutron star/black hole (massive stars). Elements heavier than iron form in supernovae.

5. Universe (Extended)

The Sun is one star in the Milky Way; the Milky Way is one of billions of galaxies. Redshift: receding galaxies show stretched wavelengths → the Universe is expanding → Big Bang model; CMB is the afterglow. Hubble: farther ⇒ faster recession.

6. Scales

light-year = distance light travels in a year (9.5 × 10¹⁵ m); astronomical unit = Earth–Sun distance (1.5 × 10¹¹ m).

title: Probability
content:
Statistics — Probability

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): probability scale, combined events, tree diagrams, conditional probability, relative frequency.

1. Basics

P(event) = favourable/total; 0 ≤ P ≤ 1; P(not A) = 1 − P(A). Probabilities of a complete set sum to 1 — use to find a missing probability. Key: P(event) = the probability of that event, a number between 0 and 1 with no unit; A = any event in the set being described.

2. Combined events

  • Independent: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
  • Mutually exclusive: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).
  • With replacement ⇒ independent; without replacement ⇒ denominators shrink.

Example: bag 4 red, 6 blue; two draws without replacement: P(both red) = 4/10 × 3/9 = 2/15.

3. Tree diagrams

Multiply along branches; add between outcome paths. Label end products like 4/10 × 6/9 = 4/15.

4. Conditional probability

P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). From tree diagrams it is the "given the first branch happened" re-weighting. Key: P(A|B) = the probability of A once B is known to have happened; P(A ∩ B) = the probability that both occur; P(B) = the probability of the given event, which must not be zero.

5. Relative frequency (experimental)

Relative frequency = successes ÷ trials. More trials → closer to theoretical probability; compare with expected counts (n × P).

Exam tips: always reduce fractions for final answers; in tree diagrams write the multiplication line before the product — that is where the marks are.

title: Coordinate Geometry
content:
Coordinate Geometry

Gradients and Equations of Lines

Gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). From ax + by + c = 0, the gradient is −a/b. Key: m = gradient, the change in y per unit x; (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) = two points on the line; a, b and c = the coefficients of the line's equation (no units, since they only set the line's position).

Point-slope form: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).

Example: through (4, 3) with m = −1/2: y − 3 = −(x − 4)/2, i.e. y = −x/2 + 5.

Parallel and Perpendicular

  • Parallel lines: equal gradients.
  • Perpendicular lines: m₁m₂ = −1 (gradients are negative reciprocals).

Example: perpendicular to y = 2x + 1 has gradient −1/2.

Midpoint and Distance

Midpoint of (x₁, y₁), (x₂, y₂): ((x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2).

Distance: √((x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)²). The line from (0,0) to (3,4) has length 5 — recognise 3-4-5 triangles.

Intersections and Bisectors
