Intersections: solve the equations simultaneously. The perpendicular bisector of AB passes through the midpoint of AB with gradient −1/m(AB) — equate distances PA = PB for the locus method. Key: m(AB) = the gradient of the line AB; P = a general point of the locus; PA and PB = distances from P to each endpoint, so they share the unit of the axes.

Exam tips: rationalise gradients as fractions; check perpendicularity by multiplying gradients to get −1.

title: Networks and the Internet
content:
Networks and the Internet

The TCP/IP Stack

Four layers: Application (HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS), Transport (TCP reliable, connection-oriented with sequence numbers and acknowledgements; UDP fast, connectionless), Internet (IP addressing and routing), Link (physical delivery on the local network). Layering separates concerns so each layer can change independently.

Switching

  • Circuit switching: a dedicated path is held for the call (traditional telephone) — wasteful if idle.
  • Packet switching: data split into packets routed independently; each carries source/destination addresses and a sequence number, reassembled at the destination. Efficient and fault-tolerant; packets may arrive out of order (TCP fixes ordering).

Addressing and Subnetting

IPv4 addresses are 32 bits, written dotted decimal, split into network + host portions by the subnet mask. ANDing an IP with the mask yields the network ID. 192.168.4.0/26 means the first 26 bits are network, leaving 6 host bits: 64 addresses, 62 usable. NAT maps private addresses to one public IP.

Models and Protection

Client-server centralises services (web, email, files); peer-to-peer shares directly (torrents, small LANs). Firewalls filter traffic by rules; proxy servers sit between clients and the internet, caching and filtering; ports identify services (80/443 web, 25 SMTP).

Exam tips: compute usable hosts from a given prefix; trace a packet through the four layers naming one protocol per layer; explain one advantage of packet over circuit switching.

title: Hypothesis Testing
content:
Hypothesis Testing

The Framework

The null hypothesis H₀ is the default claim (no change, p = p₀). The alternative H₁ is what a suspicious observation suggests (p > p₀, p < p₀, or p ≠ p₀). The significance level α is the probability of rejecting a true H₀ — the false-alarm rate, usually 5% or 1%. Key: p = the true success probability being tested; p₀ = the value H₀ pins it to (a number from 0 to 1); α = significance level, also a probability — 5% is written 0.05, never 5.

Test for a Binomial Proportion

With X ~ B(n, p₀) under H₀, compute the probability of results at least as extreme as the observed count in the direction of H₁.

Example: H₀: p = 0.3 against H₁: p > 0.3, observed 10 successes in n = 20. Compute P(X ≥ 10) under B(20, 0.3). If that tail probability is below α, reject H₀.

One-Tailed vs Two-Tailed

One-tailed tests take the whole α in one direction. Two-tailed tests split α across both tails: compare against α/2 on each side, or equivalently check whether the observation falls in the extreme 2.5% (for α = 5%). Choose the tails from the wording of H₁, not from the data.

Critical Regions

The critical region is the set of values of the test statistic that would lead to rejection. Its boundary is the critical value. For B(20, 0.3) at the 5% level with H₁: p > 0.3, find the smallest k with P(X ≥ k) < 0.05 — that k opens the critical region.

Conclusions in Context

Never just say "reject H₀". Conclude in the language of the problem: "there is sufficient evidence at the 5% level that the proportion has increased". State the significance level, the direction, and the real-world quantity.

Exam tips: define H₀ and H₁ with symbols AND words. Verify which tail the observation sits in before computing. If the observed value lies in the critical region, evidence supports H₁; otherwise there is insufficient evidence — never "prove H₀ true".

title: Respiration
content:
Respiration

Cambridge IGCSE 0610 (2023–2025): 12.1 respiration; 12.2 aerobic respiration; 12.3 anaerobic respiration.

1. Respiration is not breathing

Respiration is the chemical release of energy from food in every living cell. Breathing is the ventilation that supplies oxygen and removes carbon dioxide. Energy released by respiration powers muscle contraction, growth, active transport and maintaining body temperature.

2. Aerobic respiration

C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O, releasing about 38 ATP per glucose. It happens mainly in the mitochondria, which is why active cells (muscle, liver) have many of them. Glucose is the preferred substrate; fat and protein can also be respired.

3. Anaerobic respiration

Without oxygen, glucose is partly broken down. In human muscle: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₃H₆O₃ (lactic acid), releasing about 2 ATP. Lactic acid builds up and causes fatigue; oxygen is later used to break it down, and the extra oxygen consumed is the oxygen debt. In yeast: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂, the basis of brewing and bread-making.

4. Demonstrating it

Limewater turns milky with carbon dioxide (test with hydrogencarbonate indicator: yellow at high CO₂). Yeast in warm glucose solution with a layer of oil respires anaerobically; a thermometer shows heat, and the gas given off turns limewater milky. Germinating seeds show the same, and their temperature rise is measurable in a vacuum flask.

Exam focus

Q: Explain the benefit of anaerobic respiration to a sprinter.

A: It releases a small amount of ATP without oxygen, so muscles can keep contracting briefly after oxygen supply is exhausted, which sustains the sprint.

title: Thermal Physics
content:
Thermal Physics

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): kinetic particle model; thermal expansion; specific heat capacity; melting/boiling; conduction, convection, radiation.

1. Kinetic model

Solid: fixed positions, vibrate — fixed shape/volume. Liquid: move around, touching — fixed volume, flows. Gas: far apart, fast random motion — fills container. Brownian motion evidences random molecular motion.

2. Gas pressure and temperature

Pressure from wall collisions. Heating at fixed volume → faster particles → more frequent, harder collisions → higher pressure.

3. Thermal expansion

Heating → particles vibrate more → solids expand slightly (gases expand most). Applications: bimetallic strip (fire alarm/thermostat), gaps in bridges/rails; the liquid-in-glass thermometer.

4. Specific heat capacity

c = ΔE/(mΔθ). Heating: ΔE = mcΔθ. Key: ΔE = energy supplied (J); m = mass (kg); c = specific heat capacity (J kg⁻¹ °C⁻¹); Δθ = temperature rise (°C or K — a difference is the same in both).

Example: 2 kg water (c = 4200), 20→80 °C: ΔE = 2×4200×60 = 504 kJ.

High c of water → coolant; temperature rise measured with known heater power P in time t: c = Pt/(mΔθ). Key: P = heater power (W = J s⁻¹); t = heating time (s), so Pt is the energy supplied (J); m = mass of the sample (kg); Δθ = its temperature rise (°C).

5. State changes

Melting/boiling at fixed temperature despite heating (energy breaks bonds, not temperature). Condensation/ freezing release energy. Impurities raise melting point of mixtures/lower freezing; boiling needs nucleation.

6. Transfer: conduction, convection, radiation

  • Conduction: mainly metals (delocalised electrons + lattice vibration); non-metals poor; insulators trap air.
  • Convection: hot fluid expands, density falls, rises; denser cool fluid sinks — currents.
  • Radiation: infrared EM waves; no medium; matte black best absorber/emitter, shiny silver worst.

Applications: vacuum flask, house insulation, car radiators, solar heating panels.

title: Forces & Motion
content:
Forces & Motion

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): motion (speed, acceleration, graphs); mass & weight; density link; force basics (F = ma, resultant); momentum (Extended); turning effects; equilibrium.

1. Kinematics

  • Speed = distance/time; average speed = (u + v)/2 for uniform acceleration. Key: u = initial speed (m s⁻¹); v = final speed (m s⁻¹); time in s, distance in m — the averaging formula holds only when the acceleration is constant.
  • Acceleration a = (v − u)/t. Key: a = acceleration (m s⁻²); v = final velocity; u = initial velocity (both m s⁻¹); t = time for the change (s) — a negative answer means deceleration, so keep the sign.
  • SUVAT (uniform a): v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as. Key: s = displacement (m); u = initial velocity; v = final velocity (m s⁻¹); a = acceleration (m s⁻²); t = time (s) — each equation omits one of these, which is how you choose it.

2. Motion graphs

  • Distance–time: gradient = speed.
  • Speed–time: gradient = acceleration; area = distance. Negative gradient = deceleration.
  • Free fall 1: g ≈ 9.8 m/s² (use 10) — v = gt from rest.

3. Mass, weight, density

W = mg (g ≈ 10 N/kg). Weight acts at the centre of mass; mass is invariant. Density ρ = m/V. Key: W = weight (N); m = mass (kg); g = gravitational field strength (N kg⁻¹); ρ = density (kg m⁻³); V = volume (m³).

4. Newton's laws and resultant force

  • Resultant: colinear addition/subtraction; perpendicular by Pythagoras.
  • F = ma. Terminal velocity: drag grows with speed until it balances weight. Key: F = resultant force (N); m = mass (kg); a = acceleration (m s⁻²) — F is the sum of all forces, not any single one, and at terminal velocity F = 0 so a = 0.
  • Third law pairs: equal magnitude, opposite direction, different bodies.

5. Momentum (Extended)

p = mv; impulse Ft = Δ(mv); conservation: Σpbefore = Σpafter (explosions, collisions). Key: p = momentum (kg m s⁻¹); m = mass (kg); v = velocity (m s⁻¹, sign matters); F = force (N); t = time the force acts (s); Δ means "change in"; Σ means "sum of" over every object.

Example: 2 kg at 3 m/s hits 1 kg at rest, combined 1 m/s: 6 = 3v ⇒ v = 2 m/s.

6. Moments and equilibrium

  • Moment = F × perpendicular distance from pivot. Key: moment = turning effect (N m); F = force (N); the distance is measured perpendicular to the force's line of action, from the pivot — not along the lever.
  • Principle of moments: Σclockwise = Σanticlockwise.
  • Equilibrium: resultant force = 0 and resultant moment = 0.

Example: 100 N at 0.3 m balances F at 0.5 m: F = 60 N.

title: Biological Molecules
content:
Biological Molecules

Cambridge IGCSE 0610 (2023–2025): 4.1 carbohydrates; 4.2 fats (lipids); 4.3 proteins; 4.4 tests for food substances.

1. The three large groups

MoleculeMade ofFunctionTest
carbohydrateC, H, Oenergy, structurestarch: iodine
proteinC, H, O, Ngrowth and repair, enzymesBiuret
lipidC, H, Oenergy store, insulation, membranesethanol emulsion

Starch is a storage polysaccharide; glycogen stores energy in animals; cellulose builds plant cell walls from long unbranched chains. Proteins are chains of amino acids; lipids are glycerol with three fatty acids.

2. The food tests

  • Starch: add iodine solution — blue-black is positive.
  • Reducing sugar: add Benedict's solution and heat in a water bath — green to brick-red indicates the amount.
  • Protein: add Biuret reagent — lilac/purple is positive.
  • Lipid: add ethanol then water — a cloudy white emulsion forms.
  • Vitamin C: DCPIP solution is decolourised by vitamin C.

3. Water, vitamins and minerals

Water is the solvent for all cell chemistry and a reactant in hydrolysis. Vitamin C prevents scurvy and is found in citrus; vitamin D is needed for calcium absorption and is made in skin in sunlight. Calcium strengthens bones and teeth; iron is needed for haemoglobin; fibre (cellulose) adds bulk so the gut muscles can push food along.

Exam focus

Q: A student tests a food and obtains a lilac colour with Biuret reagent and a brick-red precipitate with Benedict's. What does this show?

A: The food contains protein (lilac) and a reducing sugar such as glucose (brick-red), so it could be, for example, milk.

title: Ratio, Rate and Proportion
content:
Number — Ratio, Rate and Proportion

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): ratio notation, sharing, direct & inverse proportion (including squares/cubes), unit rates.

1. Simplifying and sharing ratios

  • Scale both parts by the same factor: 250 g : 0.4 kg = 250 : 400 = 5 : 8.
  • Share $200 in 3 : 5 → 8 parts → $75 : $125.
  • Part–whole: 3 : 5 ⇒ 3/8 of the total. Given one share, find others by scaling.

Example: A : B = 3 : 4 and B : C = 2 : 5 ⇒ A : B : C = 3 : 4 : 10 (make B equal: ×2).

2. Direct proportion

y = kx. Best method: find the unit value, then multiply. Key: y = the quantity that grows; x = the quantity it grows with; k = the constant of proportionality, found from any one matching pair of values and carrying y's unit per unit of x.

Example: 5 pens cost $3.25 → 1 pen $0.65 → 8 pens $5.20.

Squared/cubed proportion: y ∝ x². y = 54 when x = 3 ⇒ k = 6 ⇒ y = 6x²; at x = 5, y = 150.

3. Inverse proportion

y = k/x (product constant). 4 workers 6 days ⇒ 24 worker-days ⇒ 8 workers take 3 days. Square-law: y ∝ 1/x². Key: y and x = the two inversely related quantities; k = the fixed product, so x × y never changes; under a square law it is y × x² that stays constant.

4. Rates

Unit rates (per item, per litre), exchange rates (draw the arrow to the target currency), best buys (price per unit, careful with multi-packs). Speed/density/pressure are compound-measure rates (Mensuration).

Exam tips: write the proportional equation with k before substituting; check proportion type — "more workers, fewer days" = inverse.

title: Trigonometry
content:
Trigonometry

Exact Values
