Key Identities

  • sin²θ + cos²θ = 1
  • tan θ = sin θ / cos θ
  • sec²θ = 1 + tan²θ

Solving Equations

Use the symmetry of the graphs. For sin x = 1/2 in 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π: the acute answer is π/6, and the second solution is π − π/6 = 5π/6.

For cos x = 0.5 in 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°: x = 60° and 360° − 60° = 300°.

Always check the required interval and give every solution.

Graphs and Transformations

y = a sin(bx) + c has amplitude a, period 2π/b, and vertical shift c. Key: a = amplitude, in the unit of y (measure it peak-to-midline and take the positive value); b = the angular multiplier, which shortens the period to 2π/b in radians (360°/b in degrees); c = the vertical shift, in the unit of y.

Example: y = 3 sin(2x) has amplitude 3 and period π.

Using Identities

If sin x = 0.6 with x acute, then cos x = √(1 − 0.36) = 0.8 (positive in the first quadrant).

Exam tips: write the general second solution using graph symmetry rather than memorising CAST blindly; square both sides only with care, as it can add false solutions.

title: Waves
content:
Waves

Basics

A wave transfers energy without net transfer of matter.

  • Transverse: oscillation ⊥ propagation (EM waves, water surface)
  • Longitudinal: oscillation ∥ propagation (sound)

The Wave Equation

v = fλ. Frequency f is set by the source; speed v by the medium. Key: v = wave speed (m s⁻¹); f = frequency (Hz); λ = wavelength (m) — a wave crossing into another medium keeps f and changes v, so λ must change with it.

Example: sound at 340 m s⁻¹, f = 512 Hz: λ = 340/512 ≈ 0.66 m.

Intensity

I = P/A. Intensity ∝ amplitude² — doubling the amplitude quadruples the intensity. Key: I = intensity (W m⁻²); P = power carried by the wave (W); A = area the wave passes through (m²), taken perpendicular to the direction of travel.

Doppler Effect

Observed frequency changes with relative motion: f′ = f(v ± v_o)/(v ∓ v_s). Approaching sources sound higher.

Example: an ambulance passing you: high pitch approaching, low pitch receding.

EM Spectrum

Radio → micro → IR → visible (400–700 nm) → UV → X-ray → gamma. All travel at c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ in vacuum.

Polarization

Only transverse waves can be polarised — proof that light is transverse. Malus' law: I = I₀ cos²θ between polariser axes. Key: I = transmitted intensity (W m⁻²); I₀ = intensity after the first polariser; θ = angle between the two polarising axes (°) — at 90° nothing gets through, which is how glare is cut.

Exam tips: distinguish wave speed (set by medium) from frequency (set by source); in Doppler problems, signs depend on approach or recession.

title: Transport in Animals
content:
Transport in Animals

Cambridge IGCSE 0610 (2023–2025): 9.1 transport systems; 9.2 the heart; 9.3 blood vessels; 9.4 blood.

1. Why a transport system

A large, active organism cannot rely on diffusion: the distance is too great and the demand too high. Blood carries oxygen, nutrients, hormones, antibodies and heat, and removes carbon dioxide and urea. Mammals have a double circulation: blood passes the heart twice per circuit, so the lungs receive low-pressure blood and the body receives high-pressure blood.

2. The heart

Right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta. The left ventricle wall is thickest because it pumps blood round the whole body. Valves prevent backflow: the tricuspid and bicuspid valves close when the ventricles contract, and the semilunar valves close when they relax.

3. Blood vessels

VesselWallLumenRole
arterythick, elastic, muscularnarrowcarries blood away, withstands pressure
veinthinnerwide, with valvesreturns blood at low pressure
capillaryone cell thickvery narrowexchange with tissues

4. Blood and its parts

Plasma carries dissolved substances; red cells carry oxygen as oxyhaemoglobin (no nucleus, biconcave, packed with haemoglobin); white cells defend against pathogens; platelets clot blood. Coronary heart disease is caused by fatty deposits narrowing the coronary arteries; risk factors include smoking, high saturated fat, obesity, inactivity and family history.

Exam focus

Q: Explain why the wall of the left ventricle is thicker than that of the right.

A: The left ventricle pumps blood at higher pressure around the whole body, whereas the right ventricle pumps only to the lungs, so it needs less muscle.

title: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages
content:
Number — Fractions, Decimals and Percentages

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): conversions between fractions, decimals and percentages; percentage change; reverse percentages; compound change.

1. Conversions

Fraction → decimal by division; decimal → percentage ×100. Recurring decimals: let x = 0.7̄, then 10x − x = 7 ⇒ x = 7/9.

Compare fractions by common denominator or by converting to decimals.

2. Operating on fractions

  • Add/subtract: common denominator. 2/3 + 1/4 = 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12.
  • Multiply: top×top, bottom×bottom. Divide: flip and multiply — 2/3 ÷ 4/5 = 2/3 × 5/4 = 5/6.
  • Of: 3/5 of 45 = 27.

3. Percentage change

change ÷ original × 100. Increase $80 by 15%: 80 × 1.15 = $92.

4. Reverse percentages

Original = new ÷ multiplier. "After a 20% increase a coat is $72" → 72 ÷ 1.2 = $60. "After 12% discount a phone is $440" → 440 ÷ 0.88 = $500.

5. Compound change

Multiplierⁿ. Simple interest I = Prt/100 vs compound P(1 + r/100)ⁿ. Key: I = simple interest earned (in the money unit); P = principal, the starting amount; r = the annual rate in per cent; t = time in years; n = the number of compounding periods.

Example: $800 at 3% for 4 years → 800 × 1.03⁴ = $900.41. Successive +10% then −10% ⇒ ×0.99 (net 1% decrease).

Exam tips: identify "increase TO" vs "increase BY"; for reverse questions divide, never subtract the percentage; quote money to 2 d.p.

title: Complex Numbers
content:
Complex Numbers

Basics

i² = −1. A complex number z = a + bi has real part a and imaginary part b. Two numbers are equal iff both parts match. Key: z = the complex number; a = Re(z), the real part; b = Im(z), the imaginary part — both are ordinary real numbers; i = √−1, the unit that cannot be plotted on the real axis.

Arithmetic: add/subtract parts; multiply with brackets and replace i² with −1.

Example: (2 + 3i)(1 − i) = 2 − 2i + 3i − 3i² = 5 + i.

Conjugates

z̄ = a − bi. zz̄ = a² + b² (real). Dividing: multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate.

Example: 1/(3 − i) × (3 + i)/(3 + i) = (3 + i)/10.

Argand Diagram

Plot z as the point (a, b). |z| = √(a² + b²) is the modulus (distance from origin); arg z = tan⁻¹(b/a) is the argument (angle). Multiply two numbers: moduli multiply, arguments add. Key: a and b = the coordinates of z on the Argand diagram (the modulus takes their unit, if any); arg z = the angle from the positive real axis, in radians or degrees as the question asks.

Modulus–Argument Form

z = r(cos θ + i sin θ), r = |z|, θ = arg z. Useful for powers and roots. Key: r = modulus of z, the distance from the origin; θ = argument of z, the angle it makes with the real axis; cos θ and sin θ are dimensionless, so r carries the unit.

de Moivre and Roots

[r(cos θ + i sin θ)]ⁿ = rⁿ(cos nθ + i sin nθ).

Example: (1 + i)⁸: |1 + i| = √2, arg = π/4, so z⁸ = (√2)⁸ cis 2π = 16.

An nth root gives n evenly spaced solutions, 2π/n apart on a circle of radius r^(1/n).

Exam tips: always give arguments in the required interval; when solving equations, remember complex roots come in conjugate pairs for real polynomials.

title: Redox Equilibria
content:
Redox Equilibria

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH15, Topic 16. Redox reactions transfer electrons. Standard electrode potentials let you predict whether a reaction is feasible and quantify the reducing and oxidising power of species.

Oxidation and reduction

  • Oxidation is loss of electrons and an increase in oxidation state. Reduction is gain of electrons and a decrease in oxidation state.
  • The reducing agent is oxidised; the oxidising agent is reduced.

Standard electrode potentials

  • Each half-cell has a standard electrode potential, E⁰, measured under standard conditions: 298 K, 1.0 mol dm⁻³ solutions and 100 kPa for gases.
  • E⁰ is measured against the standard hydrogen electrode, which is defined as 0 V.
  • A more positive E⁰ means a stronger oxidising agent on the left of the half-equation. A more negative E⁰ means a stronger reducing agent.

Predicting feasibility

  • E⁰cell = E⁰(reduction) − E⁰(oxidation). A positive E⁰cell means the reaction is feasible under standard conditions. Key: E⁰ = standard electrode potential (V), measured at 298 K, 100 kPa and 1.00 mol dm⁻³.
  • ΔG = −nFE. A negative ΔG (positive E⁰cell) means the reaction is spontaneous. Key: ΔG = standard Gibbs free energy change (J mol⁻¹); n = moles of electrons transferred (mol); F = Faraday constant (96 500 C mol⁻¹); E = cell e.m.f. (V).

Redox titrations

  • Manganate(VII) is its own indicator: it is purple in solution and becomes colourless at the end point when Mn²⁺ forms.
  • Acidified dichromate(VI) turns from orange to green as Cr³⁺ forms. Iodine and thiosulfate use starch, which turns blue-black with iodine and loses that colour at the end point.

Exam tip: write the ion-electron half-equations first, balance the electrons, then combine them. The ratio of electrons sets the mole ratio in titration calculations.

title: Variation and Selection
content:
Variation and Selection

Cambridge IGCSE 0610 (2023–2025): 18.1 variation; 18.2 adaptive features; 18.3 selection.

1. Types of variation

Continuous variation gives a range of values (height, mass) and is usually affected by many genes plus the environment. Discontinuous variation puts individuals into distinct groups (blood group, tongue rolling) and is usually controlled by one or a few genes. Plotting continuous data gives a normal curve; discontinuous data gives separate bars.

2. Causes

Variation comes from genes (meiosis creates new combinations of alleles; mutation makes new alleles) and from the environment (diet, exercise, light). Identical twins show how much of a characteristic is environmental.

3. Natural selection

Organisms produce more offspring than survive; there is variation; some variants are better adapted; those individuals survive and reproduce, passing their alleles on; the frequency of the advantageous allele rises. This is why bacteria become resistant to antibiotics and why insects become resistant to pesticides.

Adaptive features can be structural (long roots), behavioural (migration) or physiological (water conservation).

4. Artificial selection

Humans choose individuals with desirable features to breed. It has produced high-yield crops, dairy cattle and breeds of dog. It reduces genetic diversity and can spread inherited defects, because the population is narrowed deliberately.

Exam focus

Q: Explain how a population of bacteria can become resistant to an antibiotic.

A: A random mutation gives some bacteria resistance; the antibiotic kills the non-resistant ones; the resistant bacteria survive, reproduce and pass on the resistance allele, so the proportion resistant rises.

title: Superposition
content:
Superposition

The Principle of Superposition

When waves meet, displacements add. In phase → constructive (big amplitude); antiphase → destructive (cancellation).

Coherence and Path Difference

Two sources are coherent if they share frequency and constant phase difference. Maxima occur where path difference = nλ; minima where it = (n + ½)λ. Key: n = any whole number (0, 1, 2 …), the order of the fringe; λ = wavelength (m); path difference = the extra distance one wave travels (m) — a whole number of wavelengths arrives in phase.

Double-Slit (Young)

Fringe spacing x = λD/a (D = slit–screen distance, a = slit separation). Key: x = distance between adjacent bright fringes (m); λ = wavelength (m); D = distance from the slits to the screen (m); a = separation of the two slits (m) — move the screen further away and the fringes spread out.

Example: λ = 600 nm, D = 2 m, a = 0.5 mm: x = 2.4 mm.

Red light gives wider fringes than blue; smaller slit separation also widens fringes.

Diffraction Grating

d sin θ = nθth order maximum. More slits → sharper, brighter maxima. The number of visible orders is the largest n with sin θ ≤ 1.

Example: 600 lines/mm → d = 1.67 μm; for 500 nm light, n_max = 3.

Stationary Waves

Two identical waves travelling opposite directions (e.g. wave + reflection) create nodes (no movement) and antinodes (max movement), spaced λ/2 apart. Strings and closed pipes resonate at f₁ = v/2L (fundamental) and harmonics.

Exam tips: always compute d from 'lines per mm' first; state 'path difference = nλ' explicitly in explain-the-fringe questions.

title: Electricity: D.C. Circuits
content:
Electricity: D.C. Circuits

Current and Charge

I = Q/t — charge per second, in amperes. Conventional current flows + to − (electrons drift the other way). Key: I = current (A); Q = charge passing a point (C); t = time (s) — one ampere is one coulomb per second.

I = nAvq links microscopic drift to macroscopic current (n = carrier density).

Voltage and Power

  • V = W/Q (joules per coulomb) Key: V = potential difference across the component (V); W = work done on the charge, i.e. energy transferred (J); Q = charge moved (C).
  • P = VI = I²R = V²/R Key: P = power dissipated (W); V = potential difference across the component (V); I = current through it (A); R = its resistance (Ω) — use V²/R when the voltage is fixed and I²R when the current is.

Resistance and Resistivity

R = V/I; R = ρL/A. Resistivity ρ is a material property (Ω m). Metals' resistance rises with temperature; thermistors' falls (NTC). Key: R = resistance (Ω); V = potential difference (V); I = current (A); ρ = resistivity (Ω m), a property of the material alone; L = length of the conductor (m); A = its cross-sectional area (m²).

Example: a wire 2 m long, 0.5 mm² cross-section, ρ = 5 × 10⁻⁷: R = 2 Ω.

Series and Parallel

  • Series: same current, R_total = R₁ + R₂ + …
  • Parallel: same voltage, 1/R_total = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + …

EMF and Internal Resistance

ε = I(R + r) — some voltage is 'lost' inside the battery. Terminal voltage V = ε − Ir drops as load current rises. Key: ε = electromotive force of the source (V); I = current (A); R = external resistance (Ω); r = internal resistance (Ω); V = terminal p.d. across the external circuit (V).

Potential Dividers

V_out = V_in × R₂/(R₁ + R₂). Used with LDRs/thermistors to make sensor circuits. Key: V_in = supply p.d. (V); V_out = p.d. across R₂ only (V); R₁ and R₂ = the two resistors of the potential divider (Ω) — swapping which one is the sensor inverts the response.

Exam tips: redraw messy networks with clean junctions; always account for internal resistance in 'maximum power' questions.

title: Human Influences on Ecosystems
content:
Human Influences on Ecosystems

Cambridge IGCSE 0610 (2023–2025): 20.1 food supply; 20.2 habitat destruction; 20.3 pollution; 20.4 conservation.

1. Feeding a growing population

Intensive farming raises yield with fertilisers, pesticides, irrigation and monoculture, but can pollute water, reduce soil quality and lower biodiversity. Organic farming uses manure and biological control instead. Genetically modified crops can resist pests or drought, with the risk of genes spreading to wild relatives.

2. Habitat destruction

Deforestation removes habitats, causes soil erosion and increases atmospheric CO₂; draining wetlands and building on land do the same. Biodiversity falls and species may become extinct. Tropical rainforests matter globally because they store carbon and hold most terrestrial species.

3. Pollution

  • Water: sewage and fertiliser cause eutrophication — algae bloom, die, decompose, and oxygen is used up so fish die.
  • Air: sulfur dioxide from fossil fuels causes acid rain; CO₂ and methane enhance the greenhouse effect; CFCs damaged the ozone layer.
  • Land: non-biodegradable plastics and toxic waste persist and enter food chains.

4. Conservation

Conservation protects habitats and species: national parks, seed banks, captive breeding, fishing quotas and reforestation. Sustainable use means taking resources at a rate the ecosystem can replace. Education and legislation are as important as biology, because most causes are economic.

Exam focus

Q: Describe how fertiliser washing into a lake can kill fish.

A: Nitrates cause algae to grow rapidly; they die and are decomposed by bacteria that use up dissolved oxygen, so fish cannot respire and suffocate.

title: Descriptive Writing
content:
Descriptive writing succeeds when the reader can see, hear, smell or feel the scene. It is built from precise detail, controlled sentence rhythm and a clear sense of focus.

Sensory detail

Use all five senses where they fit, not only sight. Specific nouns and verbs do more work than general adjectives.

Precision

  • Replace weak words such as "nice" or "went" with exact ones: "gleaming", "stumbled".
  • Use concrete nouns: "rust-flecked railings" rather than "old fence".
  • Choose one striking image and develop it, rather than listing many.

Show, do not tell

Show a feeling through action and detail rather than naming it. "She was furious" tells the reader. "Her jaw tightened and she slammed the cupboard door" shows it.

Sentence variety

Varying sentence length controls pace. Long sentences can build a scene slowly, and short ones can cut the mood or create a jolt. Vary your openings too, rather than starting every sentence with the subject.

Structure

Organise the piece around a clear focus. Options include:

  • A close-up that moves outward, from a detail to the wider scene.
  • A changing viewpoint, following a person through a place.
  • A fixed point in time that shows change, such as dawn to dusk.

End with an image or a reflection that returns to your focus. Avoid ending on a plain statement of fact.

title: Integration II
content:
Integration II

Standard Integrals

  • ∫ sin x dx = −cos x + c
  • ∫ cos x dx = sin x + c
  • ∫ e^x dx = e^x + c
  • ∫ 1/x dx = ln|x| + c Key: for every standard result above: c = the constant of integration, in the same unit as the antiderivative; the absolute value keeps the logarithm defined for negative x; each answer differentiates straight back to the integrand.
  • ∫ sec²x dx = tan x + c

With linear arguments: ∫ e^(3x) dx = e^(3x)/3 + c; ∫ cos 2x dx = sin 2x/2 + c.

Substitution

Reverse of the chain rule. For ∫ 2x e^(x²) dx, let u = x²: du = 2x dx, so the integral is ∫ e^u du = e^(x²) + c.

Integration by Parts

∫ u (dv/dx) dx = uv − ∫ v (du/dx) dx. Choose u to be the part that simplifies when differentiated (LIATE: logs, inverse trig, algebraic, trig, exponential). Key: u = the factor you differentiate (first in the LIATE order); v = the factor you integrate; both are functions of x — for a definite integral, evaluate uv between the same limits and the constants cancel.

Example: ∫ x e^x dx = x e^x − ∫ e^x dx = x e^x − e^x + c.

Partial Fractions

Break rational functions into pieces like ∫ 1/(x+1) dx = ln|x + 1| + c.

Example: ∫ 4x/(x² − 1) dx = ∫ [2/(x − 1) + 2/(x + 1)] dx = 2 ln|x − 1| + 2 ln|x + 1| + c.

Exam tips: definite integrals: substitute limits into the transformed variable directly; for by-parts integrals like ∫ ln x dx, take u = ln x, dv/dx = 1.

title: Angles and Polygons
content:
Geometry — Angles and Polygons

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): angle facts, parallel lines, polygon angles, circle theorems (Extended).

1. Core angle facts

  • Line 180°; point 360°; vertically opposite equal.
  • Parallel lines: corresponding (F), alternate (Z), co-interior (C, sum 180°).
  • Triangle 180°; isosceles/equilateral properties; exterior angle = sum of two remote interior angles.

2. Polygons

Interior angle sum = (n − 2) × 180°. Regular polygon: exterior = 360° ÷ n; interior = 180° − exterior. Key: n = the number of sides (a count); every result is an angle in degrees.

Example: regular octagon: exterior 45°, interior 135°.

3. Circle theorems (Extended)

  1. Angle at centre = 2 × angle at circumference (same arc).
  2. Angle in a semicircle = 90°.
  3. Angles in the same segment are equal.
  4. Cyclic quadrilateral: opposite angles sum to 180°.
  5. Tangent ⊥ radius; two tangents from an external point are equal.
  6. Alternate segment theorem.

Quote the reason in brackets every time: "∠ACB = 62° (angles in same segment)".

4. Algebra with angles

Set up equations from the theorem: cyclic quad (2x + 10) + (3x − 5) = 180 ⇒ x = 35.

Exam tips: mark every found angle on the diagram immediately; use radii to create isosceles triangles; never leave a theorem unquoted.

title: Networking & Communication
content:
Networking & Communication

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): transmission modes, serial/parallel, packet switching, protocols, LAN/WAN, hardware, security layers.

1. Transmission basics

  • Serial: one bit at a time — reliable over distance, cheaper cable.
  • Parallel: several bits at once — faster over short runs; skew/crosstalk limit distance.
  • Simplex / half-duplex / full-duplex direction; bandwidth (bits/s) vs bit rate.

2. Packets

Header (sender/receiver addresses, sequence number) + payload + trailer (checksum). Packet switching: routes vary, packets reassembled at destination; checksum failure → re-request. Benefits: robustness, shared lines; delays/reassembly overhead.

3. Protocols

TCP/IP stack layers (application, transport, network, link). HTTP/HTTPS (TLS encryption), FTP (with login + commands), email: SMTP send, POP3/IMAP retrieve. Bluetooth/Wi-Fi for WPAN/WLAN.

4. Network types & hardware

LAN (site) vs WAN (internet). Router (joins networks, IP), switch (MAC frames within LAN), gateway (protocol translation), NIC, WAP. MAC address (burned-in, layer 2) vs IP address (assigned, layer 3).

5. Security in transmission

Encryption scrambles plaintext → ciphertext (key needed); HTTPS = HTTP over TLS; firewall packet filtering by port/IP; authentication (user+pass, 2FA); access levels.

Exam tips: explain why skew limits parallel over distance; compare MAC vs IP in a table; protocol questions want "rules for communication", not acronyms alone.

title: Organic Synthesis
content:
Organic Synthesis

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH15, Topic 20. Organic synthesis plans a route from a starting material to a target molecule. You need to choose reagents and conditions, track functional groups and calculate the overall yield.

Planning a route

  • Retrosynthesis works backwards from the target: identify the functional group, then find a precursor that converts into it in one step.
  • Each step should be a known functional group interconversion with suitable reagents and conditions.
  • Carbon chain length can be increased with KCN, which turns a haloalkane into a nitrile. The nitrile can then be hydrolysed to a carboxylic acid or reduced to an amine.

Key interconversions

  • Primary alcohol to aldehyde: distillation with acidified dichromate(VI), so the aldehyde is removed before it oxidises further.
  • Primary alcohol to carboxylic acid: reflux with excess acidified dichromate(VI).
  • Aldehyde or ketone to alcohol: NaBH₄ (or LiAlH₄ for carboxylic acids and nitriles).
  • Alkene to haloalkane: addition of HBr. Alkene to alcohol: steam with an acid catalyst.
  • Nitrobenzene to phenylamine: reduction with Sn and concentrated HCl. Nitration of benzene is the first step of a route to phenylamine.

Yield calculations

  • Percentage yield = actual mass ÷ theoretical mass × 100. Key: both masses are in the same unit (g), so the percentage has no unit; the theoretical mass comes from the limiting reagent.
  • Overall yield for a multi-step route is the product of the individual step yields. Two steps at 80% and 70% give 0.80 × 0.70 = 0.56, or 56% overall.
  • Atom economy measures the proportion of reactant atoms that end up in the desired product: (molar mass of desired product ÷ sum of molar masses of all products) × 100.

Exam tip: state the reagent, the condition (reflux, distillation, heat under pressure) and the product of each step. Marks are often given for the condition, not just the reagent.

title: Articles and Determiners
content:
Articles (a, an, the) and determiners (some, many, much, each) tell the reader whether a noun is specific, general, countable or uncountable. Small words like these are often where accuracy is lost in writing.

Indefinite article: a and an

Use a or an with a singular countable noun when it is first mentioned or not specific.

  • I bought a bag.
  • He arrived after an hour.

Choose the form by sound, not spelling. Use an before a vowel sound, even when the spelling begins with a consonant: an hour. Use a before a consonant sound, even when the spelling begins with a vowel: a university, a European.

Definite article: the

Use the when both speaker and listener know which thing is meant.

  • The café we visited last week was closed.
  • The sun rises in the east.

No article

Use no article for general plural or uncountable nouns.

  • I like coffee in the morning.
  • Children need sleep.

Determiners with countable and uncountable nouns

  • Many and few go with countable nouns: many books, few students.
  • Much and little go with uncountable nouns: much water, little time.
  • Some and any work with both.

Checking your writing

Ask two questions: is this noun specific to the reader? Is it countable? Those two answers decide the article and the determiner.

title: Acids, Bases and Salts
content:
Acids, Bases and Salts

Cambridge IGCSE 0620 (2023–2025): 7.1 the characteristic properties of acids and bases; 7.2 oxides; 7.3 preparation of salts.

1. Definitions and everyday behaviour

An acid is a proton donor; a base is a proton acceptor; an alkali is a soluble base that releases OH⁻ in water. Acids turn litmus red and methyl orange red, and they react with metals, bases and carbonates. Strong acids ionise completely (HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄); weak acids ionise partially (ethanoic, citric), which is why they have a higher pH at the same concentration.

2. pH and indicators

The pH scale runs 0–14: below 7 acidic, 7 neutral, above 7 alkaline. Universal indicator gives a colour for each pH. Neutralisation is acid + base → salt + water; the ionic equation is H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.

3. Oxides

TypeExampleBehaviour
acidicCO₂, SO₂non-metal oxide, reacts with alkali
basicMgO, CuOmetal oxide, reacts with acid
amphotericAl₂O₃, ZnOreacts with acid and with alkali
neutralCO, H₂Ono acidic or basic behaviour

4. Making a named salt

Pick the route from solubility. Soluble salts: acid + excess insoluble base or carbonate, filter off the excess, evaporate to crystallise (copper(II) sulfate from CuO and H₂SO₄). Sodium, potassium and ammonium salts: titration, because both reactants are soluble (NaOH + HCl gives NaCl). Insoluble salts: precipitation, mixing two solutions (BaCl₂ + Na₂SO₄ gives BaSO₄).

Tests worth memorising: carbonate + acid gives CO₂ (limewater milky); sulfate + barium chloride gives a white precipitate; chloride + silver nitrate gives a white precipitate soluble in ammonia.

Exam focus

Q: Describe how to prepare pure, dry crystals of copper(II) sulfate from copper(II) oxide and dilute sulfuric acid.

A: Warm the acid, add copper(II) oxide in excess until no more dissolves, filter off the excess solid, then heat the filtrate to the point of crystallisation and leave it to cool so crystals form; dry them between filter papers.

title: Enzymes
content:
Enzymes

Cambridge IGCSE 0610 (2023–2025): 5.1 enzyme action; 5.2 effects of temperature and pH.

1. What an enzyme is

Enzymes are proteins that act as biological catalysts: they speed up reactions and are not used up. Each has an active site with a shape complementary to its substrate — the lock-and-key model. The substrate binds, the reaction happens, and the products leave. Enzymes lower activation energy, so reactions proceed at body temperature.

2. Temperature

Rate rises with temperature because molecules move faster and collide more often, up to an optimum (about 37 °C in humans). Above the optimum the bonds holding the enzyme's shape break, the active site loses its shape irreversibly, and the enzyme is denatured — the rate falls sharply and does not recover on cooling.

3. pH

Each enzyme has an optimum pH. Pepsin works at pH 2 in the stomach; pancreatic enzymes work at about pH 8 in the small intestine; amylase in saliva at about pH 7. Extreme pH denatures the enzyme the same way heat does.

4. Named enzymes and uses

  • Amylase: starch → maltose (saliva, pancreas).
  • Protease: protein → amino acids (stomach, pancreas).
  • Lipase: lipids → fatty acids and glycerol (pancreas).
  • Catalase: hydrogen peroxide → water and oxygen.

Industrially, enzymes clarify fruit juice, tenderise meat, and in biological washing powders digest protein and fat stains at low temperature, which saves energy.

Exam focus

Q: Explain why an enzyme stops working after being boiled, but works again if it is only chilled.

A: Boiling breaks the bonds that hold the active site's shape, denaturing the enzyme permanently. Chilling slows molecular motion so the rate falls, but the shape is unchanged and activity returns on warming.

title: Circular Measure
content:
Circular Measure

Radians

One radian is the angle subtending an arc equal in length to the radius. π radians = 180°.

  • Degrees → radians: multiply by π/180.
  • Radians → degrees: multiply by 180/π.

Common angles: 30° = π/6, 45° = π/4, 60° = π/3, 90° = π/2, 180° = π, 360° = 2π.

Arc Length

s = rθ (θ in radians). Key: s = arc length, in the same unit as r; r = radius; θ = the angle at the centre in radians, which is a pure number — never put degrees in here.

Example: r = 6, θ = π/3 gives s = 2π.

Sector Area

A = ½r²θ. Key: A = area of the sector, in square units of the length used; r = radius; θ = angle at the centre in radians (not degrees).

Example: r = 5, θ = 1.2 gives A = ½ × 25 × 1.2 = 15.

Segment Area

A = ½r²(θ − sin θ). For r = 2, θ = π/2: A = 2(π/2 − 1) = π − 2. Key: A = area of the segment between the chord and the arc (square units); r = radius; θ = angle subtended at the centre in radians — sin θ is dimensionless, so it can be subtracted from θ.

Rearranging

  • θ = s/r (must be radians)
  • θ = 2A/r²

Exam tips: never mix degrees into s = rθ; convert first. Sketch the sector and mark r and θ before computing, and check whether a question asks for the major or minor sector.

title: Databases and Data Definition
content:
Databases and Data Definition

Relational Concepts

A table (relation) stores rows (tuples) and columns (attributes). The primary key uniquely identifies each row; a foreign key references a primary key in another table, creating the relationship. A composite key uses two or more columns together.

Normalisation

  • 1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups.
  • 2NF: 1NF plus every non-key attribute depends on the whole key (kills partial dependency in composite keys).
  • 3NF: 2NF plus no transitive dependency — non-key attributes must not depend on other non-key attributes.

Normalisation reduces redundancy and prevents update, insert and delete anomalies.

DDL and DML

DDL defines structure: CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, DROP. DML manipulates data: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE, INSERT INTO, UPDATE, DELETE. Joins combine related tables: FROM Student s JOIN Enrolment e ON s.id = e.StudentID. Aggregates: COUNT, SUM, AVG with GROUP BY and HAVING.

Transactions and Concurrency

A transaction is a unit of work obeying ACID: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (rules preserved), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not interfere), Durability (committed data survives crashes). Record locking blocks conflicting simultaneous edits; a deadlock occurs when two transactions each hold a lock the other needs.

Exam tips: normalise a small table through 1NF, 2NF, 3NF naming the dependency removed at each step; write a two-table SELECT with JOIN; state which ACID property a scenario breaks.

title: Data Representation
content:
Data Representation

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): binary/hex, two's complement, BCD, text/image/sound encoding, file sizes, compression.

1. Number systems

  • Binary place values 128…1; hex digits 0–9, A–F; one hex digit = one nibble (4 bits).
  • Conversions: binary ↔ decimal ↔ hex. 0101 1010 → 5A; FF = 255.
  • BCD: 4 bits per decimal digit — 0029 → 0000 0000 0010 1001. Used in clocks/calculators; easier digit conversions, more bits than pure binary.

2. Two's complement (signed)

MSB is negative: −128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1. −5 = 1111 1011. Range 8-bit: −128…+127.

Negating: invert bits, add 1. Subtraction: add the negated number — 7 − 5 = 7 + (−5) = 0000 0111 + 1111 1011 = 0000 0010.

3. Text

ASCII 7-bit (128 chars) → extended sets; Unicode for all scripts (UTF-8 variable width). Character sets map codes to glyphs; uppercase/lowercase codes differ by one bit.

4. Images and sound

  • Bitmap: pixels; colour depth = bits per pixel. File size (bits) = W × H × depth. Metadata (width, height, depth) stores dimensions. Key: W = width in pixels; H = height in pixels; depth = bits used per pixel; the product is in bits, so divide by 8 for bytes.
  • Sound: sample rate (Hz), resolution (bits per sample), track duration × channels. Higher rate/depth = better fidelity, larger files.

5. Compression

  • Lossless (RLE, ZIP): exact restore — text/code must use it. RLE example: AAABBBCC → 3A3B2C; effective with runs.
  • Lossy (JPEG, MP3): discards perceptually minor data — photos/music OK, text never.

Exam tips: show full working in conversions; for size questions write the formula first with units; state the reason a compression type suits the file.

title: Plant Nutrition
content:
Plant Nutrition

Cambridge IGCSE 0610 (2023–2025): 6.1 photosynthesis; 6.2 leaf structure; 6.3 mineral requirements.

1. Photosynthesis

6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂, catalysed by chlorophyll and driven by light energy. Carbon dioxide enters through stomata, water arrives in the xylem, and oxygen leaves. The glucose is used for respiration, converted to starch for storage, made into cellulose, or combined with nitrogen to form amino acids.

2. Limiting factors

Light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature each limit the rate when in short supply; raising any one of them increases the rate only until another becomes limiting. A graph of rate against light levels off for that reason. The standard experiment uses pondweed and counts oxygen bubbles, or measures the distance a bubble travels in a set time.

3. Leaf structure and its reasons

  • Waxy cuticle — reduces water loss.
  • Upper epidermis — transparent, lets light through.
  • Palisade mesophyll — packed with chloroplasts for absorption.
  • Spongy mesophyll — air spaces for gas diffusion.
  • Veins — xylem brings water, phloem removes sugar.
  • Stomata and guard cells — controlled gas exchange; guard cells swell to open.

4. Mineral ions

IonDeficiency symptom
nitratestunted growth, yellowing leaves (needed for amino acids)
phosphatepoor root growth (respiration, DNA)
potassiumyellow leaves with dead spots (enzymes, stomata)
magnesiumyellow leaves between veins (chlorophyll)

Exam focus

Q: A plant is grown in distilled water with all minerals except magnesium. Predict the appearance and explain.

A: The leaves turn yellow between the veins, because magnesium is needed to make chlorophyll; without chlorophyll the plant cannot photosynthesise.

title: Movement into and out of Cells
content:
Movement into and out of Cells

Cambridge IGCSE 0610 (2023–2025): 3.1 diffusion; 3.2 osmosis; 3.3 active transport.

1. Diffusion

Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to lower concentration, down a concentration gradient, due to random motion. It needs no energy from the cell. Rate is faster with a steeper gradient, higher temperature, larger surface area and a shorter distance — which is why alveoli and villi are shaped as they are.

2. Osmosis

Osmosis is the diffusion of water through a partially permeable membrane from a dilute solution (high water potential) to a concentrated solution (low water potential). In pure water, a plant cell becomes turgid because the cell wall resists further expansion; in a concentrated sugar solution it loses water, the vacuole shrinks and the membrane pulls away — plasmolysis. An animal cell in pure water bursts (lysis); in strong solution it shrinks (crenation).

3. Active transport

Movement against the concentration gradient, using energy from respiration and carrier proteins in the membrane. Root hair cells absorb mineral ions from very dilute soil solution this way, and the ileum absorbs glucose against its gradient after diffusion has taken what it can.

4. Proving osmosis in the lab

Weigh potato cylinders, leave them in a series of sucrose concentrations for a fixed time, then reweigh. Gaining mass means water entered; losing mass means it left. Plot the change against concentration: the solution where mass does not change is isotonic to the potato. Visking tubing filled with starch and glucose in water shows the same: glucose diffuses out and is detected with Benedict's reagent, starch cannot leave.

Exam focus

Q: A plant wilts on a hot day. Explain its cells' change in terms of water potential.

A: More water evaporates than is absorbed, so cells lose water by osmosis to the surrounding tissue; the vacuoles shrink, turgor is lost and the leaves droop.

title: Experimental Techniques and Chemical Analysis
content:
Experimental Techniques and Chemical Analysis

Cambridge IGCSE 0620 (2023–2025): 12.1 apparatus; 12.2 purity; 12.3 separation techniques; 12.4 identification of ions and gases; 12.5 chromatography.

1. Choosing apparatus

A measuring cylinder is quick but imprecise (about ±1 cm³); a burette reads to 0.05 cm³ and a pipette delivers a fixed accurate volume; a volumetric flask makes a standard solution. Read at eye level, at the bottom of the meniscus, to avoid parallax error.

2. Purity and melting point

A pure substance melts and boils at a single sharp temperature; an impure one melts over a range and at a lower temperature than the pure substance. That is the standard test for purity, and it is why a melting-point apparatus is used rather than appearance.

3. Separation methods

  • filtration — insoluble solid from a liquid;
  • evaporation or crystallisation — soluble salt from its solution;
  • simple distillation — solvent from a solution, or a liquid from a less volatile solute;
  • fractional distillation — liquids with different boiling points, as in crude oil;
  • separating funnel — immiscible liquids;
  • chromatography — separating and identifying dissolved dyes.

4. Tests for ions and gases

Flame tests: lithium crimson, sodium yellow, potassium lilac, calcium orange-red, copper blue-green. Cations with sodium hydroxide: a white precipitate insoluble in excess suggests aluminium or calcium; a blue precipitate is copper(II); a green precipitate is iron(II); a red-brown precipitate is iron(III). Anions: carbonate effervesces with acid; sulfate gives a white precipitate with barium chloride and hydrochloric acid; chloride gives a white precipitate with silver nitrate that dissolves in ammonia.

Gases: oxygen relights a glowing splint, hydrogen gives a squeaky pop, carbon dioxide turns limewater milky, chlorine bleaches damp litmus, ammonia turns damp red litmus blue.

Exam focus

Q: A solution gives a green precipitate with sodium hydroxide and effervesces with dilute acid. Identify the metal ion and name a possible anion.

A: The metal ion is iron(II), Fe²⁺. The effervescence suggests carbonate, CO₃²⁻.

title: Introductory Organic Chemistry and Alkanes
content:
Introductory Organic Chemistry and Alkanes

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH11, Topic 4. Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon compounds. Alkanes are the simplest family, and their reactions introduce the radical substitution mechanism used throughout the course.

Naming and formulae

  • A homologous series has the same general formula, similar chemical properties and a gradual change in physical properties.
  • Alkanes have the general formula CnH2n+2. Names depend on the longest carbon chain: meth-, eth-, prop-, but-, pent-, hex-.
  • Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different connectivity, such as butane and methylpropane.

Fossil fuels and cracking

  • Alkanes are obtained from crude oil by fractional distillation; the fractions separate by boiling point, which rises with chain length.
  • Cracking breaks long chains into shorter, more useful alkanes and alkenes, using heat or a catalyst.

Radical substitution

  • Alkanes react with chlorine or bromine under UV light by free-radical substitution.
  • The three stages are initiation (Cl2 → 2Cl•), propagation (a radical reacts with an alkane, regenerating a radical) and termination (two radicals combine). Key: Cl2 = one chlorine molecule; Cl• = a chlorine radical, the dot standing for its single unpaired electron; the 2 in front of Cl• records that homolytic fission of one molecule gives two radicals, which is why a trace of light starts a chain that consumes many molecules.
  • Propagation steps form the product; termination steps are rare, so they do not appear in the main yield.

Combustion

  • Complete combustion gives carbon dioxide and water; limited oxygen gives carbon monoxide or carbon (soot).

Exam tip: when writing a radical mechanism, use a single-headed arrow for each electron moved and always show the radical dot.

title: Information Representation
content:
Number Systems and Ranges

Unsigned binary with n bits stores 0 to 2ⁿ − 1. Two's complement represents negatives: the MSB has value −2ⁿ⁻¹.

Example: 8-bit two's complement of −5: 11111011 (−128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 2 + 1).

SystemBaseDigits
Binary20–1
Hexadecimal160–9, A–F
BCD—4 bits per decimal digit

Binary Arithmetic

Add: 0+0=0, 0+1=1, 1+1=0 carry 1, 1+1+1=1 carry 1. Overflow happens when a result exceeds the word size.

Subtraction uses two's complement addition (A − B = A + (−B)).

Text

  • ASCII: 7 bits, 128 characters, English only
  • Unicode: universal scripts; UTF-8 is variable-width (1–4 bytes)

Images and Sound

  • Bitmap: pixels with colour depth (bits per pixel). File size = width × height × depth. Key: width and height are counts of pixels; depth = bits used for each pixel; the product is in bits, so divide by 8 for bytes.
  • Sound: sampling rate (Hz) × bit depth × duration × channels.
  • Resolution trade-off: fidelity vs size.

Compression

  • Lossless (ZIP, run-length encoding): exact reconstruction — required for text/code
  • Lossy (JPEG, MP3): discards perceptually minor data — smaller files

Example: RLE of AAABBBCC → 3A3B2C.

Exam tips: show working for two's complement conversions; state why compression type suits the data (text must be lossless).

title: Reading for Main Ideas and Detail
content:
Reading in English means knowing which reading method fits the task. Skimming, scanning and close reading are three different tools, and using the right one saves time and improves understanding.

Skimming

Skimming means reading quickly to get the general idea. Read the title, the first sentence of each paragraph, and any headings. Ask: what is this text about, and who is it for?

Scanning

Scanning means searching for a specific piece of information, such as a date, a name or a number. Move your eyes quickly over the text looking for the key word, and ignore everything else.

Main ideas

The main idea of a paragraph is the point the paragraph makes. It is often in the topic sentence, which is frequently near the start, but it is not always there. Ask: what do the other sentences support?

Supporting details

Supporting details are examples, facts, reasons and explanations that develop the main idea.

  • Main idea: The city is a centre of innovation.
  • Supporting detail: The city hosts three major universities and many technology firms.

Unknown words

When you meet an unfamiliar word:

  • Look at the words around it for clues.
  • Check whether the word is a familiar root with a prefix or suffix.
  • Decide whether you need its exact meaning to answer the question.

Do not stop reading to look up every word. Often the meaning is clear from context.

title: Data Handling and Representation
content:
Statistics — Data Handling

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): averages from lists and tables, quartiles/IQR, charts, cumulative frequency, histograms.

1. Averages

  • Mean = Σfx/Σf from frequency tables. Median = middle value (ordered data). Mode = most frequent. Range = max − min. Key: f = the frequency of each value; x = the value itself, or the class midpoint; Σ means add them all up, so the mean carries the unit of x.
  • Choose the best average: mode for shoe sizes, median when outliers distort the mean.

Example (table): goals 0,1,2,3 with f 5,8,4,3: mean = (0+8+8+9)/20 = 1.25.

2. Quartiles and IQR

Q₁ at n/4, Q₃ at 3n/4 (position); IQR = Q₃ − Q₁ — less affected by outliers than the range. Key: n = the number of data items (a count); Q₁ and Q₃ = the lower and upper quartiles, in the same unit as the data; the IQR shares that unit.

3. Charts

Bar charts, pie charts (angle = fraction × 360°), time series, pictograms. Compare data sets with like-for-like totals; comment on trends.

4. Cumulative frequency

Running totals vs upper class boundaries; the curve ends at (max, n). Median at n/2; Q₁/Q₃ at n/4 and 3n/4; box plot from the five-figure summary.

5. Histograms

Bar area ∝ frequency: FD = frequency ÷ class width. Recover frequencies as FD × width; unequal widths need FDs on the axis. Key: FD = frequency density, the count per one unit of class width; frequency is a plain count; class width is in the units the data was measured in.

Exam tips: read cumulative-frequency answers with dashed construction lines; always compare spreads, not just averages, when asked to compare data.

title: Simulation, Sensors and Real Data
content:
Simulation, Sensors and Real Data

Simulation and Modelling

A simulation is a program that models a real system to test scenarios safely and cheaply: weather models, traffic flows, epidemic spread. Models use abstractions — chosen variables and equations — with a time step. Advantages: no real-world risk, repeatable, faster or slower than real time. Limitations: only as good as the model; rare events may be missed.

Sensors and Signals

Sensors measure physical quantities: temperature (thermistor), light (LDR), pressure, humidity, sound. Most output analogue signals varying continuously; computers need digital values, so an ADC (analogue-to-digital converter) samples the signal. Resolution depends on bits — an 8-bit ADC gives 256 levels. A DAC converts digital output back to analogue for actuators or speakers.

Monitoring vs Control

  • Monitoring: sensors feed data to the computer, which only records, displays or raises alarms — no action taken on the environment.
  • Control: the computer acts via actuators (motors, valves, heaters) based on sensor input — the classic feedback loop.

Real-Time Considerations

Control systems are often real-time: late output can be wrong output. Sampling rate must exceed twice the highest signal frequency (Nyquist) to avoid aliasing.

Exam tips: distinguish monitoring from control with a named example; describe the role of ADC and DAC in a greenhouse system; explain one limitation of a simulation.

title: Ethics and AI
content:
Professional Bodies

ACM/IEEE-CS and BCS codes: public interest, competence, integrity, avoid harm, respect privacy. Violations cost trust and employment.

Ethical Scenarios

  • Collecting more personal data than needed (privacy)
  • Releasing software with known bugs that risks safety (competence/honesty)
  • Automated decisions without human review (accountability)

Laws: data protection (GDPR-style), computer misuse (unauthorised access is a crime regardless of intent).

AI Characteristics

Systems exhibiting: planning, learning, reasoning, problem-solving, perception, knowledge representation.

Machine Learning

  • Supervised: learns from labelled data (spam detection)
  • Unsupervised: finds structure in unlabelled data (clustering)
  • Reinforcement: learns by reward signals (game agents)

Training/evaluation loop: fit on training data, test on unseen data to avoid overfitting. Neural networks adjust weights via backpropagation.

Ethics of AI

Bias in training data → unfair outputs; opaque decisions → accountability gaps; job displacement; autonomous weapons.

Exam tips: structure ethics answers as: identify the principle → apply to the scenario → give consequences for stakeholders.

title: Permutations and Combinations
content:
Permutations and Combinations

The Multiplication Principle

If a task is done in successive stages with m, n, ... choices at each stage, the total is the product of the choices. This underpins every counting problem: a menu with 4 starters and 6 mains gives 24 meals.

Permutations — Order Matters

The number of ways of arranging r objects from n distinct objects is

  • ⁿPᵣ = n!/(n − r)!

The number of arrangements of n distinct objects is n!. Five books on a shelf: 5! = 120 ways.

Combinations — Order Irrelevant

The number of ways of choosing r objects from n is

  • ⁿCᵣ = n!/(r!(n − r)!)

Choosing a committee of 3 from 8 people: ⁸C₃ = 56. Choosing is not arranging — a committee has no internal order, so we divide by r!.

Restricted Permutations

  • No two specified people adjacent: arrange everyone else, then slot the restricted people into gaps. For n people with 2 who must be separated: arrange the other n − 2 (ways), then place 2 people in distinct gaps between them.
  • Specified people together: bundle them as one item, arrange the bundle, then multiply by the internal arrangements of the bundle.
  • Words with repeated letters: divide by the factorials of each repeat count. ARRANGE has 7 letters with A appearing twice and R twice, so 7!/(2!·2!) = 1260.

Combinations with Constraints

  • At least / at most: split into cases and add. A team of 5 from 6 boys and 5 girls with at least 3 girls is ⁵C₃⁶C₂ + ⁵C₄⁶C₁ + ⁵C₅⁶C₀.
  • "Must include" pairs: choose the required items first, then choose freely from the remainder.

Exam tips: state whether a scenario is a permutation or combination before computing anything. Most lost marks come from counting an arrangement where order does not actually matter. Check every answer against a small case you can enumerate by hand.

title: Data Types and File Organisation
content:
Data Types and File Organisation

User-Defined Types

A user-defined type is derived from existing types. An enumerated type lists named values in order: TYPE Months = (Jan, Feb, Mar ...). Internally each value is an integer index starting at 0. Pointer types store a memory address; the dereference operator returns the value at that address, which is how linked structures reference their nodes. Set types store unordered collections of distinct values from an ordinal base type, supporting union, intersection and difference.

Records

A record groups related fields of different types under one identifier, for example a Student record with name : STRING and mark : INTEGER. Arrays of records are the standard structure for storing a table of items in memory.

File Organisation

  • Serial: records in insertion order; searching checks every record. Simple but slow.
  • Sequential: records kept in key order; binary search possible, but insertion needs rewriting.
  • Random (direct): a hashing function converts the key into a storage address, giving near-instant access. A poor hash causes collisions — two keys hashing to the same address — resolved by chaining or overflow areas.

Hashing

A common method is division hashing: Address = Key MOD TableSize. A good hash distributes keys evenly; load factor above roughly 70 percent degrades performance. Key: Address = the slot chosen, an index from 0 to TableSize − 1; Key = the value converted to an integer; TableSize = the number of slots — all three are counts, with no units.

Exam tips: state the internal integer representation of enumerated values; define a collision before describing its resolution; compare the three file organisations in terms of search and insert cost.

title: System Software and Security
content:
Operating System Roles

  • Manage memory (paging/segmentation, virtual memory to disk)
  • Schedule processes (round robin, priorities)
  • Handle I/O via device drivers and spooling
  • Provide the UI, file systems, and security (users, permissions)

Translators

  • Assembler: assembly → machine code (1:1)
  • Compiler: whole source → machine code, reports all errors, produces standalone executables
  • Interpreter: line-by-line execution, stops at first error, needs the interpreter present

Bytecode + VM (e.g. Java) combines both: compile once, run anywhere the VM exists.

Linkers and Loaders

Static linking copies library code into the executable; dynamic linking binds at runtime (smaller files, shared libraries). The loader places the program in memory, relocating addresses.

IDEs

Editors with syntax highlighting, autocompletion, debugger (breakpoints, stepping, variable watch), and integrated compilation.

Malware and Defences

Viruses, worms, trojans, spyware, phishing. Defences: antivirus (signature + heuristic scanning), firewalls (packet filtering by port/IP), sandboxing, user education, patches.

Exam tips: compare compiler vs interpreter with concrete error-handling differences; explain firewall rules using ports and addresses.

title: Programming Concepts
content:
Programming Concepts

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): variables/constants, data types, selection/iteration, arrays, file handling, subroutines, scope, IDE tools.

1. Basics

Constants vs variables; types: INTEGER, REAL, CHAR, STRING, BOOLEAN, DATE; casting between them. Declaration with meaningful names.

2. Selection and iteration

IF score >= 50 THEN
  grade ← "pass"
ELSE
  grade ← "fail"
ENDIF

CASE OF grade
  "A" : OUTPUT "excellent"
  OTHERWISE : OUTPUT "keep going"
ENDCASE

REPEAT
  INPUT pin
UNTIL pin = storedPin

FOR i ← 1 TO 10 STEP 2 ... NEXT i

WHILE: condition first (may not run); REPEAT: runs at least once.

3. Arrays

Fixed size, indexed (0- or 1-based per spec); 2D arrays: row, column. Bounds errors when index leaves range. Traversal with FOR loops.

4. Files

OPENFILE "data.txt" FOR READ
READFILE "data.txt", line
CLOSEFILE "data.txt"

OPENFILE "log.txt" FOR APPEND
WRITEFILE "log.txt", record

Modes: READ, WRITE (overwrites), APPEND (adds).

5. Subroutines

Procedure (no return) vs function (returns value). Parameters by value (copy) vs reference (original). Local scope inside; global shared — declare deliberately, avoid overuse.

6. IDE tools

Syntax highlighting, autocompletion, breakpoints, single stepping, variable watch — name the tool and its debugging benefit.

Exam tips: use the exam pseudocode style exactly; for 2D arrays, loop rows outer/columns inner; choose WHILE vs REPEAT by "must it run once?"

title: Sine Rule, Cosine Rule and Triangle Area
content:
Trigonometry — Sine and Cosine Rules

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): area formula, sine rule, cosine rule, multi-step bearing and 3-D problems (Extended).

1. Area of a triangle

A = ½ab sin C (C = included angle between sides a and b). Key: A = the area of the triangle, in square units of the length used; a and b = the two sides enclosing angle C; C = that included angle, taken in degrees.

Example: a = 8, b = 5, C = 48° → A = ½ × 8 × 5 × sin 48° = 14.8.

2. Sine rule

a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C. Use when a matching angle–side pair is known. Key: a, b and c = the sides of the triangle; A, B and C = the angles opposite them; the common ratio carries the unit of length, because sin of an angle has no unit.

Example: A = 40°, a = 7, B = 65°: b = 7 sin 65°/sin 40° = 9.98.

Ambiguous case: two triangles possible when finding an angle — check the obtuse option (180° − θ).

3. Cosine rule

a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A. Use with two sides + included angle, or all three sides (then cos A = (b² + c² − a²)/(2bc)). Key: a = the side opposite angle A; b and c = the other two sides; cos A takes A in degrees; every term is a length squared, so the square root at the end returns a length.

Example: b = 7, c = 5, A = 52°: a² = 74 − 70 cos 52° = 30.9 → a = 5.56.

4. Bearing problems

Draw both north lines, transfer angles via parallel lines, then pick sine/cosine rule.

Example: QP = 60 km bearing 070° from Q; QR = 45 km bearing 150°. ∠PQR = 80° → PR² = 60² + 45² − 2·60·45 cos 80° → PR = 68.4 km.

5. 3-D trigonometry

Identify the plane containing the required angle; use 3-D Pythagoras d² = x² + y² + z² for space diagonals; angle between a line and a plane uses the projection onto the plane.

Exam tips: state which rule you are using and why; sketch a separate 2-D triangle for 3-D questions; answers to 3 s.f. / bearings as three digits.

title: Bearings and Loci
content:
Mensuration — Bearings and Loci

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): compass bearings, scale drawings, constructions (perpendicular/angle bisectors), loci regions.

1. Bearings

  • Measured clockwise from north; three figures: 065°, 128°, 300°.
  • Back bearing = front bearing ± 180°. Key: a bearing is measured clockwise from north and written in three figures (000°–360°); add 180° when the front bearing is under 180°, subtract 180° when it is over — the sign is chosen so the answer stays inside 000°–360° — it is one rule, not two answers.
  • Draw a north line at both points; north lines are parallel, giving Z-angles.

Example: B is on bearing 070° from A → A is on bearing 250° from B.

2. Scale drawings

1 cm : 500 m style scales; measure, convert, and quote distances/bearings from your drawing to the accuracy allowed.

3. Constructions

  • Perpendicular bisector of a segment: equal arcs from both ends, join the crossings.
  • Angle bisector: equal arcs from the vertex arms.
  • 60° and 90° constructions with compasses; leave all arcs visible.

4. Loci

Fixed distance from a point = circle; from a line = parallel lines with rounded ends; equidistant from two points = perpendicular bisector; from two lines = angle bisector.

Example: a goat tied by a 5 m rope to a corner of a 4 m × 6 m shed: the reachable region is ¾ circle radius 5 m + two ¼ circles radius 1 m where the rope wraps.

Exam tips: state "clockwise from north" in bearing definitions; shade/label locus regions clearly; use a ruler for construction lines too.

title: Excretion in Humans
content:
Excretion in Humans

Cambridge IGCSE 0610 (2023–2025): 13.1 excretion; 13.2 the kidney; 13.3 urine and dialysis.

1. Excretion and egestion

Excretion is removing metabolic waste made in cells: carbon dioxide from respiration and urea from the breakdown of excess amino acids in the liver. Egestion is removing undigested food. Sweat removes water, salts and urea; the lungs remove carbon dioxide and water vapour.

2. The kidney

Each kidney is supplied by a renal artery and drained by a renal vein and a ureter. Inside, the cortex contains the glomeruli and the medulla the collecting ducts. Nephrons do three things:

  • Ultrafiltration: pressure in the glomerulus forces water, glucose, urea and salts into the capsule; proteins and blood cells are too large.
  • Selective reabsorption: glucose is reabsorbed entirely, most water and salts partly, in the proximal tubule.
  • Urine forms from what is left and passes to the bladder via the ureter.

3. Dialysis

A dialysis machine passes blood on one side of a partially permeable membrane and dialysate fluid on the other. Urea and excess salts diffuse out down their gradients; glucose and proteins keep the correct concentration and stay. It must be repeated several times a week because waste accumulates between sessions.

4. Water balance

ADH from the pituitary increases water reabsorption when blood water potential falls, so urine becomes more concentrated; it falls on a hot day or after salty food, and rises after drinking a lot.

Exam focus

Q: Explain why glucose is not found in the urine of a healthy person.

A: It is filtered at the glomerulus but then completely reabsorbed by active transport in the proximal tubule, so none remains in the urine.

title: Thermal Physics
content:
Thermal Physics

Internal Energy

Sum of random kinetic + potential energies of molecules. Temperature rise → KE up; phase change → PE up (bonds stretch) at constant temperature.

Specific Heat and Latent Heat

  • Heating: Q = mcΔθ (c = specific heat capacity) Key: Q = heat energy added (J); m = mass (kg); c = energy needed to raise 1 kg by 1 K (J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹); Δθ = temperature rise (K) — no phase change happens while this applies.
  • Phase change: Q = mL (L = specific latent heat) Key: Q = energy needed to change state (J); m = mass changing state (kg); L = energy per kilogram for that change (J kg⁻¹) — temperature stays constant throughout, which is what distinguishes it from Q = mcΔθ.

Example: melting 0.2 kg ice: Q = 0.2 × 334,000 ≈ 67 kJ — no temperature change during the change.

Mixtures: heat lost = heat gained.

Gas Laws

  • Boyle: pV = constant (T fixed)
  • Charles: V/T = constant (p fixed)
  • Pressure law: p/T = constant (V fixed)
  • Combined/ideal: pV = nRT, R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ Key: p = pressure (Pa); V = volume (m³); n = amount of gas (mol); R = molar gas constant (8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹); T = thermodynamic temperature (K) — T must be in kelvin, never °C.

Example: 2 mol at 300 K in 0.05 m³: p = nRT/V = 2 × 8.31 × 300/0.05 ≈ 100 kPa.

Kinetic Theory

½m⟨c²⟩ = (3/2)kT — temperature measures mean translational KE. Also pV = ⅓Nm⟨c²⟩. Key: m = mass of one molecule (kg); ⟨c²⟩ = mean square speed of the molecules (m² s⁻²); k = Boltzmann constant (1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹); T = temperature (K); N = number of molecules; p and V are pressure (Pa) and volume (m³).

Exam tips: use kelvin in every gas equation; in mixture problems, work per substance with a common final temperature.

title: Organic Chemistry: Halogenoalkanes, Alcohols and Spectra
content:
Organic Chemistry: Halogenoalkanes, Alcohols and Spectra

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12, Topic 10. Halogenoalkanes and alcohols are the first families where a functional group changes the reactivity of the molecule. Spectra are the tools that identify those groups in an unknown compound.

Halogenoalkanes

  • A halogenoalkane has a halogen atom bonded to a carbon atom. The C–X bond is polar because the halogen is more electronegative, so the carbon is slightly positive.
  • Reactivity rises down the group because the C–X bond gets weaker (C–I is weakest), so the iodoalkane reacts fastest.
  • Nucleophilic substitution with aqueous hydroxide ions gives an alcohol. The nucleophile donates a pair of electrons to the carbon atom.
  • Halogenoalkanes can be tested by warming with aqueous silver nitrate in ethanol: the precipitate forms at different rates, and iodoalkanes react fastest.

Alcohols

  • Alcohols contain the –OH group. Primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols depend on how many other carbons are attached to the carbon bearing the –OH.
  • Oxidation of primary alcohols with acidified potassium dichromate(VI) gives aldehydes, which can be oxidised further to carboxylic acids; excess oxidant and heat give the acid.
  • Secondary alcohols oxidise to ketones; tertiary alcohols are not oxidised under these conditions.
  • Dehydration with hot concentrated sulfuric acid or aluminium oxide forms an alkene.

Mass spectrometry

  • The molecular ion peak gives the relative molecular mass. Fragmentation patterns reveal structural features.
  • Peaks at m/z 15 and 29 can indicate CH3 and C2H5 fragments.

Infrared spectroscopy

  • Bonds absorb infrared radiation at characteristic wavenumbers. A broad absorption near 3200–3550 cm⁻¹ indicates an O–H group in an alcohol. A strong absorption near 1700 cm⁻¹ indicates a C=O group. Key: wavenumber (cm⁻¹) = 1/λ with λ measured in cm, so it counts how many wavelengths fit in one centimetre — a larger wavenumber means a shorter wavelength and a higher-energy vibration. The O–H band is broad because hydrogen bonding varies its energy; C=O is sharp and strong.
  • Use tables of characteristic absorptions with the spectrum, rather than memorised single values.

NMR (introduced)

  • The number of peaks in a proton NMR spectrum gives the number of environments of hydrogen atoms; the relative areas give the ratio of hydrogens.

Exam tip: when identifying an unknown, combine evidence: the molecular formula from mass spectrometry, the functional groups from infrared, and the environments from NMR.

title: Abstract Data Types
content:
Abstract Data Types

What is an ADT?

An abstract data type is a logical description of a collection of data plus the operations on it, independent of implementation. Stacks, queues, linked lists, binary trees and hash tables are all ADTs; in A Level you must show how they are built from arrays or records with pointers.

Linked Lists

Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node; a start pointer marks the head and a null marks the end. Insertion rewires two pointers — no shifting — giving O(1) insertion at a known position, but access requires walking the list, O(n).

Stacks and Queues

A stack is LIFO (push and pop at the top); a queue is FIFO (enqueue at the rear, dequeue from the front). Both can be arrays with index pointers or linked lists. Stack uses include call stacks and expression evaluation; queue uses include print buffers and breadth-first search.

Binary Search Trees

Each node has up to two children; left subtree keys are smaller, right subtree keys larger. Search, insert and (average-case) delete are O(log n). An in-order traversal outputs keys in ascending order. A degenerate (linear) tree from sorted input degrades to O(n).

Hash Tables

Covered in file organisation, but as an ADT a hash table pairs a hash function with bucket storage for O(1) average access.

Exam tips: be able to draw a tree after a sequence of insertions and write its three traversals; state the pointer changes for a linked-list insertion; compare ADT operations with Big-O.

title: Drugs
content:
Drugs

Cambridge IGCSE 0610 (2023–2025): 15.1 medicinal drugs; 15.2 misuse of drugs; 15.3 the effects of alcohol and tobacco.

1. Medicinal drugs

Antibiotics kill bacteria by attacking their cell wall or protein synthesis; they do not work on viruses. Painkillers relieve symptoms without killing pathogens. Insulitis, asthma inhalers and insulin are examples of drugs that replace a missing function. Antibiotic resistance develops when courses are incomplete or antibiotics are used for viral infections, so resistant strains such as MRSA survive.

2. Recreational drugs and their effects

DrugEffectHarm
alcoholdepressantliver damage, impaired judgement, fetal harm
nicotinestimulantaddiction, raised heart rate, and tar harms lungs
heroinstrong painkiller, depressantaddiction, overdose, infected needles
cannabisaltered perceptionimpaired memory, mental health risk

3. Alcohol and pregnancy

Alcohol crosses the placenta; heavy drinking can cause fetal alcohol spectrum disorder, with learning and behavioural difficulties. Smoking in pregnancy reduces oxygen supply and raises the risk of low birth weight.

4. Performance-enhancing drugs

Anabolic steroids build muscle but damage the liver, raise blood pressure and upset hormone balance. Stimulants raise heart rate and risk cardiac problems. They are banned in sport because they are unsafe and give an unfair advantage.

Exam focus

Q: Explain why antibiotics should not be prescribed for influenza.

A: Influenza is caused by a virus, and antibiotics only act on bacteria; unnecessary use also selects resistant bacteria and wastes the drug.

title: Tenses in Context
content:
Tense choice depends on time, not only on the verb. The same action can be described with different tenses, and the difference changes the meaning. Learn the tenses by the situations where you use them.

Present simple

Use the present simple for facts, general truths and routines.

  • Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius.
  • The bus leaves at seven every morning.

Past simple

Use the past simple for a finished action at a stated or clearly understood past time.

  • She went to the cinema yesterday evening.
  • We moved to Leeds in 2015.

Present perfect

Use the present perfect for an action connected to now. It is common with since, for and ever, and when the exact time is not important.

  • I have lived in London since 2019. (It continues now.)
  • Have you ever tried sushi?

Compare: I lived in London in 2019. This finishes in the past and does not connect to now.

Past continuous

Use the past continuous for an action in progress at a past moment, often interrupted by a shorter action.

  • When the phone rang, I was taking a shower.

Future forms

Use will have plus a past participle for an action completed before a future time.

  • By next summer, they will have finished the course.

Common errors

  • Using the past simple with since: write "I have lived here since 2019", not "I lived here since 2019".
  • Forgetting that a general fact uses the present simple even in a past context.

title: Databases
content:
Relational Basics

Tables (relations) of records with fields. Keys:

  • Primary key: unique identifier
  • Foreign key: references another table's PK — creates relationships
  • Candidate/secondary keys: other unique identifiers

Normalisation

  • 1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups
  • 2NF: 1NF + no partial dependency on a composite key
  • 3NF: 2NF + no transitive dependencies (non-key → non-key)

Example: (StudentID, Course, CourseFee) has CourseFee depending on Course, not StudentID — move course data to its own table (3NF).

SQL

SELECT name, grade FROM students
  WHERE grade >= 'A' ORDER BY name;
INSERT INTO students VALUES (...);
UPDATE students SET grade = 'B' WHERE id = 5;
DELETE FROM students WHERE id = 5;

Joins combine tables: FROM students s JOIN enrolments e ON s.id = e.sid.

Transactions

ACID: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (rules hold), Isolation (no interference), Durability (committed = permanent). Record locking prevents conflicting simultaneous edits.

Exam tips: justify each normal form step with the dependency removed; write SQL with correct WHERE clauses to avoid accidental full-table updates.

title: Right-Angled Trigonometry
content:
Trigonometry — Right-Angled Triangles

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): SOH CAH TOA, exact values, angles of elevation/depression.

1. The ratios

Label sides first (opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse) with respect to the marked angle, then choose:

  • sin θ = opp/hyp; cos θ = adj/hyp; tan θ = opp/adj. Key: θ = the marked angle (in degrees or radians); opp = the side opposite θ; adj = the side next to θ that is not the hypotenuse; hyp = the longest side, opposite the right angle — all three are lengths, so each ratio has no unit.

Example: hyp 10, angle 35°, find opposite: x = 10 sin 35° = 5.74 (3 s.f.).

2. Finding angles

Use inverse keys: θ = sin⁻¹(opp/hyp). tan θ = 3/4 ⇒ θ = 36.9° (1 d.p.).

3. Exact values (Extended)

4. Elevation and depression

Elevation: angle up from horizontal; depression: down. Both measured from the horizontal line at the observer.

Example: tower 20 m, elevation to top 42° → horizontal distance = 20/tan 42° = 22.2 m.

5. Pythagoras combinations

Find a missing side with Pythagoras before applying a ratio when two sides are known instead of an angle.
