title: Magnetic Fields and Electromagnetism
content:
Magnetic Fields and Electromagnetism

Force on a Current

F = BIL sin θ (Fleming's left hand: field-index, current-first-finger, force-thumb). Key: F = force on the wire (N); B = flux density (T); I = current (A); L = length of wire in the field (m); θ = angle between the wire and the field — the force is maximum at 90° and zero when the wire lies along the field.

Example: 0.5 m wire carrying 3 A at 90° to a 0.2 T field: F = 0.3 N.

Force on a Moving Charge

F = BQv sin θ, always perpendicular to v → circular paths: r = mv/(BQ) (basis of cyclotrons and mass spectrometers). Key: F = magnetic force (N); B = flux density (T); Q = charge of the particle (C); v = its speed (m s⁻¹); θ = angle between v and B; m = mass (kg); r = radius of the circular path (m) — the force does no work, so the speed stays constant and only the direction turns.

Example: an electron (m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg) at 2 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ in 0.5 mT: r ≈ 2.3 cm.

Fields from Currents

  • Long straight wire: B = μ₀I/(2πr), circling by the right-hand grip rule Key: B = flux density at distance r (T); μ₀ = permeability of free space (4π × 10⁻⁷ H m⁻¹); I = current (A); r = perpendicular distance from the wire (m) — the field falls off as 1/r and circles the wire.
  • Solenoid: B = μ₀nI inside Key: B = flux density inside the solenoid (T); μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H m⁻¹; n = turns per metre of length (m⁻¹); I = current (A) — the field is uniform inside and weak outside.

Electromagnetic Induction

Faraday: induced EMF = rate of flux cutting = N dΦ/dt. Lenz: induced effects oppose the change (negative sign). Key: EMF = induced p.d. (V); N = number of turns in the coil; Φ = magnetic flux through one turn (Wb); dΦ/dt = rate of change of that flux (Wb s⁻¹); the minus sign of Lenz's law says the induced current opposes whatever changed the flux.

Example: a coil of 100 turns, flux changing 2 mWb in 50 ms induces EMF = 100 × 0.002/0.05 = 4 V.

Flux Φ = BA (B ⊥ A). Generators rotate coils in fields; transformers link two coils by a shared changing flux with V₁/V₂ = N₁/N₂.

Exam tips: use left hand for motors (force on current), right hand for generators (induced current); state Lenz's law in explain questions.

title: Waves & Sound
content:
Waves & Sound

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): general wave properties; reflection/refraction/diffraction; sound.

1. Wave basics

v = fλ. Transverse (oscillation ⊥ travel — light, water, S-waves) vs longitudinal (parallel — sound, P-waves). Amplitude, wavelength, frequency f = 1/T; wavefront diagrams. Key: v = wave speed (m s⁻¹); f = frequency (Hz); λ = wavelength (m); T = period, the time for one complete oscillation (s) — the medium sets v, the source sets f, and λ follows from v = fλ.

2. Ripple tank behaviours

  • Reflection: angle in = angle out; speed/frequency unchanged, direction changes.
  • Refraction: speed change at boundary bends wavefronts (shallow water slows ripples).
  • Diffraction: spreading through gaps ≈ λ wide; around edges.

3. Electromagnetic spectrum (order)

Radio → micro → IR → visible (red 700 nm – violet 400 nm) → UV → X → gamma. All travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum; transverse; uses and dangers (IR heating; UV skin; X/gamma ionising).

4. Sound

  • Longitudinal; needs a medium (bell in vacuum demo). Speed ~340 m/s air, faster in liquids/solids.
  • Range 20 Hz–20 kHz; ultrasound > 20 kHz (sonar, prenatal scans, cleaning).
  • Pitch ↔ frequency; loudness ↔ amplitude.

5. Echo problems

Distance = (v × t)/2 (there and back). Key: distance = one-way distance to the reflector (m); v = speed of the pulse in the medium (m s⁻¹, 340 for sound in air); t = total time between sending and hearing the echo (s); dividing by 2 is what makes it one-way.

Example: echo after 0.6 s, v = 340 → cliff 102 m away.

Exam tips: in diagrams always label wavelength as crest-to-crest; for refraction, state "changes speed" first, then direction; quote EM uses with the hazard.

title: The Periodic Table
content:
The Periodic Table

Cambridge IGCSE 0620 (2023–2025): 8.1 arrangement of elements; 8.2 Group I properties; 8.3 Group VII properties; 8.4 transition elements; 8.5 noble gases.

1. How the table is built

Elements are ordered by increasing proton number. A new period starts when a shell fills, so elements in the same group have the same number of outer electrons and therefore similar chemical properties. Metals are on the left, non-metals on the right, with the metalloids along the staircase.

2. Group I — the alkali metals

Lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, caesium. Down the group: reactivity increases, melting point decreases, density increases. They react with water to give a metal hydroxide and hydrogen (2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂), and with oxygen to form oxides. Reactivity rises because the outer electron is further from the nucleus and lost more easily.

3. Group VII — the halogens

Fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine. Down the group: colour deepens, melting and boiling points rise, reactivity falls. A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one from its salt: chlorine + potassium bromide gives bromine and potassium chloride. They form ionic halides with metals and covalent compounds with non-metals.

4. Transition elements and noble gases

Transition metals (iron, copper, zinc, silver, gold) are hard, dense, good conductors, often form coloured compounds and can show several oxidation states; they are also useful catalysts. Noble gases (Group VIII/0) have full outer shells, so they are unreactive and are used where inertness matters: argon in lamps, helium in balloons, neon in signs.

Exam focus

Q: Explain why potassium is more reactive than sodium.

A: Potassium's outer electron is in a shell further from the nucleus and is shielded by more inner shells, so it is lost more easily, making the reaction faster and more vigorous.

title: Organic Nitrogen Compounds: Amines, Amides, Amino Acids and Proteins
content:
Organic Nitrogen Compounds: Amines, Amides, Amino Acids and Proteins

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH15, Topic 19. Amines, amides, amino acids and proteins contain nitrogen. The lone pair on nitrogen controls basicity, and the amide and peptide links join molecules into polymers.

Amines

  • Primary amines have one alkyl group on the nitrogen, for example ethylamine.
  • Alkyl groups push electron density onto nitrogen, so ethylamine is a stronger base than ammonia.
  • In phenylamine the lone pair is delocalised into the ring, so it is a weaker base than ammonia.
  • Amines form salts with acids: CH₃NH₂ + HCl gives CH₃NH₃⁺Cl⁻.
  • Preparation: a haloalkane heated with excess ethanolic ammonia gives a primary amine. The excess ammonia limits further substitution. A nitrile reduced by LiAlH₄ gives a primary amine.

Amides

  • An acyl chloride reacts with ammonia or an amine to form an amide. Ethanoyl chloride with ammonia gives ethanamide.
  • Hydrolysis of an amide with hot dilute acid gives a carboxylic acid and an ammonium salt.

Amino acids and zwitterions

  • Amino acids contain –NH₂ and –COOH. In the solid and near neutral pH they exist as zwitterions, ⁺H₃NCH(R)COO⁻, with no net charge.
  • At the isoelectric point the zwitterion has no net charge. In strong acid it is a cation; in alkali it is an anion.
  • Amino acids can be separated by electrophoresis because their charge depends on pH.

Peptides and proteins

  • A peptide link forms when the –COOH of one amino acid condenses with the –NH₂ of another, releasing water.
  • Proteins have primary (sequence), secondary (alpha helices and beta sheets, held by hydrogen bonds) and tertiary structures. Complete hydrolysis with hot acid gives amino acids.

Exam tip: when comparing base strength, explain the availability of the nitrogen lone pair, not just the names of the groups.

title: Further Trigonometry
content:
Further Trigonometry

Compound Angles

  • sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B
  • cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B Key: A and B = two angles in the same unit (degrees or radians); the ± pairs with ∓ — a plus on the left is a minus on the right; every term is dimensionless, being a ratio of lengths.

Example: sin 75° = sin(45° + 30°) = (√2/2)(√3/2) + (√2/2)(1/2) = (√6 + √2)/4.

Double Angles

  • sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A
  • cos 2A = cos²A − sin²A = 2cos²A − 1 = 1 − 2sin²A Key: A = the angle (the same identity holds for sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A above); the three forms are interchangeable — pick the one that matches what you know, cos²A for cos values, sin²A for sin values.

Example: express 4 sin x cos x in one term: 2 sin 2x.

The R-Form

a sin x + b cos x = R sin(x + α) with R = √(a² + b²) and tan α = b/a. Key: a and b = the original coefficients (they share a unit, so √(a² + b²) means anything); R = the amplitude of the combined wave; α = the phase shift, in the same angular unit as x — read both R and α from a sketch of the triangle, since tan α alone loses the quadrant.

Example: 3 sin x + 4 cos x = 5 sin(x + 0.927). This instantly gives the maximum 5 and minimum −5.

Reciprocal Functions

sec θ = 1/cos θ, cosec θ = 1/sin θ, cot θ = 1/tan θ. Key identity: 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ.

Exam tips: choose the cos 2A form that eliminates the unwanted function; when solving with R-form, divide by R before using inverse trig, and translate intervals carefully.

title: Inequalities
content:
Algebra — Inequalities

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): solving linear inequalities, integer solution sets, shading regions on graphs (linear programming context).

1. Solving

Like equations, but reverse the sign when multiplying/dividing by a negative: −2x ≥ 6 ⇒ x ≤ −3.

Example: 3x − 5 < 2x + 1 ⇒ x < 6.

2. Integer solutions

−1 ≤ x < 4 ⇒ x ∈ {−1, 0, 1, 2, 3}. Closed endpoint for ≤/≥, open for </>.

3. Double inequalities

Handle both sides: −3 < 2x + 1 ≤ 7 → −4 < 2x ≤ 6 → −2 < x ≤ 3.

4. Shading regions

  • Draw the boundary line: dashed for </>, solid for ≤/≥.
  • Test a point (usually (0,0)) to pick the wanted side; shade the unwanted side or label the wanted region.
  • Feasible region satisfies all constraints simultaneously.

Example: y ≤ 2x + 1: solid line, test (0,0): 0 ≤ 1 ✓ → region containing origin.

Exam tips: never divide by an unknown sign — move x terms first; list integer solutions inside curly brackets; state which region you shade.

title: Chemical Equilibria
content:
Chemical Equilibria

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH14, Topic 13. In a closed system a reaction reaches a dynamic equilibrium, where the forward and reverse rates are equal. The equilibrium constant tells you the position of that equilibrium at a given temperature.

The equilibrium constant Kc

  • For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, Kc = [C]^c [D]^d / ([A]^a [B]^b). Only species in solution or gas phase appear in the expression. Key: a, b, c, d = stoichiometric coefficients from the balanced equation (no units); [X] = equilibrium concentration of X (mol dm⁻³).
  • Kc is constant for a given temperature. Changing concentration or pressure shifts the position but not the value of Kc.
  • The units of Kc depend on the stoichiometry. For N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, Kc has units of mol⁻² dm⁶.

Worked example

  • For H2 + I2 ⇌ 2HI, at equilibrium [HI] = 1.60, [H2] = 0.20 and [I2] = 0.20 mol dm⁻³. Kc = 1.60² / (0.20 × 0.20) = 64.

Partial pressure and Kp

  • In gas equilibria, the partial pressure of a gas is its mole fraction multiplied by the total pressure.
  • Kp uses partial pressures instead of concentrations. For N2O4 ⇌ 2NO2, Kp = p(NO2)² / p(N2O4). Key: p(X) = partial pressure of X at equilibrium (Pa or atm); the powers 2 and 1 are the coefficients from the balanced equation.

Effect of changes

  • Adding reactant or removing product shifts the position towards the products. Adding product shifts it towards the reactants.
  • Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules. Changing the volume has the same effect as changing pressure.
  • Raising the temperature favours the endothermic direction. For an exothermic forward reaction, Kc decreases as temperature rises.
  • A catalyst changes the rate at which equilibrium is reached but not the position or Kc.

Exam tip: a change in temperature is the only change that alters Kc. Concentration, pressure and catalyst changes alter the position or rate, but not the constant.

title: Dynamics
content:
Dynamics

Newton's Laws

  • A body stays at rest or in uniform motion unless acted on by a resultant force.
  • F = ma — the resultant force equals mass × acceleration. Key: F = resultant force (N); m = mass (kg); a = acceleration (m s⁻²), in the same direction as F — resolve forces before applying it.
  • Forces occur in pairs: equal magnitude, opposite direction, on different bodies.

Example: a 2 kg mass with a 10 N resultant accelerates at 5 m s⁻².

Weight and Mass

Weight W = mg — a force in newtons; mass in kg is invariant. A 70 kg person weighs about 687 N. Key: W = weight (N); m = mass (kg); g = gravitational field strength (9.81 N kg⁻¹ on Earth) — g is the same number as the free-fall acceleration, which is why W = mg and F = ma agree.

Momentum

p = mv (vector, kg m s⁻¹). Resultant force = rate of change of momentum: F = Δp/Δt. Key: p = momentum; m = mass (kg); v = velocity (m s⁻¹); Δp = change in momentum (kg m s⁻¹); Δt = time over which it changes (s) — this form of Newton's second law still holds when the mass changes.

Conservation: in a collision with no external forces, total momentum is unchanged.

  • Elastic: kinetic energy also conserved
  • Inelastic: some KE becomes heat/sound

Example: a 3 kg trolley at 4 m s⁻¹ hits a stationary 1 kg trolley and they couple: 12 = 4v, so v = 3 m s⁻¹.

Friction and Connected Bodies

Draw free-body diagrams, then apply F = ma along each axis. For a towed car and trailer, the tow-bar tension appears as an internal pair (equal and opposite).

Exam tips: 'constant velocity' means zero resultant force, not zero friction; impulse questions want FΔt = Δp.

title: Quadratics
content:
Quadratics

A quadratic has the form ax² + bx + c with a ≠ 0. Master three tools: completing the square, the discriminant, and inequalities.

Completing the Square

Rewrite x² + bx + c as (x + b/2)² − (b/2)² + c.

Example: x² + 6x + 5 = (x + 3)² − 9 + 5 = (x + 3)² − 4, so the vertex is at (−3, −4).

For a > 1, factor out a first: 2x² + 12x + 19 = 2(x² + 6x) + 19 = 2(x + 3)² − 18 + 19 = 2(x + 3)² + 1.

Vertex form a(x − h)² + k gives the minimum/maximum value k at x = h — this is how you find a maximum area or minimum cost. Key: a = the shape coefficient (positive opens upward, negative downward); h = the x-coordinate of the turning point; k = the function's value there, in the unit of y — so the max or min answer is k itself, not h.

The Discriminant

Δ = b² − 4ac decides how the curve meets the x-axis:

ΔRootsGraph
Δ > 0two distinct real rootscrosses x-axis twice
Δ = 0repeated roottouches (tangent)
Δ < 0no real rootsnever meets x-axis

Example: kx² + 4x + 1 = 0 has equal roots when 16 − 4k = 0, so k = 4.

Quadratic Inequalities

Solve by sketching. For x² − 5x + 4 < 0, factorise: (x − 1)(x − 4) < 0, and the curve is below the axis between the roots, so 1 < x < 4.

Tip: flip the inequality when dividing by a negative number, and always sketch to check which interval you need.

Curve and Line Intersections

Set the equations equal; the resulting quadratic's discriminant tells you if the line is a secant (Δ > 0), tangent (Δ = 0) or misses (Δ < 0).

Exam tips: complete the square before reading off turning points; state the discriminant condition explicitly before solving for an unknown coefficient.

title: Cell Structure, Reproduction and Development
content:
Cell Structure, Reproduction and Development

Edexcel IAL Biology WBI12, Topic 3. Cells are the basic units of life. Their structure reflects their function, and cell division produces the new cells needed for growth, repair and reproduction.

Cell structure

  • Prokaryotic cells have no nucleus; their DNA is a circular loop in the cytoplasm, and their ribosomes are 70S. Eukaryotic cells have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
  • The nucleus holds DNA. Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration. Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis in plant cells. Rough endoplasmic reticulum has ribosomes and makes proteins; the Golgi apparatus modifies and packages them.
  • Electron microscopes have higher resolution than light microscopes because electrons have a much shorter wavelength than visible light.
  • Magnification = image size ÷ actual size. For an image 40 mm across at a magnification of ×400, the actual size is 0.1 mm. Key: magnification is a ratio with no unit; image size and actual size are measured in the same unit, so the units cancel.

Cell division

  • The cell cycle has interphase (G1, S and G2) and mitotic division. DNA replicates in the S phase.
  • Mitosis produces two genetically identical diploid daughter cells. It is used for growth and repair.
  • Meiosis has two divisions and produces four genetically different haploid gametes. Crossing over happens in prophase I, and independent assortment happens when homologous pairs line up at metaphase I.

Stem cells and development

  • A totipotent cell can form any cell type, including the cells of the placenta. Embryonic stem cells are pluripotent: they can form any cell type of the body. Adult stem cells are multipotent.
  • Differentiation switches on particular genes so that a cell becomes specialised.

Cancer

  • Cancer results from mutations that disrupt the control of the cell cycle. The cells divide in an uncontrolled way and can form a tumour.

Exam tip: when you compare mitosis and meiosis, name the number of divisions, the number of daughter cells, their ploidy and whether they are genetically identical.

title: Transformations and Vectors
content:
Transformations and Vectors

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): reflection, rotation, translation, enlargement (incl. negative SF); vector notation, resultant, magnitude, vector geometry.

1. Transformations — full descriptions

  • Reflection: mirror line (x = 0, y = x, y = −x…).
  • Rotation: centre, angle, direction (anticlockwise positive).
  • Translation: column vector.
  • Enlargement: centre + scale factor; negative SF inverts through the centre.

"Enlargement, SF 2, centre (0, 3)" — every word earns a mark.

2. Combined transformations

Apply right-to-left: "reflect in y = x, then rotate 90°" — rotate the reflected image.

3. Vectors

  • Column vector (x; y); magnitude = √(x² + y²). Key: x = the horizontal displacement and y = the vertical displacement, both in the same unit as the axes; the magnitude is a length in that unit.
  • Resultant by component addition; parallel vectors are scalar multiples.
  • Position vectors: AB = OB − OA. Key: AB = the vector running from A to B; OA and OB = the vectors from the origin O to each point; subtracting gives the journey that starts at A and ends at B.

Example: A(1, 2), B(4, 6): AB = (3; 4), |AB| = 5.

4. Vector geometry

Midpoint of AB = ½(a + b). Prove collinearity: show AB = k·BC (shared point). Prove parallelogram: AB = DC. Use route paths: AC = AB + BC. Key: a and b = the position vectors of the two endpoints; k = any scalar multiplier, a pure number that keeps AB parallel to BC; AB, BC, AC, DC are all vectors.

Exam tips: tracing paper is allowed for transformations; in proofs, end with a conclusion sentence ("hence A, B, C are collinear").

title: Chemistry of the Environment
content:
Chemistry of the Environment

Cambridge IGCSE 0620 (2023–2025): 10.1 water; 10.2 fertilisers; 10.3 air quality and climate.

1. Water and its treatment

Water is tested with anhydrous copper(II) sulfate, which turns from white to blue, and with cobalt(II) chloride paper, which turns from blue to pink. Natural water is treated by filtration to remove solids and chlorination to kill bacteria; in the lab, distilled water is made by boiling and condensing, which removes dissolved ions.

2. Fertilisers

Plants need nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. Ammonium salts, nitrates and phosphates are applied as fertilisers; the ammonium ion is made industrially by the Haber process and converted to ammonium sulfate or ammonium nitrate. Over-application is an environmental problem: rain washes nitrates into rivers, causing eutrophication, where algae bloom, die, and their decay removes oxygen from the water.

3. Air, pollution and climate

PollutantSourceEffect
carbon dioxidecombustion of fossil fuelsenhanced greenhouse effect
carbon monoxideincomplete combustiontoxic, binds haemoglobin
sulfur dioxideburning sulfur-containing fuelsacid rain
oxides of nitrogenhigh-temperature enginesacid rain, photochemical smog

Acid rain damages buildings (carbonates dissolve) and lakes. Clean-up measures include catalytic converters, flue-gas desulfurisation with calcium oxide, and using renewable energy. The greenhouse effect itself is natural; the enhanced effect comes from extra CO₂ and methane trapping more outgoing infrared radiation.

Exam focus

Q: Explain how sulfur dioxide causes acid rain and give one effect.

A: Sulfur dioxide from burning fossil fuels is oxidised in the air to sulfur trioxide, which dissolves in rain to form sulfuric acid; the acidic rain corrodes limestone buildings and lowers the pH of lakes.

title: Magnetism & Electromagnetism
content:
Magnetism & Electromagnetism

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): magnets & fields; magnetic effect of a current; force on a current-carrying conductor; motor effect; electromagnetic induction (Extended); transformers (Extended).

1. Magnets and fields

Iron/steel/cobalt/nickel; like poles repel. Field lines exit N, enter S; compass plotting; plotting compass aligns with field. Induced magnetism: iron (temporary) vs steel (permanent).

2. Electromagnets

Solenoid field like a bar magnet; strength ↑ with current, turns, iron core. Uses: relays, scrapyard crane, electric bell, speaker. Hard/soft magnetic materials choose permanent vs core use.

3. Force on a current-carrying conductor

F = BIL, direction by Fleming's left hand (fIeld, current, force). Reversing current or field reverses force. D.C. motor: coil, commutator reverses current each half-turn for continuous rotation; speed/torque ↑ with current, field strength, turns/area. Key: F = force on the wire (N); B = magnetic flux density (T); I = current (A); L = length of wire inside the field (m) — the motor turns because each side of the coil carries current in the opposite direction, so the two forces form a couple.

4. Electromagnetic induction (Extended)

Induced e.m.f. when a conductor cuts field lines or flux changes. Fleming's right hand (generator). Factors: speed, field strength, turns. A.C. generator: slip rings; dynamo effect; Lenz's law opposes change (direction of induced current).

5. Transformers (Extended)

Vp/Vs = Np/Ns; Pin ≈ Pout (100% assumed): IpVp = IsVs. Step-up raises V, lowers I → lower I²R transmission losses; a.c. required (changing flux).

title: Word Formation: Prefixes and Suffixes
content:
Many English words are built from a root with prefixes (added to the front) and suffixes (added to the end). Knowing common parts lets you understand new words and spell them correctly.

Prefixes

A prefix changes the meaning of the root.

  • un- means not: unbelievable, unclear
  • im-, in-, il-, ir- also mean not: impossible, incorrect, illegal, irregular
  • dis- means not or the reverse: disagree, dishonest
  • re- means again: rewrite, replay
  • pre- means before: preview, pre-war

Suffixes that change word class

Suffixes often change a word from one class to another.

  • Noun suffixes: -ness (happiness), -tion (decision), -ment (development), -ity (possibility)
  • Adjective suffixes: -ful (helpful), -less (careless), -able (readable), -ous (dangerous)
  • Adverb suffix: -ly (quickly)

Changing the form

Changing happy to happiness, or imagine to imagination, needs care with spelling. Some words change the final letter or drop an e before a suffix.

The suffix -less

-less means without: hopeless means without hope, careless means without care.

Practice strategy

Learn words in families. Write the noun, verb, adjective and adverb forms together, for example: decide, decision, decisive, decisively. This builds range and helps your writing.

title: Sets and Venn Diagrams
content:
Number — Sets

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): set notation, Venn diagrams, shading, universal set, subsets.

1. Notation

  • ∈ belongs to; ∉ not in; ∅ empty set; ξ (or U) universal set; n(A) = number of elements.
  • A ∩ B intersection (AND); A ∪ B union (OR); A′ complement (NOT A).
  • A ⊆ B: every element of A is in B.

2. Venn diagrams

Fill the intersection first, then work outwards. Two sets: only A, both, only B, neither.

Example: 30 students; 18 maths, 15 physics, 7 both ⇒ neither = 30 − (11 + 7 + 8) = 4.

3. Shading

For A ∩ B′ shade where A and outside-B overlap. (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′ (De Morgan) — check every region.

4. Regions algebra

With region variables x, y, z: use the totals to form equations, e.g. n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B). Key: n(S) = the number of elements in set S (a count, so no unit); A and B = the two sets; ∪ = union, everything in either set; ∩ = intersection, everything in both; x, y, z = the counts in the three regions of the diagram. The intersection is subtracted because adding n(A) and n(B) counts it twice.

5. Probability links

P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) — inclusion–exclusion from the diagram.

Exam tips: "neither" sits outside both circles — subtract from the universal set last; label regions with numbers, not expressions, as you fill.

title: Robotics & AI
content:
Robotics & AI

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): AI characteristics, machine learning basics, robotics/simulation contexts, automated systems.

1. AI characteristics

Systems exhibiting: planning, learning, reasoning, problem-solving, perception, knowledge representation. Narrow (task-specific) vs general AI distinction for discussion answers.

2. Machine learning

Supervised (labelled data — spam filters), unsupervised (clusters — segmentation), reinforcement (rewards — game agents). Training/evaluation loop: train on a set, test on unseen data; overfitting = memorising rather than generalising.

3. Robotics

Components: sensors (input), processors (decision), actuators/motors (output), power. Examples: manufacturing arms, delivery drones, autonomous vehicles (LIDAR + vision). Benefits: precision, 24/7 operation, dangerous jobs; concerns: job displacement, safety, cost.

4. Automated systems & simulation

Sensors → processor → actuators loops (greenhouses, traffic lights, self-checkouts). Simulation models real systems cheaply and safely (flight training, weather, crash tests) — limitations: model quality, missing variables.

5. Ethics of AI

Bias from unrepresentative training data; opacity of decisions; accountability for errors; privacy of training data; effect on employment.

Exam tips: for "describe how AI could be used in X" — tie each AI characteristic to a concrete step in the scenario; for evaluations, give both sides then a justified conclusion.

title: Respiration, Muscles and the Internal Environment
content:
Respiration, Muscles and the Internal Environment

Edexcel IAL Biology WBI15, Topic 7. Respiration releases energy as ATP for muscle contraction. Homeostasis keeps the internal environment stable, and the kidney is central to this. The topic links biochemistry to physiology.

Aerobic respiration

  • Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm. Glucose is split into two pyruvate molecules, with a small net gain of ATP and reduced NAD.
  • The link reaction converts pyruvate to acetyl coenzyme A in the mitochondrial matrix, releasing CO₂.
  • The Krebs cycle takes place in the matrix. It releases CO₂ and produces reduced NAD and FAD, and a little ATP.
  • Oxidative phosphorylation takes place on the inner mitochondrial membrane. Electrons pass along the electron transport chain, a proton gradient forms, and ATP synthase makes ATP. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor.

Anaerobic respiration in mammals

  • Without oxygen, pyruvate is reduced to lactate. This regenerates NAD so that glycolysis can continue, but it gives far less ATP.
  • The oxygen debt is the extra oxygen needed after exercise to oxidise the lactate.

Respiratory quotient

  • RQ = volume of CO₂ produced ÷ volume of O₂ consumed. Carbohydrate gives an RQ of about 1.0 and fat gives about 0.7. Key: RQ = respiratory quotient (no units, because it is a volume divided by a volume); both gases are measured at the same temperature and pressure.

Muscle contraction

  • A sarcomere is the unit between two Z lines. Thick filaments of myosin and thin filaments of actin slide past each other; the sarcomere shortens but the filaments do not change length.
  • Myosin heads bind to actin, and the power stroke pulls the actin along. ATP binds to myosin to break the link, and hydrolysis of ATP resets the head.
  • Calcium ions bind to troponin, which moves tropomyosin and exposes the binding sites on actin.

Homeostasis and the kidney

  • Negative feedback corrects a change from the set point. Receptors detect the change, and effectors bring the level back.
  • In the nephron, ultrafiltration occurs at the Bowman's capsule under high hydrostatic pressure. Glucose and amino acids are reabsorbed by active transport in the proximal convoluted tubule.
  • The loop of Henle creates a salt gradient in the medulla. ADH increases the permeability of the collecting duct, so more water is reabsorbed by osmosis.

Exam tip: when you describe the link between ADH and water reabsorption, follow the steps in order: osmoreceptors, ADH release, collecting duct permeability, water reabsorption.

title: Chemical Reactions
content:
Chemical Reactions

Cambridge IGCSE 0620 (2023–2025): 6.1 physical and chemical changes; 6.2 rate of reaction; 6.3 reversible reactions and equilibrium; 6.4 redox.

1. Rate and collision theory

Particles must collide with at least the activation energy for a reaction to happen. Four factors change the rate, and each one has a particle-level explanation:

  • higher temperature — more frequent and more energetic collisions;
  • higher concentration or pressure — more particles in the same volume;
  • larger surface area — more solid exposed to the other reactant;
  • a catalyst — provides an alternative path with lower activation energy.

Measuring rate: mass lost on a balance, gas volume in a syringe, or the time for a cross to disappear behind a precipitate. A steeper initial gradient means a faster rate; the graph flattens as reactants are used up.

2. Reversible reactions and equilibrium

In a closed system a reversible reaction settles at dynamic equilibrium: both directions continue at equal rates, so concentrations stay constant but are not equal. Changing conditions moves the position of equilibrium — increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction, increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles, and a catalyst only speeds up reaching equilibrium.

The Haber process is the standard example: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ is exothermic forwards, so a compromise temperature around 450 °C, high pressure and an iron catalyst are used.

3. Redox in one line

Oxidation is loss of electrons (and gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen); reduction is gain of electrons. In Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, zinc is oxidised and copper ions are reduced. An oxidising agent is itself reduced.

Exam focus

Q: Explain why increasing the temperature increases the rate of reaction, using collision theory.

A: Particles move faster and collide more frequently, and a greater proportion of collisions have energy at least equal to the activation energy, so more successful collisions occur per second.

title: Plant Structure and Function, Biodiversity and Conservation
content:
Plant Structure and Function, Biodiversity and Conservation

Edexcel IAL Biology WBI12, Topic 4. Plant tissues are arranged to transport water, move sugars and carry out photosynthesis. Biodiversity measures and conservation methods show how ecosystems are monitored and protected.

Plant tissues

  • Xylem vessels are dead, hollow cells with lignified walls. They carry water and mineral ions up the plant.
  • Phloem sieve tube elements have sieve plates and few organelles. They carry sucrose and amino acids in both directions.
  • Palisade mesophyll cells are packed with chloroplasts near the upper surface of the leaf. Sclerenchyma gives support through thick lignified walls.

Stomata and transpiration

  • Stomata open when guard cells become turgid by taking in water. They close when the guard cells become flaccid.
  • Transpiration is faster in high temperatures, dry air and wind, because these increase the water potential gradient out of the leaf.
  • Xerophytes reduce water loss with a thick waxy cuticle, sunken stomata and hairs.

Measuring biodiversity

  • Species richness is the number of different species in a habitat.
  • Simpson's index of diversity is D = 1 − Σ(n/N)², where n is the number of individuals of each species and N is the total. For two species with 10 individuals each, D = 1 − (0.25 + 0.25) = 0.50.

Sampling

  • Quadrats estimate the abundance of sessile or slow-moving organisms, often as percentage cover.
  • Transects show how species change along an environmental gradient.
  • Mark-release-recapture estimates the population of a mobile animal with the Lincoln index: N = (n₁ × n₂) ÷ m₂. Here n₁ is the number marked in the first sample, n₂ the number caught in the second, and m₂ the number of marked animals in the second sample.

Conservation

  • In situ conservation protects species in their natural habitat, for example in national parks and reserves.
  • Ex situ conservation keeps species outside their habitat, for example in seed banks and zoos.
  • The IUCN Red List classifies species by their conservation status.

Exam tip: when you are asked to explain a transpiration result, relate it to water potential and the diffusion gradient out of the stomata.

title: Continuous Random Variables
content:
Continuous Random Variables

Probability Density Functions

A continuous variable X is described by a density f(x) with f(x) ≥ 0 and ∫f(x)dx = 1 over all x. Probabilities are areas: Key: f(x) = the probability density, measured per unit of X (so it is not itself a probability); the total area under it must be exactly 1.

  • P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx Key: a and b = the limits, values of X in its own unit; the integral is the area under the density between them, which comes out as a probability between 0 and 1.

Single points have zero probability, so strict or loose inequalities make no difference: P(X < 2) = P(X ≤ 2).

Finding Unknown Constants

Piecewise densities carry an unknown k: impose that the total area is 1 (and continuity at joins where required). One equation, one unknown.

Example: f(x) = kx on 0 ≤ x ≤ 2. Total area: k·(2²/2) = 2k = 1, so k = ½.

Expectation and Variance

  • E(X) = ∫x·f(x) dx Key: E(X) = the mean of X, in X's own unit; f(x) = the density per unit of X, which is what leaves the integral in that unit; integrate over the whole range of X.
  • E(X²) = ∫x²·f(x) dx
  • Var(X) = E(X²) − (E(X))² Key: Var(X) = the variance, in X's unit squared; E(X²) = ∫x²f(x) dx, the expectation of the squares — compute it separately from the square of E(X), the two are never the same thing.

The mean is the balancing point of the area under the density. For symmetric densities the mean sits at the symmetry point — worth spotting before integrating.

The Median and Mode

The median m solves ∫₋∞ᵐ f(x) dx = 0.5 (left half of the area). The mode is the x maximising f(x). For uniform densities the median is the midpoint.

Uniform Distribution

If f(x) = 1/(b − a) on [a, b], every point is equally likely. Then E(X) = (a + b)/2 and Var(X) = (b − a)²/12 — memorise both; they are quick exam marks.

Exam tips: always verify ∫f = 1 before computing anything else. Sketch the density — area intuitions catch algebra slips. Median questions are integration-to-0.5 questions; set them up before calculating.

title: Probability Distributions
content:
Discrete Random Variables

Probability Distributions

A discrete random variable X takes values xᵢ with probabilities pᵢ where each pᵢ ≥ 0 and Σpᵢ = 1. A probability distribution can be given as a table, a formula, or a function. Any missing probability is found by subtraction.

Example: X = number of heads in 2 fair tosses: P(0) = 1/4, P(1) = 1/2, P(2) = 1/4.

Expectation

The mean of X is

  • E(X) = Σxᵢpᵢ Key: X = the random variable; xᵢ = each value X can take; pᵢ = the probability of that value; Σ = add the products over every value; E(X) has X's own unit — it is the long-run average.

It is a weighted average — the long-run average value over many repetitions. E(X) need not equal any value X can actually take.

Variance

  • Var(X) = E(X²) − (E(X))² Key: Var(X) = the variance, in X's unit squared; E(X²) = the expectation of the squares (compute Σxᵢ²pᵢ, not the square of E(X)) — the gap between the two is the spread.

where E(X²) = Σxᵢ²pᵢ — square the values before multiplying by probabilities. The standard deviation is √Var(X).

Linear Transforms

For constants a and b:

  • E(aX + b) = a·E(X) + b and Var(aX + b) = a²·Var(X) Key: a = a scaling constant (pure, so it takes X's unit with it); b = a shift in X's own unit; expectations move with both, while variance only feels the scale, and feels it squared.

Adding a constant shifts but does not spread; multiplying scales the spread by |a|.

Independent Variables

If X and Y are independent: E(X + Y) = E(X) + E(Y) and Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y). The addition rule for expectation always holds; the variance addition needs independence. The same applies to differences: Var(X − Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) — the subtraction does not cancel spread.

Exam tips: first verify Σp = 1 in any given table. Write E(X²) and (E(X))² separately; merging them is the most common exam error. In games of chance, set the expected profit to zero to find a fair entry fee.

title: Motion in a Circle and Gravity
content:
Motion in a Circle and Gravity

Circular Motion

Angular speed ω = v/r = 2π/T (rad s⁻¹). Centripetal acceleration a = v²/r = ω²r, always directed to the centre; centripetal force F = mv²/r. Key: ω = angular speed (rad s⁻¹); v = speed (m s⁻¹); r = radius (m); T = period (s); a = centripetal acceleration (m s⁻²); F = centripetal force (N); m = mass (kg) — the force is not a new kind of force but whatever supplies it (tension, gravity, friction).

Example: a 0.5 kg ball on a 1 m string at 2 m s⁻¹ needs F = 2 N inward.

Gravitational Field

Newton's law: F = Gm₁m₂/r², G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². Key: F = gravitational force between the masses (N); G = gravitational constant; m₁, m₂ = the two masses (kg); r = distance between their centres (m) — the force is always attractive and equal on both bodies.

Field strength g = GM/r². At Earth's surface g ≈ 9.81 N kg⁻¹. Key: g = gravitational field strength (N kg⁻¹ = m s⁻²); G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²; M = mass of the body creating the field (kg); r = distance from its centre (m) — g falls with the square of the distance, so it is not constant for satellites.

Orbits

For a circular orbit, gravity supplies the centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r, so v = √(GM/r) — higher orbits move slower but have longer periods (Kepler's third law: T² ∝ r³).

Geostationary satellites: T = 24 h, r ≈ 42,300 km from the centre.

Potential

Gravitational potential φ = −GM/r (zero at infinity). Potential gradient gives field strength: g = −dφ/dr. Key: φ = gravitational potential (J kg⁻¹); G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²; M = mass (kg); r = distance from the centre (m); the potential is negative everywhere and rises towards zero as r grows, which is why g carries the minus sign.

Exam tips: speed in orbit is independent of the satellite's own mass; don't confuse g at the surface with orbital equations using r from the planet's centre.

title: Human Nutrition
content:
Human Nutrition

Cambridge IGCSE 0610 (2023–2025): 7.1 diet; 7.2 the alimentary canal; 7.3 physical and chemical digestion; 7.4 absorption; 7.5 assimilation.

1. A balanced diet

Carbohydrates for energy, proteins for growth and repair, lipids for energy and insulation, vitamins and minerals in small amounts, fibre for bulk, and water. Energy needs depend on age, sex and activity. Deficiency diseases: scurvy (vitamin C), rickets (vitamin D or calcium), anaemia (iron), marasmus and kwashiorkor (protein-energy malnutrition).

2. The journey through the canal

OrganWhat happens
mouthchewing; amylase begins starch digestion; bolus formed
oesophagusperistalsis pushes the bolus down
stomachchurning; pepsin digests protein at pH 2; acid kills bacteria
small intestinepancreatic and intestinal enzymes complete digestion; absorption in the ileum
large intestinewater reabsorbed; faeces formed
rectum and anusstorage and egestion

Bile from the liver is stored in the gall bladder; it emulsifies fats and neutralises stomach acid.

3. Absorption

The ileum is folded and covered in villi, each with a thin epithelium, a rich blood supply and a lacteal. These three features give a large surface area, a short diffusion distance and a steep gradient. Glucose and amino acids enter capillaries; fatty acids and glycerol enter lacteals.

4. Teeth and decay

Incisors cut, canines grip, premolars and molars crush. Enamel is the hardest layer and is not replaced. Bacteria on plaque ferment sugar into acid, which dissolves enamel and then dentine; fluoride, less sugar and regular brushing prevent decay.

Exam focus

Q: Explain two ways the structure of a villus helps absorption.

A: Its finger-like shape and large number provide a large surface area; its wall is one cell thick, so the diffusion distance into the blood is short.

title: Forces and Equilibrium
content:
Forces and Equilibrium

Free-Body Diagrams

Draw every force on one body: weight (down), normal reactions (perpendicular to surfaces), tension (along strings), friction (opposing motion).

Resolving Forces

Any force F at angle θ splits into F cos θ (along) and F sin θ (perpendicular).

Example: a 50 N pull at 30° above horizontal drags with 50 cos 30° ≈ 43.3 N horizontally.

An object on a slope of angle θ has components mg sin θ down the slope and mg cos θ into it.

Equilibrium

A body is in equilibrium when the resultant force is zero in every direction and the resultant moment is zero.

Moments and the Principle of Moments

Moment = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot. Key: moment = turning effect of the force (N m); force in N; the distance in m is measured at 90° to the force's line of action.

For equilibrium: Σ clockwise moments = Σ anticlockwise moments. Key: Σ = sum over every force; each moment is force × perpendicular distance (N m); equilibrium also needs the forces themselves to cancel, so the body has no resultant force and no resultant turning effect.

Example: a 600 N child 2 m from a pivot balances an adult 1.2 m away: 600 × 2 = W × 1.2, so W = 1000 N.

Centre of Gravity

The point where the weight appears to act. For stable equilibrium the line of action must pass through the base.

Exam tips: take moments about the point with the most unknown forces; include the normal reaction and friction of any support, and check units of perpendicular distance.

title: Analysing Language Choices
content:
Language analysis asks how a writer uses words to create an effect. A device is only worth naming if you explain what it does and why the writer chose it.

Identifying devices

Name the device precisely, then move straight to its effect.

Common devices

  • Simile: a comparison using like or as, for example "like a black curtain drawn across the sky".
  • Metaphor: a direct comparison with no like or as.
  • Personification: giving human qualities to something non-human, for example "the city devoured the last of the daylight".
  • Onomatopoeia: a word that imitates a sound, such as buzz or crack.
  • Hyperbole: deliberate exaggeration for effect.

Explaining the effect

A strong comment has three parts: the word or phrase, what it suggests, and the reader's likely response.

Word-level analysis

  • Consider connotations: the feelings a word carries beyond its literal meaning.
  • Compare a chosen word with a plausible alternative to show why this one works better.
  • Notice verbs and adjectives, since they often carry the emotional weight of a description.

Sentence-level analysis

  • A short sentence after several long ones creates emphasis or sudden impact.
  • A list of three can build rhythm or momentum.
  • A rhetorical question makes the reader pause and consider the point.

Structuring your answer

Choose two or three clear examples rather than listing everything. Each paragraph should name the device, quote the words, and explain the effect in full sentences.

title: Sampling and Estimation
content:
Sampling and Estimation

Populations, Samples, Statistics

A parameter describes the population (μ, σ²); a statistic describes the sample (x̄, s²). A statistic is unbiased if its expectation equals the population parameter: E(x̄) = μ always holds for the sample mean.

Unbiased Variance

The estimator with divisor (n − 1) is the unbiased sample variance:

  • s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1)

Why n − 1: deviations are measured from x̄ rather than μ, slightly underestimating spread; the smaller divisor corrects it. At A2, state which estimator you are using — the unbiased one is the default.

Distribution of the Sample Mean

For a sample of size n from a population with mean μ and variance σ²:

  • E(x̄) = μ and Var(x̄) = σ²/n

Averaging shrinks spread — bigger samples give steadier estimates.

Central Limit Theorem

Whatever the population shape, for large n (rule of thumb n ≥ 30) the sample mean is approximately normal: x̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n). This is why the normal appears constantly in inference.

Example: population mean 50, s.d. 12, n = 36. Then x̄ ~ N(50, 4) and P(x̄ > 51) = P(Z > 0.5) = 0.3085. Key: x̄ = the sample mean, in the data's own unit; 4 = σ²/n = 144/36, the variance of x̄, so the spread shrinks with √n; Z = (x̄ − μ)/(σ/√n), the standardised distance, with no unit.

Using x̄ to Estimate

Given sample data, estimate μ by x̄ and σ² by the unbiased s². When the population is normal, x̄ is exactly normal for any n — the CLT is only needed for non-normal populations.

Exam tips: distinguish σ²/σ (population) from s²/s (sample) in notation. Standard error means √(σ²/n) — smaller with larger n. Quote probabilities for x̄ with the variance divided by n; forgetting that division is the classic error.

title: The Normal Distribution
content:
The Normal Distribution

The Model

A continuous distribution with the familiar bell shape, symmetric about the mean, described by two parameters: X ~ N(μ, σ²). The curve is fully determined by μ (centre) and σ (width). Total probability is 1, and because X is continuous, P(X = a) = 0 for any single point — inequalities do not need strictness. Key: X = the random variable, in its own unit; μ = the mean of the distribution (that unit); σ² = the variance (that unit squared), so σ is the standard deviation.

Standardising

Convert any normal variable to the standard normal Z ~ N(0, 1) with

  • Z = (X − μ)/σ Key: X = the value being tested; μ = mean of the distribution; σ = standard deviation; Z = how many standard deviations X sits from the mean — it has no unit, because a length in X-units is divided by a length in the same units, which is why one table serves every distribution.

Then read probabilities from the normal table. For X ~ N(50, 4²): P(X > 56) = P(Z > 1.5) = 1 − 0.9332 = 0.0668.

Backwards Problems

Given a probability, find μ or σ. Convert the target percentile to a z-value from the table, then solve (x − μ)/σ = z.

Example: P(X < 30) = 0.15 with unknown σ. From tables z = −1.036, so (30 − μ)/σ = −1.036 — one equation per unknown; use a second condition if both are missing.

Symmetry Shortcuts

P(X > μ) = 0.5. P(X < a) for a above the mean uses the complement. Tables usually give Φ(z) for z ≥ 0 only; use Φ(−z) = 1 − Φ(z). Key: Φ(z) = P(Z < z), the area under the standard normal curve up to z, read straight off the table (a probability, so 0 to 1 with no unit).

Normal Approximation to the Binomial

For large n with p near ½, X ~ B(n, p) ≈ N(np, np(1 − p)). The condition usually quoted at this level is np > 5 and n(1 − p) > 5. Apply a continuity correction: to approximate P(X ≥ 12) for a binomial, compute P(Y > 11.5) for the normal Y.

Example: B(100, 0.5) ≈ N(50, 25). P(X ≥ 55) ≈ P(Y > 54.5) = P(Z > 0.9) = 0.1841.

Exam tips: always sketch and shade — the picture prevents complement errors. State the standardisation step explicitly; marks sit in the working. Check whether a question says "mean and standard deviation" (σ) or "variance" (σ²) before standardising.

title: Poisson Distribution
content:
The Poisson Distribution

The Model

X ~ Po(λ) counts events in a fixed interval of time or space when events occur independently, at a constant average rate λ, and never twice at the same instant. Classic settings: calls per hour at a helpdesk, typos per page, cars per minute at a quiet junction.

The Formula

P(X = r) = e^(−λ) λʳ / r! for r = 0, 1, 2, ... Key: X = number of occurrences in the fixed interval; λ = the mean number expected in that interval (a count, e.g. 2 arrivals per minute); r = the value being evaluated (0, 1, 2, …); e = 2.718…, so the whole expression is a probability between 0 and 1.

Example: X ~ Po(2). P(X = 0) = e⁻² ≈ 0.1353. P(X = 1) = 2e⁻² ≈ 0.2707.

Mean and Variance

The defining signature of the Poisson:

  • E(X) = λ and Var(X) = λ — the mean and variance are equal. Key: E(X) = the mean count; Var(X) = the variance of that count; they are numerically identical for a Poisson, which is the quickest way to recognise one — if the mean and variance disagree, the data is not Poisson.

If a question gives a mean m, then λ = m; the variance is also m.

Scaling the Interval

If X ~ Po(λ) per hour, then 3 hours gives Y ~ Po(3λ). Rates must be adjusted to the same interval before computing anything. Halving an interval halves λ.

Adding Poissons

If X ~ Po(λ₁) and Y ~ Po(λ₂) are independent, then X + Y ~ Po(λ₁ + λ₂). Two independent queues merging into one server produce a Poisson with summed rate.

Exam tips: check independence and constant rate before modelling — if events cluster (rush hours), Poisson fails. Convert the interval first: a rate of 8 per 20 minutes becomes 24 per hour. In "at least" questions use the complement exactly as with the binomial.
